#4400. Tesla quietly sets up a company at German machine maker EMAG’s HQ

Tesla has registered a new German company whose business address is the headquarters of EMAG, a struggling machine-tool maker that builds production equipment for the gears inside humanoid robots.

Neither company confirmed a deal. But the paper trail is hard to ignore, and it lines up neatly with Tesla’s push to mass-produce Optimus.

The company is called Tesla Machining Technologies Management SE. Germany’s official company register lists it under HRB 315756 at the Munich district court, with €120,000 in share capital and a business address of Austraße 24 in Salach, a small town east of Stuttgart. That’s EMAG’s home base.

It didn’t start out as a Tesla company. The register shows it was first entered on August 26 as “Blitz 26-299 SE,” a shell company. Law firms sell these pre-registered shells so buyers can skip weeks of incorporation paperwork, and Tesla renamed this one earlier this month.

Business Insider Germany, which reported the change based on a notice in the federal gazette, says three people run it: Maximilian Stromberger, Tesla Germany’s 33-year-old head of sales, an American robotics engineer, and the head of HR at Tesla’s Grünheide factory.

The HR chief is the interesting name. You don’t need one to hold a passive stake in a supplier, but you do if you’re about to take on employees.

Neither Tesla nor EMAG answered Business Insider’s repeated requests for comment.

Local press near Salach has been on this for over a week. On November 23, the Stuttgarter Nachrichten reported that signs of a Tesla entry were piling up and that EMAG had briefed its workforce at a large staff meeting the week before. Business Insider dates that meeting to November 16.

Today, the same paper went further. It reports that around 220 EMAG employees will move to Tesla, that the two companies have been working together for some time, and that the deal is about humanoid robots. The full story is paywalled, and none of it has been confirmed by either company.

EMAG, with roots going back to 1867, makes turning, grinding, and gear-cutting machines, mostly for car parts like transmissions and drivetrains. The auto slowdown hit it hard. A year ago, EMAG said it would cut 455 jobs in Germany, roughly 300 of them in Salach, which is about a third of its domestic staff. It lost €42 million on €496 million of revenue in 2024, per Business Insider. It has been talking to potential investors ever since.

But EMAG has also been chasing a new market. Its website has an entire section on manufacturing humanoid robot actuator parts: flexsplines, wave generators, and planetary gears.

The first two make up a strain wave gear, the compact, high-reduction gearbox used in robot joints. Planetary gears go in the bigger joints that carry more load. EMAG says its machines hold these parts to ISO 1328 Class 4 gear quality, with runout under 5 micrometers, and can repeat that in high-volume production.

That’s right where Tesla says it’s stuck. On the Q3 earnings call last month, Musk called the hand Optimus’ main hardware problem and flagged custom gears as a reliability worry, as we reported at the time. Tesla is installing a Fremont line designed for a million robots a year, and the Optimus design it showed in 2022 used 28 structural actuators per robot. At that volume, you’re talking about tens of millions of actuators a year, many of them built around precision gears that few suppliers can make consistently.

Tesla moving directly into precision tooling highlights a brutal reality for robotics founders: software gets the spotlight, but high-tolerance actuator supply chains dictate your unit economics and scale. Building physical AI means mastering industrial manufacturing long before mass production begins. When navigating high-stakes hardware trade-offs and specialized talent, having early backers who have built hardware companies matters. Grove Ventures works hands-on from pre-seed with deeptech and AI founders, offering real operator experience to help scale complex physical architectures.

Tesla is already building the German side of this. In July, Tesla started recruiting in Reutlingen to develop and manufacture Optimus parts, including sensors, gearboxes, and actuators, plus the equipment to mass-produce them. Reutlingen is the former Manz site that Tesla took over in early 2025, along with about 300 of its employees.

Tesla has done this before. It agreed to buy Grohmann Engineering in Prüm in late 2016, which became Tesla Automation, and that unit absorbed the Manz operations. Tesla is also putting €3 billion into a Cybercab factory at Giga Berlin.

Tesla briefly acquired Wiferion in Germany. Tesla did buy the wireless charging startup in 2023, but it sold the business a few months later and kept the engineers.

Robots are still years away from your home, but solar isn’t. #4399. Narrowed Focus: 1997 Toyota Camry LE Tested

One of America’s favorite family haulers gets a full makeover.

Over 3,000,000 sold! Call it the McCamry. Along with the Ford Taurus and the Honda Accord, this Toyota is right at the top of the list when Amer­ican families go new-car shopping, and right at the top of the ratings in our last family-sedan comparison test (November 1995). Since its introduction here in 1983, Toyota has diligently smoothed up, slicked up, and suaved up the Camry till the only remaining awkwardness is the unlikely spelling of its name.

That won’t change as Toyota introduces its fourth-­generation Camry in Sep­tember, and neither will the mix of virtues that make this model a favorite. We’re talking refinement of the Camry theme, not reinvention. In fact, the basic platform and powertrain carry on, though engineering improvements seem to touch every part of the car. It’s slightly bigger in each exterior dimension—0.7 inch longer, 0.4 inch wider, 2.1 inches longer in wheelbase; the same four­-cylinder and V-6 engines are modestly more powerful (up 8 hp in the four, up 6 hp in the V-6); and the interior has been upgraded to meet all the safety standards scheduled in the next few years, including the 1997 side-impact and 1999 head-­impact requirements. The aerodynamic drag coefficient has been improved to 0.30, from 0.33.

See all results for used 1997 Toyota Camry for sale near 30022

Toyota is, however, tightening the Camry’s focus. It’s available only as a four-door now in three trim levels: CE, LE, and XLE. Gone is the coupe, which won over just five percent of Camry buyers. Gone, too, is the station wagon, a shape that convinced only three per­cent of Camry buyers in its losing battle against the tide of minivans. (Production of a Camry-based minivan begins next spring.)

In the past, we’ve joked that the Camry’s personality is one of aggressive bland­ness. Unlike the frisky feeling of the Accord and the athletic tautness of the Dodge Intrepid, both of which come through loud and clear before you’ve driven to the first corner, the Camry’s subtlety grows on you over time. It’s smoother, softer, quieter than the others, less com­municative, less mechanical. Instead of talking to you in the very pleasant way of those others, it’s the silent type that, you soon notice, goes expertly about its job.

In this new Camry, Toyota sharpened the expertise without changing the per­sonality. It’s still a car that’s light to the touch: easy to steer, easy to brake. The ride is commendably free of harshness, thanks in part to mounting the suspension on isolated crossmembers front and rear. The four­-cylinder version, with its 195/70SR-14 tires, rides very smoothly and ignores almost completely the road textures that create so much droning in sporting cars. The V-6s come with 205/65HR-15s on six­-inch-wide wheels. These tires are noticeably harsher and noisier than those on the four-cylinder cars, though road nose is still quite reasonable when compared with other cars in this class. Road grip and handling predictability are well above the minimums we’d set for family cars.

See all results for used 1997 Toyota Camry for sale near 30022

The Camry V-6 has been one of the top performers in this class. The 1997 model gains six horsepower (now 194 hp at the same 5200 rpm as the previous peak), gets shorter final-drive gearing (3.93 versus 3.43), and weighs about the same as last year’s smaller car. Another performance plus: A manual transmission has returned to the V-6 lineup, available only on CE models. How­ever, our LE V-6 auto­matic was no quicker than the last LE V-6 we tested, managing 0 to 60 mph in 8.3 seconds. Expect the five-speed to trim that by about four-tenths.

On the road, the automatic’s eagerness to change down a gear or two when you press the pedal, even slightly, and the seamless smoothness of those changes give this car quick reflexes in traffic. The engine revs with the hushed moan of a Lexus. This year, traction control is optional on LE and XLE V-6 models. When it comes to powertrain pleasures, the Camry is world-class.

Still, it’s the more subtle details of pas­senger accommodation that make this Toyota a family favorite. In the previous­-generation Camry, our comparison tests show two adults fit in the back seat more comfortably than in some other brands up to 10 inches longer. We expect this Camry advantage to widen fractionally in this new model because both legroom and head­room in back are increased by a half-inch. Although the Camry is wider on the out­side, energy-absorbing padding to protect in side impacts takes up the extra space and, in certain spots, a little more. The Camry still has pockets in the front doors, unlike the Taurus, which sacrificed them for crash-protection equipment.

Those who wish to maximize rear-seat space should think twice about opting for power front seats (standard equipment on the top-of-the-line XLE). The manual­adjust buckets have excellent toeroom under them, which the power adjuster interrupts with a transverse bar. Tall folks won’t like that.

As in most modern sedans, the Camry has fold-forward rear seatbacks split one­-third and two-thirds, allowing the cargo compartment to be extended into the pas­senger area. Here’s another think-twice: Camrys equipped with the optional child seat—it’s built into the two-thirds section of the rear seat—have that section fixed in place, ruling out all but a narrow passage into the trunk.

At the rear, the trunklid opens wider and lower than before. Space inside, however, is a bit less in the new body—14.1 cubic feet versus 14.8 before. And the new car still has the conventional trunk hinges with the sickle arms that swing down into your luggage when the lid is closed.

Conventional is the right description for the new instrument panel, certainly more conventional than the old one, which tried to visually compartmentalize the cockpit by emphasizing a huge black field in front of the driver. That was the good part. The bad part was the deemphasized and totally boring padding it left for the passenger’s amusement. Now the all-new panel stretches its padding across the inte­rior in an equal-opportunity gesture that makes the interior seem brighter and wider. The glove box is 29 percent larger. The audio controls were raised to a mid­dash height, making them easy to see and reach. The climate controls have changed over to the increasingly common turn-to-adjust knobs. They’re large enough, and so obvious in their workings, that they are easy to operate in their less prominent location. The Camry continues to position its ignition switch in the dash where you can readily see it, instead of hiding it on the side of the steering column.

Toyota has proven itself to be the master of those little conveniences that add up to an exceptionally pleasing car. In this new Camry we see more clever trade-offs as the engineers cut costs, reduce weight, and usually end up serving the customer better, too. For example, the new front bumper cuts the part count nearly in half and saves weight, yet it increases protec­tion to 5 mph from 2.5. Inside, the seats recline in stepless increments now, and the buckets’ height adjusters use a single knob instead of two. Both of these changes cut costs, Toyota says. We say they make the car better, too. Models that previously would have had retracting antennas now have the antenna screened on the rear glass, saving weight and cost. The new Bosch anti-lock brake system weighs half as much as the old one.

Still, not every cost saver is a benefit. The LCD odometer is simply gray num­bers on a gray field, making it less visible than the glowing digits in competitors like the Chrysler Cirrus and the Dodge Stratus. And the new one-piece front-bumper cover now incorporates the grille into its overtly ordinary Rubbermaid-looking façade.

There’s been much speculation in the automotive-trade press about a possible price cut. Don’t hold your breath. Sales of the old Camry hit records earlier this year with no apparent price cutting. Were there sweeteners for the dealer? Sure, but other brands had them, too. Toyota knows all the tricks for selling cars without collapsing its price structure-tricks, we think, that mostly won’t be needed to move this shrewdly updated Camry.

#4397. One More Than GT40: The Ford GT41 Le Mans Hypercar Is Finally Here

Yes, it’s about 41 inches tall. But that’s not really why it bears that name.

Ford’s return to the top class of the 24 Hours of Le Mans was finally unveiled during the Thanksgiving Day NFL game between the Detroit Lions and Chicago Bears, along with an official name that clearly evokes the company’s past success: GT41.

Of course, there weren’t 39 cars before the GT40, as that name comes from the fact that the car was 40 inches tall. The GT41, for what it’s worth is 41 inches tall… almost. Technically, the car is 41.7 inches from the ground to the top of its air intake, a dimension dictated by the current FIA regulations for the LMDh class. But GT42 doesn’t quite have the same ring to it.

And while the GT41 is based off the same Oreca chassis as used by the Genesis GMR-001 and outgoing Alpine A424 and Acura ARX-06, the car and team is a wholly internal Ford effort. “Everything that we’re building, it’s in-house,” said Mark Rushbrook, global director of Ford Racing, “It's the design, the engineering, the development, all the technical elements of the car.”

That internal approach particularly applies to the engine, which Rushbrook calls the heart of the car. The naturally aspirated 5.4-liter V-8 is based off Ford’s production engines, so much so that the block is shared with the supercharged 5.2-liter in the Mustang Dark Horse SC and F-150 Raptor R and is pulled straight from the line at the Essex Engine Plant in Windsor, Ontario. Assembled inside Ford’s dyno lab at the company’s headquarters in Dearborn, Michigan, every part inside the racing engine “is designed by a Ford engineer,” according to Joseph Hendrickson, motorsports powertrain calibration engineer. “The engines are also tested on a dynamometer inside the same building. It’s a huge point of pride for us,” he said.

The final livery of the GT41 that will race at Le Mans will be revealed closer to the start of the 2027 WEC calendar, which being at Qatar in March. The car seen here features a camouflage pattern made of the Ford Racing wordmark, with Easter eggs hidden throughout that reflect the team’s pride as an American and Detroit-based automaker; look closely, and you’ll see an American flag, a bald eagle head, the Statue of Liberty, the Spirit of Detroit, and a football.

Until then, testing of the GT41 continues at several tracks around the world (and, as a reminder, Ford has no plans to run in IMSA or the 24 Hours of Daytona in 2027), while its new “Go Like Hell” ad campaign—directed by Zac Snyder and narrated by Matt Damon—will make regular appearances on your various screens for the rest of the year. Including this one, if you click on the video below.

Executive Editor Mike Austin has worked as a writer, editor, and occasional video host across titles such as Car and Driver, Autoblog, Popular Mechanics, and Hemmings (plus a few more). Prior to joining Road & Track he finally put his engineering degrees to use as an EV analyst. His personal cars skew slightly oddball, including a 1991 Honda Beat, 2001 Volkswagen Eurovan, 1987 Alfa Romeo Spider, and 2007 Saab 9-3 wagon.

#4396. Kia, Lucid, and Volkswagen are slashing EV prices by $10,000+ for Black Friday

Forget waiting in line for a discounted TV or other gadget you probably don’t need. If you’ve been looking to go electric, Black Friday may be the time to do it. Several brands, including Kia, Lucid, and Volkswagen, are offering $10,000 or more off select EVs right now.

While electric vehicle sales have slowed in the US after last year’s rush of buyers trying to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, the market is bouncing back.

Nearly 263,000 EVs were sold in the US in the third quarter, according to Kelley Blue Book, marking the most since the record-setting third quarter of 2025.

With new models hitting the market, prices have also come down over the past year. The average transaction price (ATP) for a new EV in October was $56,221, down 2.9% from a year ago.

For Black Friday, several automakers are sweetening the deal this year, offering a generous $10,000 or more off select EVs.

Lucid launched its Black Friday offers this week. Through November 30, you can score a $15,000 Black Friday Credit on a new 2027 Lucid Gravity Touring.

Prefer a sedan? Lucid is also offering a $10,000 Black Friday Credit on a new 2027 Lucid Air Touring. To take advantage of the offer, you must pay cash or use third-party financing.

The 2027 Lucid Gravity Touring starts at $79,900 and offers up to 337 miles of EPA-estimated range. It’s available to lease for as low as $749 a month. The offer is for a 36-month lease with $6,249 due at signing.

Lucid’s electric sedan, the 2027 Air Touring, is priced from $79,900 and offers up to 431 miles of range.

Both the Gravity and Air can add up to 200 miles of range in under 12 minutes with 400 kW DC fast charging.

Lucid’s Black Friday offers end on November 30, 2026.

Kia is offering $10,000 off several electric vehicles for Black Friday, including the three-row EV9 and the Niro EV.

The 2026 Kia EV9 is available with a $10,000 Customer Cash discount that can be applied toward the purchase price. With a $10,000 discount, prices for the base EV9 Light RWD trim can fall to as low as $44,900 ($54,900 starting MSRP).

Kia is also promoting a lease deal on the 2026 EV9 Light Long Range RWD for $339/month for 36 months, with $4,999 due at signing.

If you opt to finance, you can get 0% APR for 60 months, plus $5,000 in APR Bonus Cash across the entire 2026 EV9 lineup.

The 2026 Kia Niro EV is also available with a $10,000 Customer Cash discount, knocking the price down to as low as $29,700 ($39,700 MSRP).

With leases starting at just $289/month for 36 months (with $3,999 due at signing), the 2026 Niro EV Wind FWD is about as cheap a lease as you can get nowadays, gas or electric.

The Niro EV is also available with 0% APR for up to 72 months, including a $3,500 APR Bonus Cash discount.

While it isn’t $10,000 off, it is worth mentioning that Kia now sells the smaller EV3 electric SUV. The 2027 Kia EV3 (see our review) starts at just $28,890, making it one of the most affordable EVs you can get in the US, alongside the new Chevy Bolt and Nissan LEAF.

Kia is offering a $1,500 Customer Cash discount on the 2027 EV3, which still makes it cheaper to buy outright than the Niro EV, even with incentives.

The 2027 Kia EV3 Wind FWD is available for lease starting at $349/month for 36 months, with $3,999 due at signing. Kia is offering 0.90% APR for 48 months on all 2027 EV3 trims.

Kia’s current deals end on January 04, 2027.

As it prepares to introduce its replacement in 2027, Volkswagen introduced a $10,000 Customer Bonus for the 2026 ID.4 electric SUV.

Since the ID.4 is discontinued after the 2026 model year, it might not be so easy to find one. Volkswagen said the remaining inventory is very limited.

If you can find one, Volkswagen will apply the $10,000 discount when you purchase or lease a new 2026 ID.4 through a participating dealer.

Volkswagen’s current ID.4 offer runs until November 30, 2026. You can read more about its replacement, the ID. Tiguan here.

With the new 2027 models arriving, automakers are offering generous discounts and other financing deals on 2026 models to clear inventory.

Through its annual Winter Getaway sales event, Hyundai is offering up to $7,000 off the three-row 2026 IONIQ 9 or leases starting at just $419 a month. The offer is a 36-month lease for the IONIQ 9 S RWD trim with $4,999 due at signing.

Prefer something smaller? The 2026 Hyundai IONIQ 5 is available with up to a $3,500 discount. Leases start at just $339 a month (24 months with $4,999 due at signing) for the standard-range IONIQ SE RWD, or $349 a month (24 months with $4,999 due at signing) for the standard-range IONIQ SE RWD.

Hyundai’s Winter Getaway sales event runs through November 30.

Toyota is currently offering a deal on the 2026 bZ Woodland, its bigger, more rugged electric SUV for Black Friday that’s worth checking out.

The deal includes 0% APR financing for 72 months, plus an extra $1,000 Holiday Bonus Cash. Toyota said that if you finance a new 2026 bZ Woodland for 72 payments, it will cost $13.89 for every $1,000 financed.

None of the Kia promotions are new. They’ve been the same since September at least. (I bought an EV3 that month).

In comparison, the standard 2026 bZ is available with 1.99% interest for 72 months at $14.75 for every $1,000 financed.

The standard 2026 Toyota bZ is available to lease, starting at $369 per month. The deal is for a 36-month lease with $4,369 due at signing for an effective cost of $490 per month.

Toyota is promoting 2026 bZ Woodland leases as low as $449 a month. That’s also for a 36-month lease with $4,448 due at signing.

Toyota’s current offers also end on November 30.

#4394. ChargePoint and PistenBully have a charging plan for ski resorts

The next EV to plug in at a ski resort might be the one that groomed your trail. ChargePoint has struck a deal with Kässbohrer, the German company behind PistenBully snow groomers, to bring charging to ski resorts and indoor ski facilities across Europe and North America.

Under the agreement, Kässbohrer will connect its customers with ChargePoint for chargers, software, and support with planning, installation, and day-to-day operations. Resorts can use the same provider for the snow groomers and other vehicles they keep at the maintenance depot, as well as for the EV chargers skiers use while they’re out on the slopes.

Kässbohrer’s first fully electric groomer, the PistenBully 100 E, uses electric motors to move the machine and spin the tiller that smooths the snow. It has a 196 kWh battery and can handle up to three hours of normal grooming on a charge, according to the manufacturer. It can take up to 22 kW on AC or 150 kW on a DC fast charger. It fast charges from zero to 100% in about an hour.

ChargePoint says Kässbohrer accounts for more than half of the snow groomers sold worldwide each year. Resorts can start working with the companies now. Which resorts will install ChargePoint’s chargers first, and how many will go in, are TBC.

#4393. Tested: The 2028 Volvo XC60 T8 Is the Rangiest Plug-In Hybrid

Volvo’s aging middleweight SUV is a surprisingly strong performance contender with its revised powertrain.

On the journey to the future of automotive propulsion, Volvo was an early adopter of the all-electric ethos. The Swedish automaker initially vowed to stop selling all gasoline-powered cars—including hybrids—by 2030. A few years and three new all-electric models later, Volvo has radically altered that plan and will continue to sell hybrid models past that point. That includes extending the life of the existing lineup, with the already-near-decade-old second-gen XC60 getting a new T8 powertrain, which gives it the longest pure electric range of any plug-in hybrid on sale in the U.S.

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

We have always appreciated the charms of the current-generation XC60, with a substantial package of changes sharpening its case for a few more years. Visually, the most obvious changes are a new front end incorporating LED matrix headlights and smaller revisions at the rear. The technical highlight is an improved 78-mile EPA electric range from a mammoth 37.9-kWh battery pack, this delivered to a motor on the rear axle; a smaller starter-generator can add modest assistance at the front as well. Volvo quotes a peak electric output of 208 hp, with the 2.0-liter turbo four that drives the front wheels able to deliver 247 horses. Inside, the XC60 receives small material and trim adjustments.

Engine: 1969-cc turbocharged inline-four, hybridized

Transmission: eight-speed automatic, all-wheel drive

As I pulled into Copenhagen’s morning traffic, Volvo’s Pure drive mode, which idles the gasoline-powered engine in favor of an all-electric experience, felt prudent among the multitude of commuting bicyclists. Silent running was entirely suited to the Scandinavian environment, but the XC60 T8 wasn’t stumbling over itself either when running under electrical power, Volvo having significantly juiced up the electric motor alongside the bigger battery pack.

While 208 hp in Pure EV mode has to work against 4855 pounds of weight, the T8 felt well suited to both metropolitan driving and the open road, the effective surge of electrical power proving itself on highways and the 9.9-mile-long Øresund Link that connects Denmark to Malmö, Sweden. Power delivery definitely wasn’t as aggressive as that of a spicy EV, but it wasn’t gentle either, and the electric motor had enough punch to drive the XC60 without me yearning for the gas engine to intervene. Something that won’t happen unless the accelerator is pushed to a kickdown position or by switching drive modes. The 78-mile EPA range is genuinely class-leading, and selecting the T8’s Charge mode rapidly replenished e-miles when selected.

Switching from the Pure to Hybrid mode was where the real fun began. And fun isn’t too strong a word for the unlikely performance of the split hybrid system as the 2.0-liter turbo adds its contribution to the front axle, giving a combined peak of 455 hp and what Volvo claims is 4.5-second 0–60-mph capability. In practice, the XC60 T8 felt shockingly quick, rapidly spinning up the speedometer at wide-open throttle. The accelerator has a two-part action, with softer response at the top of its travel metering electrical power before the combustion horses arrive with a suddenness. This was fun, but the transition also felt a bit too obvious considering how subtle some hybrids now are. Switching it up to Power mode refocused the powertrain by keeping the engine running and solved the on-and-off drama. The eight-speed automatic transmission shifts without drama, and there’s enough electrical torque that I didn’t even want for the missing steering-wheel paddle shifters.

We liked the way the pre-facelift XC60 T8 drove, and the new version impressed as much. Volvos are traditionally heavy and somewhat leisurely to respond, but the XC60 successfully belied its scale with impressively neutral handling on narrow Swedish country roads. My XC60 test vehicle was fitted with the optional air suspension and active shock absorbers, fighting body roll and delivering a reactive front end.

Similarly, Volvo’s power-steering system was smooth and direct, though both weight settings skewed overly light for my tastes. It’s not as overtly sporty as some performance SUVs, but its combination of qualities was definitely appealing. My only complaints were a somewhat agricultural soundtrack under full throttle and what was often a harsh ride over rough surfaces, bumps, and imperfections being transferred into the cabin.

I didn’t get a chance to plug in the XC60, but Volvo said the 2028 model can charge at speeds up to 7.2 kWh. All told, the XC60 PHEV will take around 5.7 hours to fully charge up at maximum speed.

Volvo has long succeeded at creating minimalist cabins without them looking sparse or cheap, and the XC60 continues to carry that torch with a few exceptions. And one of these exceptions was the 11.2-inch center touchscreen, which has been blown out of the casing found on previous model years to take over the entire console.

Annoyingly, climate-control functions are integrated into this display with multiple menus required for adjustment, the Android Auto software beneath it starting to show its age. Similarly, Apple CarPlay is only available through a wired connection—that’s so 2017. That said, the infotainment system was easy to operate despite its limitations. Plus, Volvo has perfected the art of displaying turn-by-turn directions on the instrument cluster; a dial speedometer and tachometer sit opposite each other with an appropriately scaled navigation map centered in between.

Beyond the technology, the XC60’s interior was a charming place to spend time. New Scandinavian-inspired materials on the dashboard included brushed wood and knit fabric, which looked upmarket and were pleasing to the touch. The light leather seats were firm yet comfortable and included massage, heating, and cooling functions, which can be operated all at once. Other notable interior design wins include a wooden sliding cup-holder cover, an alluring crystal shift knob, and satisfying brushed steel door handles. The Bowers & Wilkins stereo system on my test car was fantastic, and Volvo deserves points for retaining a traditional volume knob, as well as tactile buttons to skip songs.

If you want a properly long-range plug-in hybrid SUV, the Volvo XC60 may be your best option, at least for now. The next longest-range mid-size luxury SUV option is the Mercedes-Benz GLC Hybrid, which offers 54 all-electric miles. Toyota also offers a RAV4 Plug-In Hybrid with 52 miles of range. Volvo has not announced finalized U.S. pricing for the 2028 XC60 T8 yet.

#4392. If I could only use one bike lock, it’d be this: FoldyLock Elite 110 review

I ride e-bikes professionally, regularly testing new bikes and biking gear. I don’t even own a car – I get around almost exclusively on two wheels. So when it comes to important gear like bike locks for my fleet of e-bikes, I’ve become pretty well-versed out of necessity. And after testing out the world’s strongest folding lock, the FoldyLock Elite 110, I’m more than impressed. If I could only have one lock for my e-bikes, it’d be this one.

Of course, the name of the game in bike theft prevention is to use more than just one lock, and I’m going to return to that idea at the end of this article.

But for now, believe me when I say that this lock is seriously good, to the point that it has become my new primary.

The FoldyLock Elite 110cm is identical in strength and security to the FoldyLock Forever 90cm that I tested a few years ago, yet is 20 cm (8 inches) longer, reaching 110 cm (43 inches).

The FoldyLock Forever 90 and FoldyLock Elite 110 are the strongest folding locks in the world, confirmed by the premier international lock certification organization ART. These are the only folding locks that have ever achieved a 3-star ART certification. The scale goes up to 5, but 4-star and 5-star certifications are motorcycle-level locks.

To make things even more impressive, the FoldyLock line achieved that ART 3-star rating three years ago, and no other lock company has matched it on a folding lock since.

If one independent and international lock testing association isn’t enough for you, the lock is also Sold Secure GOLD rated, which is just one step below Sold Secure’s highest ever rating for bike locks.

Again, more on that at the end of this article to get you to that last step for top security.

There are a lot of different styles of locks out there, and each has its own advantages and disadvantages. But as someone who rides e-bikes every day as his job, I’ve come to the opinion that a strong folding lock has the best combination of maximizing advantages and minimizing disadvantages.

For starters, folding locks allow you to lock to larger diameter anchors that would be impossible for U-locks (trees, telephone poles, multiple fence bars, etc). They’re more compact than chain locks of comparable security, both in size and weight. They’re significantly stronger than cable locks (when made with quality materials). And they mount more easily to a bike frame than nearly any other lock style, as they fold tightly and usually come with a holster.

Yes, there are disadvantages too. The segments mean they can’t form as close to a circle as a chain, meaning the maximum size of the tree or telephone pole you’re locking to is slightly smaller than for an equal length chain. And they usually aren’t quite as strong as U-Locks made with angle-grinder-resistant materials. But for their size and convenience, they make perhaps the best single style of lock for the best pairing of strength and convenience.

Since I began testing the FoldyLock Elite 110, I’ve been living with it as my main e-bike lock. I test a lot of locks, and most go onto the shelf when I’m done as backups or to give to friends/family. But the FoldyLock Elite 110 has stayed as my new primary lock, and here’s why.

First of all, as I mentioned, it’s the strongest folding lock in the world, as confirmed by multiple independent testing organizations. So if you want the advantages of a folding lock, there’s simply none more secure than this.

But beyond that, the FoldyLock Elite 110 is covered by multiple patents, including the specialized protected rivets that prevent nut splitter attacks and that take out any squeaks or rattles that are common in other folding locks. The lock also physically locks into its holster, which keeps it both secure (no bounce-outs) and helps keep it silent during the ride. There’s even a coating on the hardened steel segments to protect my bike frame from scratches and resist corrosion during winter use (plus a shutter on the locking mechanism for additional winter corrosion resistance).

Basically, it seems like the company has taken pretty much all of the learnings from previous locks in their lineup, and applied those lessons to the FoldyLock Elite, making it a perfect combination of strength, security, and convenience.

As I mentioned, after my time testing the FoldyLock Elite, I can say for sure that if I could only use one bike lock, it would be this one.

But I don’t just use one bike lock. And I recommend you don’t either, if you can swing it.

We’ve long known that the best way to keep your bike safe from thieves is to use two bike locks. It’s partly for the extra security, and partly for the extra time it takes a thief to work on defeating two locks, meaning they’re more likely to choose a different sucker’s bike to steal.

I always recommend using two different styles of bike locks. Think: folding lock plus U-lock, or U-lock plus chain lock, or chain lock plus cable lock, or cable lock plus folding lock, etc. You get the idea.

My FoldyLock Elite is now my primary lock, and it allows me to lock onto just about everything on the street, from official bike racks to chunky utility poles. For my secondary, I use a SeatyLock Mason 220. This U-lock is actually one step higher-rated by Sold Secure, reaching that testing organization’s Diamond level – its highest level of security rating.

When I can lock both the folding lock and U-lock to an anchor, I do it. But sometimes, when I’m forced to lock to something wide like a lamppost, I lock the frame and rear wheel with the FoldyLock Elite 110, then lock the front wheel to the frame with the Mason 220 U-lock, as seen in the photo above.

That keeps both of my wheels and my bike locked. Despite there only being one lock keeping the bike in place to the anchor (lamppost), the second lock adds an extra layer of frustration for a thief and is likely to convince them to just choose the next bike on the sidewalk.

That’s why I always recommend using two different locks, and ideally of different styles. I believe the FoldyLock Elite 110 offers the most advantages, but its few disadvantages are offset by a secondary lock, such as a strong U-lock.

When it comes to mounting, I’ve got the holster mounted onto my fork using the supplied flexible mounting straps.

Normally you’d mount it to one of your bottle mounts, but I only have a single set of bottle bosses on my e-bike’s frame, and they are currently taken up by a water bottle holder (surprise!).

I found that despite adding 1.9 kg or 4.1 lb to the side of my fork, my bike still rides just fine. The advantage of a rigid frame is that there’s not really much change to the unsprung mass since everything is unsprung!

I love riding hands-free in the city, and it did take me a day or two to get used to the slightly altered steering moment, but I can still ride my bike hands-free even with the extra weight there on the side of the fork.

At some point I might shift the holster onto the rear rack or swap it out for my bottle holder in favor of a new bottle spot, but so far it’s working great there and hasn’t caused me any handling issues.

When it comes to value, I think the FoldyLock Elite 110 takes the cake here, too. It’s normally priced at an MSRP of $145, though it’s currently on sale for $119 as part of the Black Friday promotions.

As I said, I test hundreds of bikes and dozens of locks as my day job. I live and breathe bikes. The fact that this lock has become my go-to everyday lock is pretty much all you need to know about how impressive it truly is. It’s a pleasure to live with and use, which means that I actually end up using it.

#4391. 2028 Honda CR-V Is a Fuel-Sipping Hybrid Family SUV Worth Waiting For

Honda’s bestseller goes hybrid only as it enters its seventh generation and will arrive in 2027 with a fresh design inside and out.

Honda’s bestselling model—and the third-bestselling vehicle in the United States through the third quarter of 2026—is getting a complete makeover. The CR-V will follow the path set forth by the sixth-generation Toyota RAV4, going hybrid only as the CR-V enters its seventh generation for the 2028 model year.

We expect the 2028 CR-V Hybrid to wear a sharp new design, with spy photos showing slim daytime running lights above a series of thin horizontal grilles, while the rear end features a light bar that stretches the full width of the SUV. It will likely also be the first vehicle in the U.S. to wear Honda’s new “H” logo, which was originally introduced for its future EVs but will now be applied to other vehicles in its lineup after Honda hurriedly canceled said EVs earlier this year.

The cabin is also expected to get a significant makeover, with the Avancier—a three-row SUV sold in Asia—providing hints about what to expect. The Avancier skips out on most real buttons and knobs, instead putting nearly every function into a large screen mounted to the dashboard, a dramatic shift from Honda’s current setup that prioritizes physical controls. The Avancier’s interior is wrapped in white upholstery, accented by glowing ambient lighting, and features a squared-off steering wheel. Honda also appears to be switching to a column-mounted gear selector.

See all results for new 2028 Honda CR-V Hybrid for sale near 20152

While Honda was once led by the Accord and Civic sedans, in today’s SUV-obsessed market, the CR-V has become the Japanese automaker’s most important model. Its biggest rival, the RAV4, was overhauled for 2026 and went hybrid only. Now, the CR-V will follow suit to stay competitive in the incredibly crowded compact SUV segment. Hybrid sales of the current-generation CR-V have been strong, accounting for over half of the SUV’s total sales so far this year, making it a perfect choice to launch Honda’s new platform and hybrid powertrain.

The CR-V will arrive on a new platform that Honda promises will be stiffer and lighter than before, taking a modular approach that will lead to greater parts sharing and reducing costs. This platform will presumably be adapted to underpin future versions of the Accord and Civic, along with Acura models such as the upcoming next-generation RDX Hybrid.

Honda will ditch the standard 190-hp 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine for the 2028 CR-V, which will arrive exclusively with the company’s new hybrid powertrain. The fifth generation of Honda’s two-motor hybrid setup will continue to use an Atkinson-cycle four-cylinder, along with a pair of electric motors, but the 2.0-liter engine will be a fresh design, featuring a new cooling system. As before, the electric motors will power the wheels most of the time, but the gas engine can also be engaged to directly drive the wheels.

See all results for new 2028 Honda CR-V Hybrid for sale near 20152

The electric motors are more compact than before, and Honda has developed a new battery too. The company says the new hybrid setup will bring improved power and efficiency, targeting 10 percent better fuel economy than the outgoing hybrid powertrain. The current CR-V Hybrid makes 205 horsepower and is rated at up to 38 mpg combined. We wouldn’t be surprised to see power increase to over 220 hp—the RAV4 makes 226 hp in FWD form and 236 hp with AWD—and fuel economy nudge up to just over 40 mpg.

The CR-V is expected to come with front-wheel drive standard and all-wheel drive optional, although it’s unclear if the latter will see the addition of a third electric motor. Honda will also likely include the S+ Shift feature seen on the Civic Hybrid and Prelude, which simulates a traditional transmission’s gearchanges and allows the driver to manually shift with the steering-wheel paddles.

The CR-V’s chief rival will continue to be the Toyota RAV4. However, the Hyundai Tucson Hybrid and Nissan Rogue Hybrid, which both enter a new generation for 2027, will also be strong competitors. The Jeep Cherokee, Kia Sportage Hybrid, and Subaru Forester Hybrid will be in the mix too, along with nonhybrid compact SUVs like the Volkswagen Tiguan.

The move to only offer a hybrid powertrain could see the CR-V’s entry price climb, which might alienate some buyers. Honda will also need to make sure it can match or exceed the efficiency of rivals like the RAV4 while still providing adequate performance and a spacious, usable cabin, given how closely matched the compact SUV space is these days. Moving away from physical interior controls could also upset the Honda faithful who are used to the company’s simple-to-use buttons.

Production is set to kick off at Honda’s factories in East Liberty, Ohio, and Greensburg, Indiana, in April 2027. Sales should begin shortly after, and with the current CR-V Hybrid starting at $37,580, we expect the next-generation model to come in at around $38,000.

#4390. These are the e-bike sales you should really care about this Black Friday

A lot of sites will throw a lot of affiliate links at you today for anything they can hawk for a few bucks (this site included from our deals team, probably). But this isn’t that. I’m a professional e-bike rider and tester, and the deals below are only for bikes I actually ride, and for companies I would actually recommend to my own family and friends. Last but not least, the Prodigy V2 Eco is just $1,295 after the $100 deal, which is literally the most affordable Bosch-powered electric bike in the world. The only thing stopping me from buying that bike is that I already have one, though at this price, part of me wonders if I should get a spare for friends to use!

Basically, Ride1Up has a ton of Black Friday Sales going on now, and you can check them all out here.

If you want to go a bit further up the quality ladder to get a more premium e-bike, but you still don’t want to spend $2k+, then you should check out Monarc Bikes. The company started by selling e-bikes that came with a free spare battery, but has recently opened up options for single or even no-battery bikes, meaning if you previously bought a Monarc model and already have that free spare battery, you can save a bunch of money by buying only the bike and using your spare battery across the line. Sure, e-bikes are my first love, but electric scooters absolutely deserve their place in the micromobility ecosystem thanks to their extreme portability and compact, space-saving size.

VMAX is my favorite electric scooter company, which brings its Swiss design to the US and European scooter markets. When it came to putting my nephew on a scooter to get to school, I made sure he had a VMAX VX2 Lite to cruise around safely and securely. There are a lot of great deals to be had, and you can see all of VMAX’s sales here.

These are the major sales that jumped out at me, but let me know what other sales you’ve seen on e-bikes you recommend.

I’ll take a look too and update if I see something I know I can stand behind. There are a lot of great e-bikes out there, and having ridden so many by now, I love being able to share my experiences, especially when there’s a good deal to be had at the end!

#4389. Ineos to Build Grenadiers in America and Sell Its French Plant to BYD

The fledgling automaker could start manufacturing its off-road-centric vehicles in the United States as soon as 2028.

The Ineos Grenadier SUV and Quartermaster pickup truck could be trading the French-flag badges that signal their Hambach production for ones that feature America’s stars and stripes. That’s because the fledgling British automaker has now confirmed plans to begin building its vehicles in the United States, with the first American-made Ineos models scheduled for 2028.

Ineos Automotive is still determining the exact location of its planned American production facility, but it says that it has developed a shortlist of potential sites. The move will bring the brand’s production to its largest market, with the United States making up around 70 percent of Ineos’s global sales.

See all results for new 2027 Ineos Grenadier Quartermaster for sale near 37347

Since Ineos already sells most of its vehicles in the U.S., the move will help make the brand more efficient. By building its vehicles in America, Ineos will also be able to avoid paying many of the lofty import tariffs that it’s currently subjected to. Plus, along with announcing plans to move to the United States, Ineos confirmed it’s in the process of selling its current Hambach facility to Chinese automotive giant BYD.

At this point, Ineos hasn’t announced whether it plans to buy an existing manufacturing facility, build a new one, or use another automaker’s excess capacity. One thing Ineos has been clear about, though, is that the move will cover its entire global production. A final decision on the facility is expected within the next few months to keep the move on schedule.

#4388. TVR Returns From The Dead. Again

The moribund British sports car brand is back and wants to build the new Griffith at Lotus's factory.

Would you wait a decade for a new car? That’s the situation for anybody who raised their hand to buy the TVR Griffith when it was announced as far back as 2017. R&T’s own interest in the story faded soon after the reborn British brand announced the car was going to be heavily delayed. But, in truth, nobody realized how long the wait would be.

Delays were reportedly caused by the failure to secure funding to build a factory in Wales among other crises. It’s fair to say that the interest of most onlookers, and surely all of the potential buyers , faded as the excuses piled up. But after a change in ownership last year, TVR's new parent MOTV Group has announced that the Griffith will be produced at the Lotus factory in Hethel, with the first customer deliveries “planned for 2028,” although those likely restricted to buyers in the U.K.

There isn’t room for any detailed history of TVR here, but the original incarnation of the sport car maker collapsed into bankruptcy in 2006, having become both famous and infamous for brutish, fiber-bodied models including the 1990 Griffith, 1996 Cerbera and 1999 Tuscan Speed Six. Also the semi-mythical, one-of-one Speed 12 which was a star of early Gran Turismo games. TVR was reborn in 2013 after software entrepreneur Les Edgar bought the rights to the brand; according to public records in the U.K., Edgar resigned from the company board earlier this month.

MOTV Group was previously known as Charge Holdings, with subsidiary Charge Cars planning to build an electrified restomod version of the 1967 Ford Mustang before it, too, collapsed into bankruptcy. In 2025, Charge was saved by a group of investors and subsequently merged with TVR.

The official announcement of TVR’s latest return was accompanied by an image of what appears to be the 2017 concept car, now wrapped in a new disguise. Comparison of the images shows the same headlight position, panel lines, side-exit exhaust and identically patterned wheels. MOTV says the car will have a spaceframe chassis, a composite body, a V-8 engine with a manual transmission, and rear-wheel drive - all details aligning the 2017 version.

The original plan was for the new Griffith to use the iStream production process created by Gordon Murray’s then technology company, but this subsidiary has since been sold to ForSeven, which subsequently acquired McLaren Automotive which presumably owns the rights. So It will be interesting to discover if this technology-sharing partnership remains in place. Similarly, there is no confirmation that Cosworth is still involved in fettling the Ford Coyote V-8 that was meant to power the car as was originally announced.

Beyond the above facts the official announcement was short on details beyond naming the senior executive team, these including CEO Paul Abercrombie and CTO Steve MacManus, who was formerly an engineering vice president at Tesla and who seems to have worked on the aborted Apple car project.

Can TVR manage it this time? Given the soap opera of the brand’s recent history, there remains a substantial question mark over that one. As does the more relevant unknown for most R&T readers as to whether there is any chance a reborn Griffith would ever reach the U.S. It would be fun if it did, but let’s not get our hopes up yet.

In the U.K. he held senior staff positions with CAR, Autocar and evo, and in the U.S. he wrote for MPH and Autoweek before becoming Car and Driver’s European Editor for ten years. #4386. Save Now, Pay Later: Why It Makes Sense to Buy a Less Expensive Old Car

Life is too short to wait for the perfect vehicle.

I have a bit of automotive ADHD. I can’t stick with a single car for too long. I get bored, reach my wit’s end with throwing money into it, or simply come across a good deal through my endless scouring of Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist. That means I’m constantly switching cars, and because of my limited wealth, those cars generally fall into the category I’d affectionately describe as shitboxes.

This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.

Look, I don’t want to buy shitboxes. It’s just the best course of action if I want to experience as many cars as possible for as reasonable a price as possible. Buying shitboxes is not for the faint of heart. Here’s how I do it and why.

When I’m searching for my next deal, I look for clean-title cars, ideally without fatal rust or debilitating powertrain issues. Pretty much every other problem—trivialities such as cosmetics and air-­conditioning—is acceptable. That mind-set is how I’ve proudly managed to own three different generations of BMW M5 and a 270,000-mile Lexus GX470 that I drove from New York to Alaska and back without issue. The shitbox mentality gets the job done, especially with Aughts enthusiast icons, which still offer modern convenience and potential reliability at the tail end of the depreciation curve.

Most recently­, I landed myself a 2009 Mercedes-­Benz G550 for about half off market value.

That story began on a slow Thursday afternoon, while I was letting the Marketplace algorithm feed me its best. The G550 popped up, and I offered the seller $3500 under asking. Instead of telling me to kick rocks, he wrote, “If you are serious huyer [sic] bring me cash today and it’s yours.” Guess what I did.

With payment cobbled together from my checking account and, to avoid the delay of a bank transfer, cash loans from a few friends who share my affliction, I drove five hours from New York through torrential rain and handed over the money in a dark lot in Northern Virginia late at night. It was sketchy and awesome. Now I own a G550 that’s stuck in second gear and has a sunroof flanked by worrisome rust holes.

Aside from paying less up front, if you buy a car at its floor, you’re only going to sell it for more. Probably. And when it comes to maintenance costs, I would rather cheap out on the purchase price, knowing what’s already broken, than drop double that on a better example and wait for something to inevitably break. Also, I could pay cash in full for the vehicle and then fix the issues I want to fix over time while enjoying what I’m able to enjoy about the car along the way. All with the assurance that whatever had to be fixed was completed under my supervision and done correctly. According to my shitbox math, it makes sense.

I turned 30 this summer. By a conservative estimate, I’ve owned at least 30 cars. But I’m not in the game of flipping. For me, it’s all about having as many adventures as I can behind the wheel of the greatest cars that have graced this world’s roads before they explode in value on Bring a Trailer’s auction pages. Holding out for perfection is not an option.

Road & Track’s digital director is often surrounded by beat-up project cars. His fleet currently consists of a problematic manual-swapped 1991 BMW 325i sedan and a Mercedes G550. Before R&T, Brown worked at Jalopnik, The Drive, and Business Insider.

#4385. Bentley CEO Says an Off-Road Bentayga Is ‘On the Horizon’

Bentley is reportedly developing a new Bentayga variant based on the X concept, which featured myriad off-road-minded upgrades.

Everyone’s going off-roading these days—or at least buying cars that look like they can. Even Bentley, the British automaker synonymous with wealth and high-class style, is reportedly getting in on the off-road action.

Earlier this year, Bentley revealed an off-road concept based on the Bentayga Speed that featured more suspension travel as well as an increased track width and ride height. The Bentley X concept rolled on forged 22-inch wheels wrapped in all-terrain tires. It also debuted at the FAT Ice Race in Austria with over a foot of ground clearance, partnership decals lining the sides and hood, spotlights, and a roof-mounted go-kart.

See all results for new 2027 Bentley Bentayga for sale near 98102

Bentley CEO Frank-Steffen Walliser said public response to the X concept was “really surprisingly positive” in a recent interview with Automotive News. He added that a production Bentayga based on the X concept is “on the horizon,” though nothing is finalized yet.

The current Bentayga is approaching its 10th year on the market, still in its first generation. Walliser also said the luxury SUV is due for a redesign, though it’s still too early for details. However, he confirmed the Bentayga is here to stay as the larger, gas-powered counterpart to the electric Torcal SUV, which is set to hit the market for the 2028 model year and will occupy a similar segment as the Bentayga.

As with most concepts, the production version of the off-road Bentayga will probably be much less flashy than the X concept—and most definitely won’t come with a go-kart. But knobby tires, a taller ride height, and more exterior lighting would be plausible in a production variant. Paired with the Bentayga Speed’s 641-hp twin-turbo V-8, a grittier version would be a notable addition to the off-road luxury SUV landscape.

Alayna Wilkening grew up reading motorsport magazines and following her grandpa around his Chevrolet dealership's showroom floor. In true Hoosier fashion, her first car was a hot pink custom cardboard "Fiero-vette" for her kindergarten Kindy 500 race. She now autocrosses a 1994 Miata with her dad, which she learned to drive the night before her first event. Alayna went to Indiana University and graduated with a degree in journalism and a minor in graphic design. As a testament to her great taste in cars, her first real one was a metallic orange 2007 Chevy HHR, which she lovingly called "The Dumptruck."

#4384. Denver man traps Waymo robotaxis with cones, eggs them at least 30 times

A man in Denver has found a cheap way to beat Waymo’s self-driving system: a few orange traffic cones and a carton of eggs.

Waymo says it has counted at least 30 egg attacks on its robotaxis in Denver, all believed to be the same man. And the Denver District Attorney’s Office has declined to file charges, calling it a civil matter, according to The New York Times.

The method is laid out in a Denver police report filed last month. The man pulls up in front of a Waymo somewhere in or around downtown, takes orange cones out of his trunk, and sets them around the robotaxi so it can’t drive off. Then come the eggs, sometimes thrown from his driver’s seat, sometimes after he gets out.

He leaves in a silver Toyota Corolla. Per the report, that car belongs to a fleet leased out to Lyft drivers. The man hasn’t been identified, and Lyft didn’t comment.

A Waymo investigator took seven of the incidents to police. Each egged vehicle had to come out of service for cleaning, and the detailing bill came to about $2,000. No permanent damage.

Police brought their findings to prosecutors, who decided “no criminal charges” were appropriate. A spokesperson for the DA told the Times the office is now collecting evidence on potential damage and will work with the city attorney to find “the most appropriate legal mechanism to make this behavior stop.”

At least one Waymo had a rider inside. Jeff Hunley was headed to the Union Station neighborhood in September when his robotaxi got hit. He filmed it, said he felt safe in the car, and got his fare refunded.

Waymo opened its Denver service to the public on September 1, alongside San Diego and Tampa. The company now runs more than 100 vehicles across 60 square miles of the city, and Mayor Mike Johnston is a fan. He called them popular and affordable, and couldn’t resist adding that “overall they’re a good egg.”

The rest of November hasn’t been as friendly. California’s DMV ordered Waymo’s driverless vehicles off state freeways on November 11 after robotaxis drove into active construction zones and one tried to get past a CHP traffic break. Waymo responded by pausing freeway rides in every US market.

And vandalism isn’t new for Waymo. We covered it when at least five of its I-Pace robotaxis were set on fire during protests in Los Angeles last year.

Putting a single cone on a Waymo’s hood to freeze it has been a known trick since San Francisco activists did it in 2023. Ringing the car with cones works for the same reason: the Waymo Driver is built to respect them, and it won’t push through.

A human driver getting pelted with eggs would just roll over a cone and leave. A robotaxi sits there and takes it.

That’s the correct default. You don’t want a driverless car deciding when a cone is optional, especially two weeks after regulators pulled Waymo off California freeways for ignoring work zones. But it means anyone with a trunk full of cones can pin a robotaxi in place for as long as they want.

We’ll try to keep the egg puns to a minimum. Mostly.

Can't help but respect the guy's dedication? This guy is causing road hazards by his childish shenanigans. There is nothing to respect about this guy. I never understood why anyone would support people that hinder technological progress that ultimately makes it safer for pedestrians, cyclists and other drivers. The more human drivers we get off the road the safer we all are.

This is small-time vandalism. Two grand in cleaning, no injuries, no lasting damage. But it shows a real weakness in robotaxis: they’re designed to be the most cautious car on the road, and a determined person can turn that caution against them in under a minute. The car can’t escape, can’t honk its way out, and apparently can’t stop the same guy from coming back 30 times.

The DA’s call is hard to follow. Prosecutors have a repeat pattern, a vehicle tied to a known fleet operator, rider video, and robotaxis that are basically rolling camera rigs. And still no charges. If someone boxed in a regular taxi with a passenger inside and started throwing things at it, we suspect the answer would be different.

At the same time, I can’t help but respect the guy’s dedication.

#4383. Pay Now, Save Later: Why It Makes Sense to Buy a More Expensive Old Car

A clean used ride is both easier and cheaper to enjoy.

One of the problems with the classic end of the automotive hobby is that everyone wants a clean car. Whether your goal is to keep it that way, preserve and use it, or modify it to suit your tastes, the road will be a whole lot smoother if you start from a healthy place. Trust me, buying a good example of an older car is better for your health. I’ve been there.

This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.

Why would you buy something with obvious issues? To save money, right? But guess what—you’re undervaluing your own time, and, except for a few rare occasions, the savings never materialize. Trying to fix up a bad car without already being an expert bad-car fixer is like trying to treat someone with a spinal injury without being a doctor: It’s going to be brutal, painful, and expensive in ways you can’t anticipate.

A clean car has fewer unknowns. With a not-so-clean car, damage from accidents may not have been repaired to factory spec. Paintwork may not quite match. “Just a little bit of rust” is almost never an accurate assessment of that metal-eating menace. “You’re not going to believe what we found in here” will become your own sad catchphrase.

This is particularly true for Aughts-era cars because they are potentially usable for everyday driving. The fantasy of dailying something like a sweet E39 BMW M5 can run into the reality of owning a 20-something-year-old specialty product. You might be thinking: It’s not like buying an old Ford Woody and needing artisan-­level skills. Most Aughts cars should be reliable enough to drive regularly at freeway speeds. The worst that could happen is I might need to replace a few still readily available parts, right? Maybe. Maybe not. You’ll quickly find out which local shops won’t touch cars that are over 10 years old.

Now, if I were a talented hobbyist mechanic, or a professional one, I could probably spot a deal where my skill set could be applied to a particular car’s needs, creating unique value for me. And yes, anyone could learn those skills with some time and effort. But do you want to spend your nights and weekends wrenching, not to customize your car but to repair it? Or do you want to spend that time driving?

For everyone who does not fix cars for a hobby and wants a cool car to drive for fun and maybe modify a bit: Get the clean car. Time is money, and if your money has to buy professional time un-shitboxing a previous owner’s mistakes, it’s going to cost you both dollars and days. You’re not just losing what you may have saved on the purchase price in repairs but also paying in the lost opportunity of a car that’s not on the road being enjoyed.

One of my recent purchases is an old Mercedes that I am having professionals modify for me. The ­difference between a great and a rough example of this car is about $15,000. Real money, but to make a bad example into a good one would be more than ­double that figure.

So yeah, you pay more on the way in. But guess what? When you go to sell it, you’re on the other end of the same equation. Money out, money in. Because everybody wants the clean example, and you’re ­holding the goods.

Matt Farah is a lifelong car enthusiast who began his automotive career at dealerships, rental agencies, and detail shops before discovering the power of YouTube in 2006, with his channel The Smoking Tire. #4382. Audi Patents Physical Buttons That Fold Out from Behind a Touchscreen

A motorized switch bar could give Audi drivers real tactile controls and an uncluttered dashboard.

Physical buttons have a lot going for them. They’re easy to find by feel, satisfying to use, and generally pretty good at staying wherever the automaker installed them. Well, it seems Audi has an idea that would change that last part. It involves hiding the buttons behind a touchscreen and deploying them when needed.

As CarMoses first discovered, Audi has filed a patent application that describes a motorized switch bar, which pivots out from behind the display’s lower edge. The screen stays fixed, while the physical controls swing into position beneath it. Interestingly, when stowed, the bar apparently has an on-screen counterpart with the same functions lined up in the same order, so those who don’t want physical buttons can avoid them entirely.

See all results for used Audi for sale near 90001

For those who do want the physical buttons, there are plenty of reasons to get excited. First, Audi says in its patent documents with the German government that the switches can deploy at startup, via voice controls, or via gestures. Moving the controls from the screen to the physical switches also provides more total screen room for users. (In one example, the physical bar deploys when a movie opens, leaving more room for the video.)

Ultimately, this could be a great way to meet the demands of more people. Designers love a clean dashboard without physical buttons and switches, but plenty of drivers really love having that switchgear. This system allows owners to pick whatever they want on the fly.

The timing makes plenty of sense too. Audi has openly said that it views moving toward more mechanical controls as the right direction. Of course, adding extra complexity to the once-simple idea of buttons can also increase the cost down the line when it comes time for repairs, but even so, this idea is certainly a fascinating solution to a very modern problem.

#4381. Tesla deploys 29 mobile Supercharger stalls for Thanksgiving travel rush

Tesla has parked a fleet of mobile Supercharger stalls at some of its busiest stations in California and Arizona to handle the Thanksgiving travel crush. The company says 29 temporary stalls are live, on top of 1,027 permanent stalls it opened in the US over the last 56 days.

It’s the most organized holiday push we’ve seen from Tesla’s charging team. And it comes with on-site attendants to manage lines and a virtual waitlist now running at 300 sites.

Tesla’s charging account shared a single composite photo showing four locations. The stall counts in it add up to exactly 29:

Firebaugh gets the biggest boost: two flatbed trailers loaded with Supercharger posts and tall power cabinets, parked right under the station’s solar canopy.

Three of the four sites are in California’s Central Valley, the stretch between Los Angeles and the Bay Area where Thanksgiving Supercharger lines have been a problem for years. Bakersfield’s Copus Rd station was already on the list of sites where Tesla offered free off-peak Supercharging in 2021 to spread out holiday demand. So Tesla knows exactly where the pain is.

Holbrook is the outlier. It’s a small town on I-40 in northern Arizona, the main corridor between Southern California and Albuquerque, where there aren’t many alternatives if a station is full.

The Copus Rd and Holbrook units sit directly on the pavement rather than on trailers. Tesla didn’t say whether any of these mobile stalls run off the grid or off onboard batteries, like the Megapack Chargers it deployed for the holidays in 2024. Those battery trailers haven’t been flawless, either: one burned at the Baker, CA Supercharger on New Year’s Day 2023.

Twenty-nine mobile stalls is a rounding error. The real holiday prep is the permanent build.

Tesla says it opened 1,027 stalls across 91 US sites in the last 56 days. That’s about 18 stalls a day, and an average of more than 11 stalls per new site.

For comparison, Paren’s data showed Tesla added 1,287 US fast-charging ports in Q3, or roughly 14 per day. The methodologies aren’t identical, but it points to Tesla speeding up deployment by about 30% ahead of the holidays. In that same quarter, IONNA added 378 ports and Walmart added 344.

Tesla also says it has boosted uptime and service dispatch for the travel window, and it’s putting attendants at its busiest sites to manage queues.

Then there’s the waitlist. Tesla launched its virtual queue pilot at just five Supercharger sites in May, a full year after it promised the feature following a fight between owners at a full station. It’s now live at 300 sites.

For context, Tesla said its US network handled more than 2 million sessions and delivered over 70 GWh between the Wednesday and Sunday of Thanksgiving 2025, with only 0.76% of sessions involving a wait.

We’ve been covering Tesla’s Thanksgiving stress test since 2018, when it was genuinely rough, and 2019 brought multi-hour waits in the Central Valley. This year looks like a network operator planning for a known spike instead of apologizing after it.

One of the few parts of the Tesla business which is and actually can stay a viable business model.

Twenty-nine stalls across four sites won’t make or break anyone’s weekend. But they’re going to be precisely the stations that get hammered every year.

The 18 stalls a day is what matters. We severely criticised Elon Musk after he needlessly fired Tesla’s entire charging team in 2024 as it resulted in a significant slowdown in deployment.

He stands by this criticism, but it finally looks like Tesla is getting back to its old supercharger deployment rate. Nobody else in the US is building at anything close to that pace.

#4380. The 2027 Cadillac Vistiq Gets A Price Bump And More Options

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

The 2027 Cadillac Vistiq just got a little more expensive, as spotted by GM Authority. For the latest iteration of the relatively young three-row electric SUV that slots under the huge Escalade IQ, Cadillac wants between $900 and $1,000 more than a month ago.

The higher starting price doesn’t necessarily mean more equipment, though the Vistiq now comes with a native Tesla-style NACS charging port, just like all the other 2027 EVs made by General Motors.

That said, the automaker is not throwing in any complimentary adapters, so owners who want a manufacturer-approved DC fast-charging adapter to use at CCS stalls will have to shell out an extra $189, even if they opt for the top-spec Platinum trim that starts at roughly $100,000.

For what it’s worth, Cadillac is offering a charging adapter bundle that includes a CCS1 adapter and an AC adapter for J1772 stations for a total of $256, which is quite good value for money.

Compared to the 2026 Vistiq, the 2027 model brings two new optional appearance packages and a few new exterior paint colors. The Onyx Package, which is only available on the top Platinum trim, comes with 23-inch black wheels, gloss black nameplates, Obsidian Chrome mirror caps, and puddle lamps that depict the Cadillac logo. Then, there’s the Onyx Lite package, which can be had on the Sport trim only. It features all of the goodies in the big Onyx pack, except the 23-inch wheels.

As standard, the 2027 Cadillac Vistiq comes with 21-inch Bright Silver alloy wheels, a dual-motor powertrain capable of outputting 615 horsepower and 650 pound-feet of torque, and a 102-kilowatt-hour battery that enables a maximum EPA-estimated range of 305 miles.

The Luxury and Sport trims come standard with an 11.5-kW on-board charger, while the Premium Luxury and Platinum trims come standard with an upgraded on-board charger capable of accepting up to 19.2 kW from a Level 2 dispenser. The uprated on-board charger can be spec’d on the first two trims, too, but it costs an additional $1,480.

For 2027, the Luxury and Premium Luxury trims cost $900 more than the outgoing model, while the Sport and Platinum trims are now $1,000 more expensive than before. As a result, the 2027 Cadillac Vistiq now starts at $80,395, while the top trim’s MSRP is now $99,495.

All trims get the same powertrain, but the more expensive versions come with more kit as standard.

#4378. Lucid Gravity Robotaxis Just Took A Major Step Toward Commercial Launch

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Lucid has its sights set on America’s burgeoning autonomous-vehicle ecosystem, and now it's one important step closer to getting robotaxis on the road. The California electric vehicle startup, along with Uber and self-driving technology company Nuro, has started testing driverless Gravity SUVs in the San Francisco Bay Area, the companies announced Tuesday.

More than 100 Gravitys have already been testing on public roads in San Francisco and Houston since January, but every one of them had a human supervisor in the driver's seat. Taking the safety operator out of the vehicle is a major step ahead of the service's planned commercial launch in the Bay Area in the first quarter of 2027.

The stakes are high for Lucid. The luxury automaker has burned through billions and struggled to meaningfully scale up its vehicle sales of the Air and Gravity. Increasingly, it's turning to the growing robotaxi market for a new source of sales volume and revenue. It plans to deploy tens of thousands of robotaxis in the U.S. and Europe.

If things go to plan, Lucid, Uber, and Nuro will join Tesla, Waymo, and Zoox as the few companies offering truly driverless paid ride-hailing in the U.S. Unlike those rivals, which offer rides through their own dedicated apps, the Gravity will be available through Uber. Uber has set out to become the go-to platform for driverless vehicles, and has struck deals to put Waymo and Zoox taxis on its app in certain cities. Uber's exclusivity deal with Waymo in Austin and Atlanta, however, will end in 2028 as the Alphabet-owned company plans to shift to its own app in those cities.

Lucid said initial phase of on-road driverless testing will take place in Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos, and Sunnyvale. More Bay Area cities will be added next year. A fleet of more than 100 Gravitys are included in these driverless tests, all of which have hardware and software upgrades compared to those in the previous phase of testing.

On paper, the Gravity has some advantages over its competitors. It is among the longest-range and fastest-charging electric SUVs in the U.S., with up to 450 miles of range on a single charge and 400-kilowatt charging that can add 200 miles in as little as 11 minutes. That should mean fewer charging stops and less downtime, which could potentially keep the vehicle earning fares for longer.

Lucid Gravity robotaxi commercial roadmap.

It will also have to maintain a high utilization rate to recover its steep starting price, which begins at $81,750 for the passenger version without any autonomous hardware and software. (Lucid hasn’t said how much the robotaxi version costs, or how much the extra weight affects range and efficiency.)

The Gravity isn’t Lucid’s only vehicle that will someday do robotaxi duty. The upcoming midsize platform will also spawn a robotaxi, although Lucid hasn’t said if it will be a version of the Cosmos or something else entirely.
