#4377. Best Cars for Snow

Snow performance is all about tires and clearance, so we selected the top-rated new vehicles that come from the factory with snow-rated rubber.

When discussing a car’s performance in the snow, it all comes down to tires and clearance. Tires are the only part of your vehicle that makes contact with the road, so the rubber mounted on your car is the number-one determiner of how much grip you’ll have while accelerating, turning, or braking on slippery surfaces such as snow and ice. All-wheel drive may help you get going in the snow, but it doesn’t help you stop.

So, when selecting this list of best vehicles for snow, we included only top-rated models that come standard from the factory with tires rated for severe snow service. These tires are marked with the all-important three-peak mountain snowflake icon (3PMSF). This icon is found on either all-weather tires or all-terrain tires that have been tested and are capable of at least 110 percent of the traction of a reference all-season tire. Not every all-terrain tire carries this marking.

It’s also important to mention that any car with winter tires would be our preferred method of transportation in snowy conditions. If you don’t want to pony up for one of these SUVs or trucks with their often pricey optional off-road packages that include the 3PMSF tires, consider outfitting a different vehicle with winter tires. Check out our Winter Tire Buying Guide for advice on which tires to choose.

The CX-50 is one of our favorite compact SUVs, and it offers a rugged-looking trim level called the Meridian Edition. This version comes with snow-rated all-terrain tires no matter whether you choose the naturally aspirated 2.5 S Meridian Edition or the more powerful Turbo Meridian Edition.

Tire: General Grabber A/T or Pirelli Scorpion XTM A/T

If you’re not willing to go all out for the Raptor version of the F-150 found later on this list, this popular pickup truck also offers a lesser off-road trim level that also comes with snow-rated tires. The F-150 Tremor doesn’t have the upgraded engine or suspension from the Raptor, but it does have style upgrades and other modifications compared with the standard F-150. There are two factory tire choices, either General or Pirelli, but both have the 3PMSF icon.

Many versions of the Ram 1500 pickup offer an Off-Road Group option package that includes Falken Wildpeak all-terrain tires in various sizes, all of which have the 3PMSF icon. Ironically enough, the Ram’s most off-road-oriented versions—the Rebel, RHO, and TRX—also have all-terrain tires, but not ones specifically rated for snow.

The GX is closely related to the Toyota Land Cruiser and is the most off-road-ready SUV in the Lexus lineup. To get snow-rated tires from the factory, you have to opt for the Overtrail model, which comes with all-terrain tires and other upgrades meant to improve the GX’s performance in the dirt and other types of off-road terrain. It has an impressive 9.8 inches of ground clearance.

Ford Ranger Raptor, Ford F-150 Raptor, Ford Bronco Raptor

Tire: BFGoodrich All-Terrain T/A K02 and K03

The BFGoodrich K0 series of off-road tires is well regarded among off-road enthusiasts. Ford’s Raptor off-road pickups, the Ranger and F-150, come with the latest K03 tires, while the Bronco Raptor SUV comes with K02s. We’re fans of all of these high-performance 4x4s, but the Ranger Raptor is our favorite of the bunch due to its smaller size, lower base price, and subdued styling.

Subaru has offered standard all-wheel drive on nearly all of its models for quite a while now, which has earned it a reputation for all-weather performance. But not every Subaru comes with tires optimized for snow. Only the Wilderness version of the Outback mid-size SUV comes with Yokohama Geolandar All-Terrain tires that carry this rating. (The Forester Wilderness and Crosstrek Wilderness also have these tires, but those models don’t rate as high in our testing.)

Mercedes-Benz G550 with G Professional Package

No, you probably don’t need a G-wagen to traipse through a few inches of snow to get to the grocery store. But this highly capable SUV has become a style icon for its distinctive aesthetic, and for good reason. The most capable version of the G-class is the G550 with the G Professional package, which adds all-terrain tires, a roof rack, a bull bar on the front, and other off-road upgrades.

The Mustang Mach-E compact electric SUV is one of the few vehicles you can get from the factory with all-weather tires, in this case the Michelin CrossClimate2. These snow-rated tires come on certain versions of the Mach-E, including the high-performance, 480-hp Rally and the new-for-2027 Trail (pictured), which also has extra ground clearance.

#4376. Review: Volvo’s 2028 XC60/90 PHEVs get 80 miles of EV range, changing the game

Volvo flew us out to Copenhagen to drive across the bridge to Sweden to check out the upcoming 2028 XC60 and XC90 plug-in hybrids. The new vehicles promise to double the EV-only range to 73-78 miles, making them a new breed of hybrid rarely seen outside China. But what can you do with so much EV-only range?

At Electrek, we’re usually pretty skeptical of plug-in hybrids. Too many are glorified gas cars with 20-mile batteries that owners often don’t bother to charge. The electric-only powertrain is often underpowered and not something you can actually use day-to-day.

Volvo’s upcoming 2028 XC60 T8 and XC90 T8 “Long-Range” PHEVs are the rare exception that actually force us to pay attention. By stuffing a 41.2 kWh floor-mounted battery (37.9 kWh usable) into its solid but aging SPA1 platform, Volvo has more than doubled the electric range of its two bestselling SUVs. Both now have more battery capacity and range than the original all-electric Nissan Leaf, Hyundai Ioniq, and many of the compliance EVs that followed. Volvo also doubled the charging speed from 3.6kW to a more reasonable 7.2 kW, meaning charge times are roughly unchanged.

Both the XC60 and XC90 share the exact same T8 AWD hardware: a 247-hp 2.0-liter turbocharged four-cylinder up front with a 70-hp front e-boost motor, and an upgraded 174-hp electric motor on the rear axle. Combined output lands at a healthy 455 horsepower and 560 lb-ft of torque.

The real headline, though, is the electric range:

Those numbers easily crown both Volvos as the longest-range plug-in hybrids coming to the U.S. market, blowing past the Mercedes-Benz GLE 450e, Toyota RAV4 Prime, and Range Rover PHEVs, which top out around 50 miles. With the average American commuting around 30 to 40 miles a day, you can genuinely treat either of these SUVs like a full EV Monday through Friday without waking up the gas engine once…or so it would appear on paper.

Sadly, there are some caveats to consider that will make these a little harder to run EV-only. First, to accelerate quickly off the line or to operate in AWD mode, the gas engine needs to engage. That makes winter driving and spirited driving a gas-usage endeavor. Also, without DC fast charging, the Level 2 charger tops out at 7.2 kW, meaning longer trips will also require gas usage.

On the plus side, even with the cold weather and snow tires, I saw range over 145 kilometers/90 miles on the XC60 when fully charged.

If you don’t need a third row, the XC60 is easily the more compelling package.

At 4,855 lbs, it’s quick—ripping from 0–60 mph in 4.5 seconds—and surprisingly efficient for a bulky crossover, sipping 48 kWh per 100 miles in electric mode and returning 29 mpg combined once the battery is depleted. Unlike the XC90, the 2028 XC60 also gets a proper visual refresh, complete with a cleaner front fascia, Matrix LED headlights, horizontal taillights, and an updated interior featuring Google Gemini on its not huge but very usable 11.2-inch touchscreen.

It’s also the easier daily driver in tight spaces, with a 37.4-foot turning circle and slightly more first- and second-row legroom than its bigger sibling. The trade-off is utility: you’re limited to 21.1 cu. ft. of cargo space behind the second row and a 3,500-lb towing capacity.

The XC90 is the family hauler for buyers who want a three-row electric SUV but aren’t quite ready to jump into an EX90 or Rivian R1S.

Because Volvo redesigned the battery into a flat, floor-mounted pack, you don’t lose the XC90’s practicality. You still get 6- or 7-passenger seating, 34.5 cu. ft. of cargo room behind the second row (up to 69.4 cu. ft. max), and a serious 5,000-lb towing rating. Even with the extra bulk, it hits 60 mph in 4.9 seconds.

The downside? Efficiency drops to 53 kWh per 100 miles (27 mpg on gas), the third row’s 31.9 inches of legroom is still best reserved for kids, and outside of the new battery and Google Gemini integration, the cabin and exterior are essentially carryovers, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing since we love Volvo interiors.

There are plenty of decently-long-range PHEVs available in Europe comparable to these things (e.g. VWAG's ones); it isn't only China. Also, a lot of them are far more affordable (and thus a reasonable alternative for people looking to save on motoring costs).

Availability isn't the issue so much as finding anyone who is interested in both owning and plugging in a PHEV. Almost anyone who is serious about minimising fuel use just gets a BEV instead.

Even with a 41.2 kWh pack, you can’t completely hide the compromises of a plug-in hybrid:

Look, we’d still rather see buyers go all-electric with the upcoming EX60 or EX90, and if Volvo prices these 2028 T8s too close to $70,000–$80,000 when deliveries start in early 2027, going full BEV will still be a no-brainer in my book.

But for those who aren’t ready to make the leap to full EV, these vehicles are incredibly compelling. Every morning, assuming you’re on a Level 2 charger, you have almost 80 miles of EV range, about double the average American daily usage. Then, of course, the backup of the 18-gallon tank and gas motor for those edge cases like trips or towing in cold weather are covered.

So the takeaway: if you’re going to build a plug-in hybrid in 2027, this is how you do it. Giving drivers 73 to 78 miles of real electric range turns the gas engine from a daily necessity into a road-trip range extender. For households with a Level 2 home charger that still have lingering charging anxiety on long highway trips, the 2028 XC60 and XC90 T8 are easily the smartest PHEVs on the market. Not to mention the smooth, quick and safe rides Volvo is known for.

#4374. Congress just passed a major e-bike safety law. Here’s what it actually means

E-bike battery safety standards that have largely been voluntary across the US are on the verge of becoming mandatory federal requirements, following the passage of a major piece of legislation in Congress.

The US Senate unanimously passed H.R. 973, known as the Setting Consumer Standards for Lithium-Ion Batteries Act, on November 19. The House previously passed the bill in April 2025 by a 365-42 vote. The legislation now heads to the president for a signature.

So what does that actually mean for e-bikes and their batteries?

The biggest change is that the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) would be required to turn three widely used UL safety standards into mandatory federal consumer product safety standards. Those include UL 2271 for light electric vehicle batteries, UL 2849 for e-bike electrical systems, and UL 2272 for personal e-mobility devices such as electric scooters.

Currently, those standards are generally voluntary at the federal level, though some jurisdictions have already made them mandatory. New York City, for example, requires certification to applicable UL standards for e-bikes, batteries, and other micromobility devices sold in the city.

If H.R. 973 becomes law, that approach would effectively go nationwide.

The bill gives the CPSC 180 days after enactment to promulgate the three standards as final consumer product safety standards. And this isn’t simply a one-time requirement based on today’s standards. Future revisions would generally become federal requirements 180 days after the CPSC is notified, unless the agency determines that a revision doesn’t improve safety.

For established e-bike companies already selling UL-certified products, the immediate impact may be relatively small. Many major brands have already moved toward UL 2849 certification, particularly as retailers and municipalities have increasingly demanded it.

The bigger impact is likely to be felt at the lower end of the market, where inexpensive e-bikes, replacement batteries, and direct-import products have continued to enter the US without certification to recognized safety standards.

Importantly, UL certification isn’t a guarantee that a lithium-ion battery can never catch fire. Damage, improper repairs, incompatible chargers, manufacturing defects, and other problems can still create hazards.

But the standards are designed to test batteries and electrical systems against foreseeable electrical, mechanical, and environmental stresses. Making those standards mandatory would establish a nationwide minimum safety floor instead of leaving compliance largely voluntary.

I’d say that’s probably the biggest change here: we aren’t talking about a new e-bike technology or a new battery chemistry. We’re talking about taking safety standards that much of the reputable e-bike industry already follows and making them the baseline for everyone selling these products in America.

#4373. The Tesla Cybertruck Is America’s Fastest-Selling Used Truck

EVs are selling faster than gas vehicles, with the Cybertruck leading used trucks and 16 EVs landing among the 25 fastest-selling models.

Even though it was recently canceled, the Tesla Cybertruck is the number-one-selling used car in America. That’s based on analysis of over 1.1 million used-vehicle sales from October 2026 by iSeeCars.com. It includes the fastest-selling trucks and the 25 fastest- and slowest-selling vehicles overall.

In fact, EVs take 25 percent less time to sell than gas vehicles in the used market, and among those EVs there are three Teslas in the top 25, including the Cybertruck, Model 3, and Model Y. And 16 of the 25 fastest-selling used vehicles are EVs.

“Why do so many electric vehicles, including the recently canceled Cybertruck, sell so rapidly on the used market? The combination of sustained high fuel prices and a dramatic drop in market value essentially ‘flips the script’ on EVs when they transition from new to used status,” said iSeeCars Executive Analyst Karl Brauer.

Here are some numbers: EVs average 45.6 days on the market compared with 54.5 days for hybrids and 61.0 days for gasoline vehicles, according to iSeeCars. Those 45.6 days are 15.4 days less than gasoline vehicles and 8.9 days less than hybrids. The overall industry average is 59.5 days. Used EVs spend 25.2 percent less time on the market than gasoline vehicles, while hybrids spend 10.7 percent less time on the market than gasoline models.

See all results for new 2026 Tesla Cybertruck for sale near 12180

And despite the fact that many electric pickup trucks have recently been axed, EV pickups in general are particularly well represented among the fastest-selling used trucks, the study says. Four of the top 10 trucks are electric, and three of them rank among the top four fastest-selling pickups.

The Tesla Cybertruck leads the rankings at 39.1 days on the market, selling in 26.4 fewer days than the average used pickup. The Ford Maverick hybrid ranks second at 43.3 days, followed by the fully electric Rivian R1T at 45.2 days and the Ford F-150 Lightning at 47.4 days.

Gasoline-powered trucks account for five of the top 10 positions, led by the Toyota Tacoma in fifth place at 50.1 days. The Ford Maverick hybrid ranks second, outperforming all electric trucks except the Cybertruck.

However, not every electric pickup sells quickly. The Chevrolet Silverado EV ranks last among all 24 trucks, averaging 107.5 days on the market. That’s 68.4 days longer than the Cybertruck and 42.0 days longer than the average truck.

EVs also perform strongly in the broader used market, per iSeeCars, where they claim 16 of the 25 fastest-selling model rankings.

The Audi A4 Allroad is the fastest-selling used vehicle overall, averaging just over a month on the market, or 33.7 days, followed by the Lexus RX 450h+ plug-in hybrid at 35.0 days and Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron at 36.3 days.

See all results for new 2026 Tesla Cybertruck for sale near 12180

Electric vehicles occupy six of the top 10 positions, including the Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron, Audi Q6 e-tron, Hyundai Ioniq 5, Lexus RZ 300e, Kia EV9, and BMW i5. All six average fewer than 39 days on the market, compared with the overall used vehicle average of 59.5 days.

The Tesla Cybertruck ranks 16th among all used vehicles, averaging 39.1 days, while the Tesla Model 3 ranks 18th at 39.5 days and Tesla Model Y ranks 24th at 39.8 days. Electric models from Kia, Rivian, Subaru, Toyota, and Volkswagen also appear in the top 25.

What are the slowest sellers on the used car market? The Cadillac Escalade IQ is the slowest-selling vehicle in the study, averaging 134.3 days on the market, more than twice the overall industry average. The Ford Escape plug-in hybrid ranks second at 127.3 days, followed by the Lincoln Corsair hybrid at 114.0 days.

The Silverado EV ranks fourth at 107.5 days, making it both the slowest-selling electric pickup and one of the slowest-selling used vehicles overall.

Two additional electric vehicles appear among the slowest-selling models: the electric Dodge Charger, averaging 98.2 days, and the GMC Hummer EV SUV, averaging 84.9 days.

“There’s clearly a big shift from new to used status for electric vehicles, especially when fuel prices have remained elevated for several months,” said Brauer. “Used shoppers are all about value, which normally plays against electric vehicles. But when consumers see their fuel budget jump 20 to 30 percent, the value of not visiting a gas station leads straight to used EVs.”

#4372. An Empty EV Tried To Park Itself 868 Times In One Night. The Video Is Hilarious

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Correcting yourself while parking isn't an abnormal event. Maybe you overshot the turn and pulled just a little bit too close to the car next to you. So you back out, adjust, and try again. It's not all that embarrassing—at least not the first time. But how many times does it have to happen before you start to go red in the face (or just give up and drive away)?

Two? Five? What about 868? Because that's how many times one Chinese EV was caught on security camera footage trying to find the perfect parking spot overnight.

An apparently empty Avatr EV was caught on camera spending the majority of the night maneuvering around marked parking spaces in a parking structure in China's Anhui Province. The car can be seen on video moving around a small area of the garage. Reversing into a space, pulling forward, repositioning, and doing it all over again.

Watching the footage is a bit confusing. If you know that it's a car with parking assist or other autonomy features, you probably assume that the car is just having trouble deciding how well it's parked—like it's some sort of programming error that makes the car's software lack confidence that its parking job is good enough. That may not have been the case here.

It turns out that this particular car wasn't alone in its parking shenanigans. In fact, other video footage soon emerged showing other Avatr and Huajing-branded cars pulling off similar parking stunts.

While the exact reasoning for the repeated parking is unknown, CarNewsChina quickly put together that the cars in the videos all sport Huawei's driver assistance software.

The footage emerged just as a contest run by Huawei was taking place. It ran through November 13th and was meant to show off the capabilities of the tech company's Qiankun Intelligent Driving system by giving users points in eight different categories depending on how they used vehicles' Qiankun-backed features while driving.

One of these categories is called "Parking Elite." It measures the use of Automatic Parking Assist, Exit-and-Park Assist, Parking Lot Navigation Assist, and Remote Parking Assist to assign points to drivers. The top 100 drivers would receive Huawei points, which can be redeemed for in-app purchases and discounts.

Of course, this reportedly led to some drivers attempting to game the system. CarNewsChina even surfaces a post where one driver claims to have completed 1,000 parking sessions in a single day. It's worth noting that Huawei's tech is technically a driver-assistance feature and not an autonomous driving function; the car is supposed to always have a human supervising these types of actions

These are just theories, of course, but the claims from drivers and security camera footage do seem like gaming the system is a plausible explanation.

Either way, you have to admit that if you saw a car parking itself 868 times overnight into various parking spaces, you'd wonder what was going on—I know I would. At least it's good for a laugh and didn't cause a traffic jam.

#4369. New York Says 'Enough Is Enough' To In-Car Subscriptions

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

If you ask the auto industry, subscriptions are the future. Consumers might disagree. They don't want basic features like heated seats being locked behind a paywall, especially when the hardware is already installed. Legislators in New York have decided those types of subscriptions are nothing more than a money grab.

A new law aims to put a stop to many forms of in-car subscriptions and after-sale purchases, meaning that if all it takes is a credit card number to switch on a feature after you buy the car, it probably isn't going to fly in New York State. But there are, of course, some exclusions.

Governor Kathy Hochul signed into law a bill that prohibits automakers, dealerships, and third-party providers from charging car buyers ongoing subscription fees in certain cases. Specifically, it prohibits recurring fees for hardware already installed in the car at the time of purchase, so long as those features don't create an ongoing cost for the manufacturer or a provider.

A snippet from the State's announcement says it best (and uses the infamous heated seat subscription as a prime example):

Amid rising consumer prices, the new law guards against a rising trend of car companies charging car owners fees to activate and use built-in features like heated seats, enhanced navigation, hands-free driving and entertainment options that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers and manufacturers.

There are, of course, provisions in the legislation of what features aren't covered by the subscription freeze.

New York says that driver assistance and automation features, connected cellular services, in-car hotspot, satellite radio, vehicle telematics, roadside assistance, navigation updates, and infotainment features are some of the items excluded from protection under the new legislation.

Notably, that means Tesla can continue charging for features like Full Self-Driving. It does, however, call into question features like Acceleration Boost, which is a $2,000 software-based performance upgrade that requires no extra ongoing costs.

This distinction tracks fairly in line with what both enthusiasts and consumers have been shouting at their phone screens for the last few years. If it's local hardware that's already installed in the vehicle and requires no ongoing costs to maintain (like heated seats, climate control, or remote start using a physical key fob), it feels like a cash grab to continue to charge owners after purchasing the vehicle. Things that cost money to provide—like internet-connected streaming features or driver assistance features that are being actively developed and upgraded over the air—are a bit more defensible.

If your $70,000 SUV still needs its manufacturer's servers, cellular network, fresh maps with to-the-minute traffic conditions, and continuously updated self-driving software—you might not get out of paying a monthly fee. But if it just needs a relay flipped on to work completely offline, then the manufacturer better just work it into the cost.

#4368. The Most Valuable Hot Wheels Cars Ever

We bet this list of 23 little cars with big price tags will make you double-check your personal collection—or start one.

Collecting cars is expensive, time-consuming, and something of a game of patience. Collecting little die-cast cars is mostly just the latter two. However, at the top end of the game, rare and hard-to-find Hot Wheels can command prices that raise eyebrows.

To get a sense of where the market is at right now and where it’s going, we caught up with Hot Wheels uber-collector Bruce Pascal. Pascal has thousands of die-cast cars in his collection, which even extends to the full-size classic hot rod “King T,” which inspired the 1968 Hot Wheels Hot Heap. Together, the collection is worth over a million dollars, and it includes an example of the most valuable Hot Wheels of them all, the one at the bottom of this list.

Before diving in on the spendy stuff, Pascal was quick to note that the Hot Wheels collecting hobby is as broad as it is deep. He notes that while eBay used to be where auction battles raised prices higher, about half of all transactions these days occur on Facebook fan pages, with regular auctions, Deal or No Deal style haggling, and sometimes even other Hot Wheels fans throwing some cash on the table to help someone else lock down a buy of a car that perhaps had sentimental value.

You can find most of these places by identifying your segment of interest in Hot Wheels, whether that's the “Redline” cars of the 1960s and 1970s, “Blackwall later cars,” or just plain typing in “Hot Wheels” for everything. Pascal notes that the vast majority of transactions are for less than $10, so feel free to wheel and deal as you build up your own toy car collection. They’re a lot easier to find parking for than a full-size one. Meantime, here’s a look at the Hot Wheels that fetch the most money when they change hands.

2026 Red Line Club Ferrari F40 - $120–$150

Values of the full-size Ferrari F40 have more than doubled over the past few years, making owning one a multimillion-dollar payout. If you’d invested on a smaller scale, you could have doubled your money too. Mattel’s Red Line Club costs under 10 bucks a year and opens up access to highly detailed die-casts for members only. The RLC F40 debuted in August for $50, and examples are now trading for as much as triple that on eBay. It's not nearly the same money as the 1960s cars, but it shows that anyone can get into the Hot Wheels collecting game.

1974 Magenta Rodger Dodger with White Interior – $3000

First issued in 1974, Rodger Dodgers with a black interior are relatively common; those with the white-colored interior are rare, as pictured here, and are the ones that collectors desire.

The Chevrolet Camaro is probably the most Hot Wheels of Hot Wheels, right out of the gate as one of the original 16 castings produced. Brown over a white interior is among the rarest combinations, although values on these haven't really changed much over the past few years.

Rare Hot Wheels Prototype Camaro Worth $100,000

1972 Pink Superfine Turbine – $3500–$4500

Designed by Larry Wood, the Superfine Turbine design dates from the early 1970s and has remained fairly stable in price recently. Wood joined Hot Wheels back in 1969 and was with the company for 50 years, collaborating with the likes of Ed “Big Daddy” Roth and George Barris.

Another Hot Wheels flight of fancy and designed by Paul Tam, the Open Fire is a stretched-out AMC Gremlin with six wheels and plenty of motor. This little green goblin is rare, but prices have held steady of late.

1969 Red Baron with White Interior – $4500–$5000

With its German helmet theme, the Red Baron incorporates a bit of 1960s biker culture and has been reissued many times. This original one, with the rare white interior, is the collector’s choice.

Datsun’s 240Z got some respect right out of the gate in the early 1970s, but fans had to wait until 1977 for Hot Wheels to get its first imported car model. These have doubled in price since 2019.

A hopped-up Mopar with flames, the Rodger Dodger was built in low quantities with blue paint. The rarity drives the price up, as it has also doubled in value over the years.

1971 Spectraflame Purple Bye Focal – $6000

Bye Focal was Mattel’s term for a range of colors in the 1970s, and this purple was the rarest of them. The twin hood scoops are a nice touch, but this model has an Achilles’ heel where the body will begin to fall apart. That just makes surviving examples more rare.

1969 Cheetah Base with Python Body – $6000

This example is a prototype Hot Wheels, one that escaped into the wild even though it wasn’t meant to. The production model was intended to be called the Python, but the original in-house name was the Cheetah. Since only a handful of cars were built with the early base plate on them, that makes this model valuable.

1968 Pink Beatnik Bandit – $6000 (in package, $20,000)

Based on an Ed Roth hot rod, the Beatnik Bandit was another of the first Sweet Sixteen original Hot Wheels. The casting came in nearly 20 colors, but the pink shade is the rarest and thus the most sought after. Prices have remained pretty steady, though an example still in the original packaging fetched five figures recently.

1970 Red Ferrari 312P with White Interior – $7000

Almost every example of this Ferrari model produced came with a black plastic interior. This casting has the white interior that collectors obsess over finding.

Said to be the very first Hot Wheels to make production, the white version of the original run Custom Camaro was supposedly meant to be a blank canvas for designers. Add flames? Chrome-look paint? By mistake, some of these cars were packaged up and sent out, finding their way to the public.

1971 Red Olds 442 with Black Interior – $8000

Another model unusual for its color combination, the Olds 442 casting almost never came in red over black. It’s rumored that fewer than 15 surviving examples of these cars currently exist.

A relative newcomer to the ultra-collectible Hot Wheels segment, this 917 sprang up the charts thanks to its combo of bright paint and association with Porsche. Even Hot Wheels isn’t immune from the air-cooled Porsche boom.

Everyone loves a Woody wagon, but Hot Wheels didn't make many of them in 1969. Again, rarity drives the price point.

A U.K. import, this AMX was made as part of a sponsorship deal with drag racer Ed Shaver. Hot Wheels made lots of AMX castings, so the critical thing is finding one with the original side decals—and making sure they’re the genuine item.

The actual valuation on this little brown Mopar is actually something of a question mark. It’s rare though the casting was very popular, as Hot Wheels didn’t make many examples with brown paint. However, none have changed hands recently, so the actual auction price for one could be much higher.

1969 Mad Maverick Base on Mighty Maverick – $15,000

Another case of a name change driving a big price boost because of rarity, a copyright issue with rival die-cast company Johnny Lightning meant Mattel had to change the name of the Mad Maverick to the Mighty Maverick. However, a few escaped with the original name.

Considered to be one of the rarest production Redline Hot Wheels, this purple 442 has steadily increased in price recently to break into the top five of the most valuable Hot Wheels. It was made exclusively in Mattel’s Hong Kong facilities for just a single year.

#4366. Here’s How To Make Your Holiday EV Road Trip Easier

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

It’s a short workweek for most of us here in the United States. In just a day or two, many of us will load up our cars and trek around the country to our loved ones. If you’re reading this, there’s a decent chance you’ll be taking on of those trips in an electric vehicle. EVs have come a long way, so in theory, range anxiety shouldn’t be much of an issue for anyone these days. Still, with so many drivers on the roads, there are bound to be annoyances that come with long EV road trips.

Here are a few tips that can take the edge off a long trip.

DC fast charging times are getting better and better, but charging still takes longer than stopping for gas. Thus, bottlenecks can occur on well-traveled routes with limited DC fast charging stops. It’s just kind of the nature of the beast when most people are stopping for 20-30 minutes. Multiply that by the plethora of drivers also trying to charge up and get home, and well, it’s not hard to see why EV charging queues can balloon, adding time to your drive home.

But you can head some of that off if you prep the night before. For those with home charging, that means simply plugging the car in and ensuring it’s fully charged for the next day’s trip. For those who don’t have access to home charging, using a DC fast charger the night before, when everyone isn’t rushing to leave, could ease some of the frustration of charging up before getting on the roads.

Also, some DC fast charging companies give a discount for charging during off-peak hours. Prepping the night before won’t just save you time, it might save you money.

We may have a set route in mind for our trip, and that could be all fine and dandy, but is it really the best route for our cars? Electric vehicles tend to consume more energy at higher speeds and when traveling up hills. Thus, it could be advantageous to maximize range by picking a flatter route, or one with lower speeds.

In most cases this won’t be necessary, but if you’re pushing the limits of your car and the infrastructure around you, it’s good to know. Most route planning apps—like A Better Route Planner, Plugshare, or even Google Maps—take into account which route is friendlier to your car’s range calculator, and may suggest detours if you get a big range boost from a route that’s nearly as quick.

These route planners will tell you exactly when and where to stop, depending on your car’s efficiency, your destination, your desired state of charge at arrival, and road conditions along the way. They can be adjusted to fit your real-world efficiency data or your need for breaks. Rather than just winging, using a route planner ensures you’re never in an uncomfortable situation without the range or charging ability to get where you need to go.

This goes hand in hand with route planning, but I think it is relevant here. The Sunday after Thanksgiving is typically the single busiest travel day of the year. You’re not the only one on the road who will need charging. Prepping the night before can help with the initial charging wait times at the start of your trip. If you’re on a long journey, chances are you’ll find yourself in a big queue at a strange charger.

When you’re planning your route with charging stops, pay attention to what brands they are and what ports they use. An increasing number of highway stops often have several competing charging stations. A Tesla Supercharging station could have an Ionna Rechargery nearby. Or maybe it’s an EV Go station. Or maybe it’s a charging station by Circle K or Shell. In any case, they tend to cluster together near high-power infrastructure. Rather than fumble with apps and payments at the station, I think it’s best if you research the charging companies on your route and pre-emptively install their apps and set up payment.

Similarly, bring an adapter. NACS is quickly making its way across the country, but not every station has NACS ports, and not every one has CCS. Some of the stations with your desired plug will likely be busy. An adapter that allows your car to access both NACS and CCS ports will save a lot of headaches.

Once again, you’re not the only one trying to get home for the holidays. Let’s keep the queue moving, and try not to charge more than 80%, if possible. Charging speeds slow substantially when EV batteries surpass 80%. It may have only taken 15-20 minutes to get to 80%, but it’ll take another 20 or so to reach 100%, or much longer in some cars. Chances are, there’s someone waiting. Not only is it courteous to unplug and move on, but it’s also probably quicker to charge again (if you need it) closer to your destination.

I know this list has mostly been about minimizing time lost due to charging, but I think it’s important to remember that it’s okay to take a break. Charging stops are inherently longer than refuelling a gas car, but I think that 15-30 minute break is helpful for safe driving. Taking a rest, using the restroom, or getting a snack can take the edge off a trip. Use an EV’s characteristics to your advantage.

I’ve been doing EV road trips since 2021, and it’s amazing to see just how far both vehicle range and charging infrastructure have come. Long trips are possible for most drivers these days, whereas years ago, it was a huge hardship or even impossible. With better apps, better infrastructure, and better cars, it’s only gotten easier. But it still pays to know what you’re doing. Drive safely out there, folks.

#4365. Stellantis Exiting the WEC and Formula E to Focus on New Hi-Po Cars

Rather than spend millions on factory-backed teams, Stellantis will focus on new-car development and customer-racing support.

Stellantis is preparing its exit from the World Endurance Championship (WEC) and Formula E, but the automaker isn’t giving up on motorsports. In fact, the decision is meant to funnel more energy into making motorsports-focused cars for customers.

The Peugeot 9X8 hypercar is Stellantis’s only factory-backed car in the WEC; that partnership will end at the end of the year. The automaker has a bit more skin in the game in Formula E, where Citroën and Opel each hold two spots on the 24-car grid this season. Both teams will exit Formula E at the end of the season in summer 2027.

See all results for used cars for sale near 37040

By ending its FIA World Championship partnerships, Stellantis says it’ll be able to focus on building motorsports-capable cars for enthusiasts. Employees who currently work in the WEC and Formula E divisions will be retained and reassigned to other areas focused on performance-vehicle development and customer racing. Those reassigned employees will likely pivot to work on high-performance Alfa Romeo and Maserati models, as well as new motorsports-inspired variants for Peugeot, Lancia, and Opel.

Stellantis says it’ll continue to build on its engineering and competition knowledge in customer racing programs—especially rally racing, where several of its brands have deep rally roots. Dismantling factory-backed teams likely frees up the automaker to invest more in smaller collaborations with privateer teams, much like its partnership with PH Sport on the Lancia Corse HF in the World Rally Championship.

The restructuring aligns with Stellantis’s FaSTLAne 2030 plan, which aims to launch more than 100 new and refreshed vehicles by 2030. Reassigning motorsports employees to other areas will undoubtedly help streamline the development process for enthusiast-focused cars to meet the automaker’s ambitious goals.

Car and Driver reached out to Stellantis to find out how this might affect its involvement in other major motorsports events in North America. After all, Ram recently returned to the NASCAR Truck Series for the 2026 season, and Dodge recently announced plans to return to the NASCAR Cup Series for the 2027 season with two Charger-based race cars. A spokesperson provided the following statement: “There are no changes to Stellantis North America motorsports programs.”

#4364. This might be the real reason Elon Musk says Tesla’s AI5 chip is going to Optimus

Elon Musk says Tesla’s cars don’t need the next-generation AI5 chip, so it’s going to Optimus first. A new report from Taiwan’s chip supply chain gives a more practical reason: Tesla won’t have enough AI5 chips for its cars until 2028.

According to Commercial Times, Tesla’s chip design partner Global Unichip (GUC) is giving its limited TSMC 3nm capacity for 2027 to Google and Microsoft data center chips first. That leaves Tesla with a relatively small AI5 allocation.

Last Sunday, a Tesla owner asked Musk when AI5 would be in new cars. His answer: “It’s going to Optimus. Cars will remain at AI4. That’s enough to solve superhuman driving.”

As we reported this week, FSD v15 is basically AI4’s last shot. Tesla engineers are already squeezing the last few percent of utilization out of the chip, and the AI4.5 refresh is mostly a move to LPDDR5X memory. Musk said Tesla cut AI4.5 from 32GB to 24GB of RAM because “RAM is super expensive,” and that AI4 itself now costs twice as much due to memory and storage price hikes.

It’s quite a change in plans. In June 2024, Musk said AI5 would be in vehicles in the second half of 2025. Tesla only taped out AI5 in April, and Musk had already started describing its focus as Optimus and Tesla’s supercomputer clusters.

The Commercial Times report, published today, describes GUC as the custom ASIC design partner on Tesla’s AI5 project. GUC is the design services house whose largest shareholder is TSMC, and it works mostly on data center silicon.

Industry sources told the paper that GUC’s 2027 allocation of TSMC’s N3 capacity is much larger than this year’s. But with AI compute demand exploding, it still can’t serve every big customer at once.

So GUC is prioritizing North American cloud projects, including Google’s Axion 2 and Axion 3 server processors and Microsoft’s in-house chips. Those orders carry high margins and good visibility. Tesla’s robot and car chip doesn’t make the front of the line.

The result, according to the report, is that Tesla’s initial 2027 wafer quota can’t support annual shipments for a fleet of millions of cars. The supply chain expects that limited AI5 volume to go first to Optimus, which needs a lot of compute but ships in small numbers, and only expects large-scale adoption in cars after N3 capacity expands further in 2028.

TSMC is adding 3nm capacity, but not fast. Its new 3nm fab in Tainan is scheduled for volume production in the first half of 2027, and its second Arizona fab, which Musk has said will produce AI5, in the second half of 2027.

Tesla does have a second source. Samsung is building its own version of AI5 on 2nm at its Taylor, Texas fab, but it expects volume production of Tesla’s AI chips there in the second half of 2027.

Now look at the numbers. Tesla delivered roughly 1.6 million vehicles last year. Every one of them needs a self-driving computer.

Optimus is a different story. Tesla now plans to put AI5 in Optimus around April 2027 and push external Optimus deliveries to late 2027. Even an aggressive robot ramp next year is measured in thousands of units, not millions.

If your 2027 AI5 supply is a fraction of what a car program needs, Optimus is the only product Tesla has that can absorb it.

Musk’s version is that cars don’t need AI5 because AI4 is “enough to solve superhuman driving.” The supply chain’s version is that Tesla can’t get enough AI5 chips to put in cars anyway. Both can be true at the same time, but only one of them explains the timing.

Musk has made it clear that his top priority for Tesla autonomous driving is to be the cheapest to produce by a large margin. So he cut lidar and other sensors then designed the low cost to produce cybercab which also has low energy cost per mile. The only problem is that Musk hasn't prioritized operational autonomous driving.

Look at how Tesla has been handling silicon this fall. It cut AI4.5 RAM. It cut AI5 RAM from 144GB to 72GB, then bumped it to 96GB a day later. It says AI4 costs double what it used to. That’s a company rationing chips and memory, not one choosing to leave a 12x compute upgrade on the shelf because it isn’t needed.

And if AI4 really were plenty, Tesla engineers wouldn’t be talking about squeezing out the last few percent of the chip for v15.

So here’s how we read it. Tesla had to pick where its scarce AI5 chips go in 2027, and it picked the low-volume product. “AI4 is enough” is the story that makes that decision sound like a choice. And it’s a story we heard about HW3, Tesla’s previous self-driving computer.

#4363. This BMW iX3 Drove Over 600 Miles On One Charge. The Catch? It Took Nearly 18 Hours

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

It’s no surprise by now that the new BMW iX3 is a great long-range electric SUV. It blew past its official range rating in several tests and beat the competition in a few independent comparisons. Now, though, the iX3 is putting another performance under its belt, but it’s a whole other story whether regular drivers would actually go to all the trouble to replicate it.

BMW Brazil wanted to demonstrate that the first Neue Klasse-based model can do the rather demanding trip from Brasília to São Paulo without recharging along the way. That’s a 631-mile (1,016-kilometer) journey, while the iX3’s official range rating in Brazil sits at 354 miles (570 km). In the U.S., the 2027 iX3 50 xDrive, the same trim as the one put to the test in South America, has an EPA-rated 434 miles of range, so nowhere near the target distance.

Still, the crew made it, but it involved a lot of planning, a very careful right foot, and plenty of patience. Here’s how they did it.

Maximizing efficiency was the main goal, so the drivers aimed for a constant pace, avoiding busy roads, unnecessary acceleration, and steep deceleration. The iX3, which is powered by a 112-kilowatt-hour battery in the U.S., ended up traveling at speeds between 37 and 43 miles per hour (60-90 kilometers per hour), with short stints at up to 56 mph (90 kph) when the road was clear.

The drivers also made full use of the Max Range mode throughout the trip, which prioritizes efficiency over performance. It’s safe to say that the car’s 469 horsepower had a pretty restful day when BMW decided to go on this trip.

After traveling 439 miles, the electric SUV still had 30% left in the battery, with 193 miles (312 km) of estimated range left. At 15% battery level, the car had traveled 538 miles (866 km), with 99 miles (159 km) of projected range left. The numbers said the trip would be possible, so the team soldiered on, starting the final stretch at around 4 a.m. to avoid the São Paulo rush hour. In the end, the iX3 reached its destination, having covered 631 miles (1,015.8 km) on a single charge, but the time it took to check off this achievement was excruciatingly long: 17 hours and 30 minutes.

The car’s trip computer showed an average energy consumption of 17.6 kilowatt-hours/100 miles (10.9 kWh/100 km), while the average speed was just 35.5 mph (57.1 kph). That’s good enough when the only goal is to squeeze as many miles out of the battery as possible, but there aren’t many people out there who are willing to spend so much time behind the wheel just to prove a point.

Seeing how the iX3 can charge at up to 400 kW and a 10-to-80% top-up can take as little as 21 minutes, a short charging session can make a big difference during a real-world road trip.

Still, BMW Brazil’s achievement tops that of its Chinese counterpart. Earlier this year, a Chinese-spec iX3 50L xDrive drove over 500 miles on a single charge, averaging 20.2 kWh/100 miles (12.2 kWh/100 km).

#4362. Hyundai’s new Mercury EV Concept will launch as the IONIQ M in 2027 [Images]

Hyundai unveiled the Mercury Concept, a preview of its upcoming entry-level electric SUV set to launch as the IONIQ M in 2027.

Following the IONIQ V, which went on sale in September, Hyundai offered a look at its upcoming IONIQ lineup for China at the Guangzhou Auto Show on November 27.

Hyundai’s Mercury Concept stole the spotlight. The concept previews its upcoming “B-segment premium smart SUV,” set to launch in China in 2027.

According to Hyundai, the IONIQ M will be “the most accessible entry-level model in the IONIQ universe.” Unfortunately, it’s designed specifically for China.

Like the IONIQ V, the electric SUV was developed by Hyundai Motor’s Chinese design and engineering team. As such, it features a unique style and advanced tech you won’t find in Hyundai’s vehicles sold in the US, Europe, or other overseas markets.

The SUV’s futuristic low-slung design is inspired by Mercury’s orbit around the sun. Up front, the shark-nose design and slim, edgy lights form Hyundai’s “H” badge, while an integrated rear spoiler adds to the compact, sporty look.

Hyundai said the production version will feature Zhuoyu L2++ ADAS and a high-tech cabin powered by ByteDance’s Doubao AI model.

A battery-swap version is also set to launch through Hyundai’s partnership with China’s CATL following the production IONIQ M.

The Mercury follows the Venus, now on sale as the IONIQ V, and the larger Earth SUV, as Hyundai’s third IONIQ Planet name designed for China. It will go on sale in 2027 as the IONIQ M, alongside the IONIQ V EREV.

In 2028, Hyundai will launch the production version of the Earth SUV, while two new energy vehicles will join the lineup in 2029.

Looks like a fantastic little car. Something like a Leapmotor B05 that I have been considering to replace our Golf and Passat, but it is hard to judge its size.

I hope it arrives here soon. The IONIQ 5 we have is great also but too big and too expensive to compete with Leapmotor, Xpeng, Geely, MG here.

While Hyundai didn’t reveal battery or powertrain specs, it will likely feature a similar setup to the IONIQ V.

The Hyundai IONIQ V is available in China with two CATL lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery packs: A 53.5 kWh battery paired with a 140 kW (188 hp) rear electric motor that offers a CLTC range of up to 540 km, or a 66.8 kWh battery paired with a 168 kW (225 hp) motor with a CLTC range of up to 650 km (404 miles).

Hyundai said the IONIQ M will be “the most accessible entry-level model in the IONIQ universe.” Given the IONIQ V starts at 109,900 yuan ($16,500), the production IONIQ M could be priced around 99,000 yuan ($15,000) in China.

#4361. BMW Cars In The U.S. Will Soon Stop At Red Lights And Automatically Drive Off Again

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

BMW is sending over-the-air software updates to roughly 16 million cars around the world, and American-spec vehicles running the latest iteration of the company’s operating system are getting a big improvement.

Starting in December, vehicles in the United States fitted with the Highway & Commuting Assistant running BMW’s Operating System X, which include the new iX3 and iX5, will be able to stop at red lights and automatically drive off again. The small but important change transforms BMW’s driver assistance feature into a stronger competitor to Tesla’s so-called Full Self-Driving (Supervised) system.

The automatic stop-and-go at red lights functionality has been available in other markets, such as Germany, for a longer time, but it’s making its way to America now, too. According to BMW, the Highway & Commuting Assistant can automatically brake to a standstill, and when the light turns green, the vehicle will automatically set off again or prompt the driver to continue, as showcased in the video below.

That’s not all, though. The December software update brings a total of five new features, as well as improvements to 19 existing functions. Most have to do with driver assistance, navigation, charging, infotainment, and comfort, and cars running BMW Operating System 8.5, 9, and X are covered.

Some of the new features include Google Maps Places data in BMW Maps for cars running Operating System 9 and X, as well as Amazon Prime Video for all Operating System X cars, plus the 1 Series, 2 Series Active Tourer, X1, and X3. Predicted occupancy for public chargers, based on historical data, is also being integrated into the plug-in hybrid 2 Series Active Tourer, X1, X3, X6, and 7 Series, plus the electric iX3 and i3.

Cars fitted with the latest full-width Panoramic Vision display get a clearer view selection and larger widgets that can be repositioned. What’s more, a new AI avatar function creates a personalized avatar from a photo that the driver can take inside the car using the built-in camera.

The update also brings the MyMoment Drive Challenge to the iX3 electric SUV. It scores acceleration, braking, and steering, and the results can be seen on the My Trips screen in the My BMW app.

The latest software version will be beamed out to 16 million cars in 88 countries starting in December. BMW said that some vehicles that are running Operating System 8 can be upgraded to 8.5 for free over the air or at the dealer for a fee. The company didn’t detail which cars would be eligible for a free upgrade, though.

#4360. Comparison Test: Audi SQ5 vs. BMW X3 vs. Genesis GV70 vs. Mercedes-AMG GLC

We audition four upscale SUVs for a role requiring maximum versatility.

From the November/December 2026 issue of Car and Driver.

The vehicles assembled here are not the starring members of their makers’ lineups. They aren’t built for lapping racetracks, crossing the Rubicon Trail, or carrying a crew of seven. Instead, compact luxury crossover SUVs, as their compound-modifier designation suggests, play multiple roles. As premium-brand offerings, there’s an expectation of luxury. As four-door utilities, they must accommodate passengers and cargo. And as the more sporting examples of their ilk, they should exhibit a degree of athleticism. Living at the intersection of a variety of vehicle types, they need to demonstrate versatility and range, rather than excel with a singular ability.

We could have made a wider casting call for this production, but to ensure that the chosen crossovers weren’t forgettable, we opted for the more muscular variants, the ones with a more potent optional engine. That dramatically narrowed the field of candidates.

See all results for new 2026 Audi SQ5 for sale near 37040

The Audi Q5 is a relatively fresh face, having just been redesigned for the 2025 model year. The SQ5 is the model that fit our bill, with its 362-hp turbocharged 3.0-liter V-6, seven-speed dual-clutch automatic, and sport-tuned adaptive air-spring suspension. The Prestige package ($5900) and Black Optic package ($1900) were the chief items pushing this crossover’s $66,795 base price to $76,370.

The BMW X3 is a seasoned player in this arena, and the M50 xDrive best met our criteria. The turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-six has bulked up and boasts 393 horsepower and a robust 428 pound-feet of torque. It’s paired with an eight-speed automatic, adaptive M suspension, M Sport brakes, and an M Sport rear differential. To the BMW’s $67,850 base price, our test example added a modest load of options, which included the Premium package ($2750) and the M Sport Professional package ($600). The result was the lowest as-tested price, at $72,050.

Where you find a BMW, you typically find a Mercedes. Here, that’s the GLC in its new-for-2027 AMG GLC53 guise. It brings an enhanced supercharged and turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-six that makes 443 horsepower, a nine-speed automatic, AMG Ride Control suspension with adaptive damping, and rear-axle steering. Its $71,350 base price soared to $85,920, inflated by extras that included the Pinnacle trim ($3900), the AMG Dynamic Plus package ($2000), and the Driver Assistance package ($1950).

The award-winning Genesis GV70, with multiple 10Best trophies on its mantel, was a natural to include. It arrives in 3.5T guise, powered by a 375-hp twin-turbocharged 3.5-liter V-6 paired with an eight-speed automatic. It surprised us by having the highest base price, at $72,045, but in Prestige Graphite trim, there was little more to add, resulting in an as-tested figure of $73,895.

See all results for new 2026 Audi SQ5 for sale near 37040

What about the many other hopefuls from Alfa Romeo, Cadillac, Lexus, Lincoln, Land Rover, and Volvo? Most were screened out due to insufficient horsepower below our 350-pony threshold, while dedicated hybrids and electrics were not invited. Casting is a cruel process.

Let’s face it; none of this quartet have movie-star looks. The GV70, though most familiar (the design dates from 2022), is still pleasing to our eyes. The GLC’s appearance doesn’t break much new ground, but its long hood and rakishly set-back greenhouse give it an aristocratic vibe. The Audi’s fresh sheetmetal somehow seems not so fresh, and also not so interesting; it was the hardest of the four to pick out in traffic. Then there’s the BMW. Like a celebrity who experiments with creative facial hair or a weird ’do, BMW periodically feels the need to challenge its fans by changing up its look. Unfortunately, that’s where the X3’s design now finds itself.

HIGHS: Comfortable seats, capable chassis, solid feature content. LOWS: Forgettable looks, cramped rear quarters, not really a standout anywhere. VERDICT: Plenty of ability but eschews the spotlight.

That change-for-change’s-sake mantra reaches full flower in the X3’s interior. The operation of the outboard air vents and the placement of their controls are just annoying, as are the haptic door-lock buttons. “What the hell is going on with the door panels?” asked associate news editor Jack Fitzgerald. The design aims to be more futuristic than luxurious, but BMW’s vision of tomorrow is somewhat dystopian. “There’s nothing I like about these design choices,” said managing testing editor David Beard, “not one thing.” Screens and lighting set the scene, the better to distract you from the cheap-looking materials. After dark, though, the offending bits recede, and the glowing mood lighting enhances the atmosphere. Space is not an issue. The back seat comfortably accommodates two, but the shape of the seatback makes it uncomfortable for three (although that’s probably a rare use case for this segment). Up front, some of us found the driver’s seat to be narrow, but it’s highly effective at holding you in place during cornering.

Look at the SQ5’s dash, and it’s more like an assemblage of screens than a coherent design—the tacked-on passenger’s display is part of the Prestige package. Our car’s red seats and suede door panels were enlivening elements, but the patterned black plastic trim would look downmarket even in an A3. The driver’s chair was deemed good for a variety of body types, and the adjustable-height center armrest ups the comfort quotient. The SQ5 was also one of two vehicles in this test with seat massagers (the Genesis was the other). Its back seat, though, was the hardest to access and the least comfortable once you fold yourself into place—a consequence of the SQ5’s shortest-in-test wheelbase.

The GLC53’s cabin looks richer than its German compatriots’, and this is one Mercedes model whose big screen isn’t larger than life. Whereas BMW tries pointlessly to reinvent the air vent, Mercedes shows what a quality execution looks like. This AMG steering wheel still has annoying touch-swipe pads, though. We also noticed that the bloated center console impinges on the driver’s kneeroom, and the inductive charging pad buried deep within made the Mercedes the car in which you’re most likely to leave your phone (it will warn you that you’ve left it inside). Finally, the GLC’s set-back cabin results in a smaller cargo hold than others here.

HIGHS: Lowest as-tested price, best fuel economy, just misses first place in most measures of performance. LOWS: Odd-duck appearance, off-putting interior, not so richly equipped. VERDICT: An SUV that dares you to like it.

The GV70’s interior is the most glam, even more so than the Mercedes’s. “Easily the nicest,” Beard said. “You notice it from the moment you sit down.” Partial credit goes to the nonboring color scheme—blue with splashes of bright red—but don’t discount the glossy carbon-fiber-weave trim, the bright stainless-steel finishes, the ovoid shapes, and the quality-feeling switchgear. We love the rotary controller for the infotainment, which feels like quality. Unfortunately, it also feels like, and is located just ahead of, the rotary shifter. That quibble aside, the user-friendly GV70 took top marks in ergonomics. The Genesis also boasts comfortable, though firm, front chairs, with bonus points for their extendable under-thigh support.

If it’s an action hero you’re seeking, look first to the Mercedes. It has the strongest résumé, with not just the most horsepower but also the most torque, at 443 pound-feet (472 with a 10-second overboost function), just shading the BMW. Though tasked with carrying the greatest mass (4669 pounds), the boosted inline-six shrugs that off, and the AMG races to 60 mph in a launch-controlled 3.7 seconds, or in 4.7 seconds from a rolling 5-mph street start. Both of these results are best in test. So, too, are the quarter-mile time of 12.2 seconds at 113 mph and, thanks to the optional AMG Dynamic Plus package, the top speed of 167 mph, should you have to outrun a hail of bullets from machine-gun-wielding bad guys. All of this was plenty evident from behind the wheel, where the Mercedes felt like it wanted to storm the autobahn.

The BMW, with its “fantastic powertrain” (Beard again), was just a beat behind. Commendably boasting the lowest curb weight of 4474 pounds, the X3 posted a 60-mph time of 4.0 seconds flat, with a street-start figure of 4.9 seconds, both second best among our foursome, as was its quarter-mile time. Exhaling through quad exhaust outlets, and piping the exhaust note through the audio system, the vocal straight-six sounds great when giving its all. “The grunt is always right there,” noted Buyer’s Guide associate editor Andrew Wendler, but if you somehow don’t trust the highly responsive transmission to deliver—or you just want a more theatrical experience—you can pull and hold the downshift paddle to trigger a 10-second Sport Boost mode. It puts the powertrain into its max-sport settings, although it had no measurable effect at the test track. It does call up a cool 10-second countdown graphic in the instrument cluster. “It reminded me of the Power Rangers activating,” Wendler said.

The Audi also has a potent powertrain that’s always ready to break into a run, although it doesn’t sound quite as good as the others when doing so. “The 90-degree V-6 doesn’t have much character,” opined Beard. Nevertheless, with 406 pound-feet of torque, the SQ5 scampers to 60 mph in 4.3 seconds, or 5.2 seconds from a rolling start. Its seven-speed was the only dual-clutch automatic here and had the expected snappy responses but almost none of the low-speed lurching behavior commonly found in such transmissions.

HIGHS: Bucks-up cabin that’s a pleasure to interact with, blissful ride, quiet cruising.LOWS: Slowest of the group, trails on the skidpad, eyebrow-raising base price.VERDICT: Not the hardest-charging but still undeniably endearing.

With the second-smallest stable of ponies at 375, along with a lowest-in-test 391 pound-feet of torque, the Genesis had noticeably less vigor than the Germans. That bore out at the track, where the GV70’s 60-mph time of 5.1 seconds was 0.8 second behind its nearest rival. The GV70 tied the Audi in 30-to-50-mph passing but otherwise brought up the rear in all acceleration tests. Still, the Genesis is hardly slow, and the V-6 makes the right noises when the virtual tach needle climbs. For the most part, fuel economy represents a bit part for these players, but the BMW’s 28 mpg in our hands bested the rest of the group and shaded the second-place Audi by 4 mpg. Meanwhile, the Genesis racked up the biggest bar tab, quaffing premium at a rate of 21 mpg.

Asked to show their softer side, the Mercedes and the BMW struggle. They remain firm even in the mellowest suspension modes, and any leftover compliance goes away if you switch into Sport. Of the BMW, Fitzgerald said, “The suspension really beats you up on this loop, especially in Sport.” The X3 suffered noticeable head toss on the more challenging secondary roads.

Driven over rumble strips or expansion joints, the SQ5 seemed a shade less solid than the others. We posited that it was the lightest car here; actually, the Audi is second to the BMW but only by 16 pounds.

HIGHS: Pavement-searing acceleration, faithful steering, loads of stick. LOWS: Stiff ride, tiresome road noise, budget-busting price. VERDICT: A hugely talented but sometimes annoying A-lister.

None of the Germans rode as well as the Genesis, which barely acknowledged broken pavement. Wendler praised it as “serene on the highway.” Furthering that impression, the GV70 was also the quietest by far, registering just 19 sones at 70 mph.

On the handling loop, the flip side for the GV70 was a bit more body lean in aggressive cornering, though that’s a trade-off many owners would be happy to make. Shod with Michelin Primacy Tour A/S tires, the GV70 didn’t have the grip of the other cars. It also turned in the longest stopping distance, although its firm pedal feel won plaudits, as did the SQ5’s.

The Audi hangs on in the corners—like the Mercedes, it wears Michelin Pilot Sport 4 SUV tires—but the steering doesn’t have much to say. We didn’t love the BMW’s steering either, but its handling chops are substantial even if its Pirelli P Zero All Season footwear placed it third in skid-pad grip with 0.85 g (a previous X3 M50 wearing Goodyear Eagle F1 summer rubber did 0.90 g). With four-wheel steering, the GLC53 turns in eagerly, and we also liked the distinct on-center accuracy. Furthermore, it turned in the best skid-pad numbers and shortest stopping distance.

Coolly capable though it may be, the BMW was hard to warm up to. It hit a lot of marks, and not just at the test track. Its potent powertrain also had the best fuel economy. The Bimmer had the lowest as-tested price, but the least money bought the least equipment, and no one was a fan of the interior—the design, the materials, or interacting with it.

The Audi had no glaring weaknesses—unless you were trying to climb into the back seat—but no scene-stealing moments either. The powertrain and the chassis are undeniably accomplished, but the SQ5 would shine brighter if Audi could recapture some of its design magic, both inside and out.

In this high-strung company, the Genesis was decidedly not the sportiest, but it should be sporty enough for most drivers. It’s easily the most comfortable, arguably the most luxurious, and just so pleasant to interact with. That was enough for second best overall, despite a last-place finish in most performance metrics.

The Mercedes ultimately stole the show after acing our track tests. The GLC53 was engaging and exciting. “This is a machine doing powerful stuff, and you’re part of it,” Wendler said. While we admired the SUV’s abilities, it was not free of irritants, with road noise, ride quality, and some ergonomic foibles trying our patience. Sharp-eyed accountants might also point out that the as-tested price was much higher than the others, but some $5K of that was costume jewelry such as black leather with red stitching, 21-inch AMG cross-spoke wheels, and the AMG Night package. All of those options could easily be shed without dimming the GLC53’s star power. And then there’s this truism: Great talent rarely comes cheap.

#4358. ChargePoint's DC Fast Chargers Are Hitting The Ski Slopes

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

The next time you hit the slopes, you might see one of ChargePoint’s EV chargers either in the ski resort’s parking lot or directly at the base of the ski run. That’s because the charging network and electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE) manufacturer has partnered with Kässbohrer, the maker of the iconic PistenBully slope groomer.

Effective immediately, the partnership puts Kässbohrer’s clients, which range from ski resort operators to public parking operators, in direct contact with ChargePoint, which builds the hardware and software for its EV charging network.

As a result, ski resorts and indoor ski facilities can get access to an entire charging ecosystem for electric snow groomers and other electric vehicles that may be in a company’s fleet.

"Electrification is reaching heavy-duty vehicles that operate under some of the toughest conditions anywhere," said John Saffrett, EVP and Managing Director, Europe at ChargePoint. "Kässbohrer is trusted by ski resorts and fleet operators around the world. Together, we're helping customers electrify entire operations, from snow groomers to public parking, while reducing emissions, improving energy management, and lowering operating costs."

As luck would have it, Kässbohrer happens to build an all-electric snow groomer, so the partnership goes both ways. ChargePoint gets to sell more chargers, while Kässbohrer gets to sell more electric snow groomers.

The PistenBully 100 E packs a massive 196-kilowatt-hour battery pack rated at 800 volts, which enables a three-hour runtime for the 7-tonne tracked EV. That’s adequate for small to moderately long ski slopes, but for longer slopes, a quick recharge may be needed, and here’s where ChargePoint’s expertise comes into play.

According to Kässbohrer, the first-ever electric PistenBully can accept up to 150 kW from a DC fast charger, with roughly one hour needed to get the battery from zero to full. With its 268-horsepower, 10,939-pound-foot electric powertrain, the 100 E can drive at up to 17 miles per hour.

"With the PistenBully 100 E, emission-free slope grooming has arrived on the mountain, said Tim Estelmann, Product Manager at Kässbohrer. “But for it to function reliably and sustainably, the right infrastructure is essential. Only when the vehicle and charging solution work together does a powerful machine become a system that operators can rely on day after day and night after night. That is precisely why we are partnering with ChargePoint, together creating the foundation for long-term operational efficiency and sustainability."

Kässbohrer also sells a series hybrid diesel-electric snow groomer that pairs a Cummins oil burner with two electric motors. The diesel engine acts as a generator, so it can keep the revs lower compared to conventional diesel snow groomers. According to Kässbohrer, the PistenBully 600 E+ has up to 20% lower carbon dioxide emissions, up to 20% lower fuel consumption, and is 20% quieter than conventional snow preparation machines.

According to ChargePoint, over half of the snow groomers sold worldwide each year are made by Kässbohrer, so there’s plenty of room to grow for both companies.

#4356. Used Tesla Cybertruck prices jump after Musk kills it, one asks $150K

Used Cybertruck prices are up 10 to 15% in the month since Tesla announced it would end production of its electric pickup, according to listing data from CarGurus and Visor.

Some dealers are pushing it much further. One in New Jersey now wants $150,790 for a used Cyberbeast, about $36,000 more than Tesla charges for a brand-new one.

CarGurus’ price index puts the average used Cybertruck at $89,715, up 9.84% over the last 30 days and 13.5% over 90 days. Over the same 30 days, the broader used car market went down 1.37%.

Visor, which tracks dealer listings hourly and compares the same trucks month to month, shows a bigger move: +15% like-for-like versus last month, with an average asking price of $101,784 across 171 used trucks. Listings that sold in the last 30 days took 17 days on average.

The curve on CarGurus’ chart is flat at around $80,000 from July to late October. Then it bends up in November.

That lines up exactly with Tesla’s moves. On November 6, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas, and Tesla raised prices by up to 10% the same day. A week later, Tesla stopped selling every Cybertruck except the Cyberbeast at $109,990. And this week, it bumped the Cyberbeast again to $114,990, which is what Tesla’s configurator shows today.

In early August, the cheapest Cybertruck you could order was $69,990. Now it’s $114,990.

Sorting CarGurus’ nationwide used Cybertruck inventory by price, the top listing is a 2026 Cyberbeast with 4,493 miles at J&S AutoHaus in Ewing, New Jersey. The asking price is $150,790 with fees.

CarGurus flags it as “Overpriced” and says it’s $35,773 above market. But the price history is the best part.

The dealer listed it at $134,995 on November 20. It went to $139,995 on November 25, the day after Tesla’s latest $5,000 Cyberbeast hike, and then to $149,995 the next day. That’s $15,000 in six days on a truck nobody has saved yet, according to CarGurus.

The same dealer also has a 2026 Cyberbeast with 851 miles at $145,790. Elsewhere, a 2024 Cyberbeast with 302 miles in Calumet City, Illinois, is listed at $148,816. And a 2024 dual-motor AWD with 1,500 miles in Lincoln, Nebraska, is at $145,306. That’s more than the $99,990 Tesla charged for a fully loaded Foundation Series AWD back in 2024.

Canadian dealers are playing the same game. The most expensive listing on AutoTrader.ca right now is a 2024 Cyberbeast with 1 km in Mississauga at C$199,999. The other 13 priced listings in the country sit between C$105,000 and C$141,995.

Sort the same CarGurus inventory from the bottom, though, and the picture changes.

A 2025 AWD with 22,495 miles is listed at $68,619 in San Bernardino, California. A 2024 Cyberbeast with 65,482 miles is at $70,118. There are several 2024 AWD trucks with 20,000 to 40,000 miles in the $77,000 to $80,000 range, and CarGurus rates many of them as good or great deals.

So the floor didn’t move all that much. What moved is the top and the middle.

There’s another detail in the CarGurus data. The 2024 model year is up 11.68% in 30 days, to $91,220. The 2025 model year is flat at $80,979, with 0% change over the same period.

The 2024 trucks include the Foundation Series, which came with Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving” package bought outright. Tesla now only sells FSD as a subscription, so those trucks have something new ones don’t. The 2025s, mostly the cheaper AWD trims, aren’t getting the same bump.

It’s good news for current owners who want out. Many of them watched their trucks lose about half their value between 2024 and 2025. This is the best window they’ve had in a long time.

Um no. ASKING prices are up. Transaction prices? They will resume their cratering momentarily.

But we wouldn’t read it as a sudden wave of love for the Cybertruck. Tesla made the cheaper versions impossible to order, so used trucks are now the only way to get anything other than a $115,000 Cyberbeast. That pushes the middle of the market up. And part of it is just dealers testing what people will pay. These are asking prices.

The bigger question is what happens after production ends. Parts and service for a low-volume stainless-steel truck that Tesla no longer makes. We’d expect that to weigh on used values far more than a configurator price hike helps them.

If you own one and you’ve been thinking about selling, now looks like a good time. If you’re buying, don’t pay discontinuation hype prices.
