#4355. Winter Weather Hits EV Range Hard. One Automaker Handles It Better Than Tesla

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

With the first signs of winter making their presence felt in some regions, it’s handy to remember that electric cars lose range when temperatures drop considerably. It happens across the board, but some automakers and models handle the cold better than others, and a new study of over 59,000 EVs from Recurrent shows which battery-powered cars retain the most range when the thermometer reaches 32°F (0°C).

This year, Tesla has been dethroned in the automaker rankings by an unexpected competitor, though the American EV manufacturer still holds the first two spots when it comes to individual models.

Polestar, the Swedish-headquartered, Chinese-owned company that’s no longer allowed to sell cars in the United States after its inventory dries up, surpassed Tesla in the EV winter range rankings. The company’s models retain, on average, 88% of their range at 32°F (0°C) compared to ideal conditions, and 83% when the thermometer reads 20°F (-7°C).

Meanwhile, Tesla, which has historically been the top performer in Recurrent’s rankings because of its early investments in heat pump systems and other winter optimizations, is second on the list this year, with an 85% average range retention at 32°F (0°C) and 77% at 20°F (-7°C).

Audi completes the automaker podium, with the German marque’s EVs retaining 79% of their range at 32°F (0°C) and 71% at 20°F (-7°C), according to Recurrent.

At this point, it’s worth noting that the comparison point for these figures is not the official EPA range figure, but the longest range achieved by a particular EV in ideal conditions, as recorded by Recurrent’s system. As a reminder, the company gathers real-world data from EVs through owners who are willing to connect their cars to Recurrent’s servers.

This year, Toyota is at the bottom of the list, with its EVs retaining just 70% of their summer range at freezing temperatures, with Mercedes-Benz not far ahead. Rivian ranked sixth, with an average range retention of 78% at 32°F (0°C), ahead of Hyundai and Porsche, but below Jaguar and Nissan.

When looking at individual electric models, Tesla still has the lead, with the heat pump-equipped Model S ranking first. The discontinued electric sedan retains 90% of its summer range at 32°F (0°C), followed by the soon-to-be-discontinued Cybertruck, with an average retention rate of 89%.

Despite Tesla losing to Polestar in the overall rankings, the Model S still has the lead in the models list.

Next up is the Polestar 2, the entry-level sedan that put Polestar on the map. The four-door EV can still deliver 88% of its summer range at 32°F (0°C), followed by the Tesla Model X with 87% and the Tesla Model 3 with 85%.

The popular Hyundai Ioniq 5 is 10th on the list, with an average range retention rate of 81%, below the Ioniq 6, Audi e-tron GT, Tesla Model Y, and Chevrolet Silverado EV, but above the Audi e-tron, Rivian R1S, and Nissan Ariya.

The pre-facelift Toyota bZ4X is at the bottom of the list with 70% of range available when the temperature is 32°F (0°C), ahead of the Mercedes-Benz EQS, Chevrolet Blazer EV, Mercedes-Benz EQS SUV, and Cadillac Lyriq. Interestingly, the Volkswagen e-Golf, which is over two decades old and doesn’t have a battery thermal management system, ranked above Cadillac’s Lyriq.

On average, the 43 electric models included in Recurrent’s dataset retain 78% of their range in freezing temperatures compared to ideal conditions. That said, the best EVs out there top out at 90% range retention, while the bottom of the pack gets only 70%.

A heat pump makes a world of difference when it comes to boosting winter range. Compared to traditional resistive heating systems, an EV equipped with a heat pump will have 8% more range in the winter, which can make the difference between getting home and calling a tow truck.

Speaking of home, home charging and preconditioning the car’s interior before setting off will also preserve precious miles when it’s time to go somewhere with a thick coat on. By using electricity from the grid to heat up the cabin, the battery will last longer before needing a recharge.

#4353. Toyota confirms the Highlander 9X will launch as its first EREV with top-tier tech in early 2027

The Toyota Highlander 9X will go on sale in early 2027 as the brand’s first extended-range electric vehicle with advanced new tech from Huawei and CATL.

Toyota joins Hyundai Motor Group, including Kia and Genesis, Ford, Volkswagen, and several other major OEMs with plans to launch its first EREV in the first quarter of 2027.

Toyota’s Chinese joint venture, GAC Toyota, announced at the Guangzhou Auto Show on November 27 that the EREV will use its flagship SUV nameplate, the Highlander 9X, when it arrives.

The Highlander 9X will blend Toyota’s classic global car heritage with some of China’s most advanced technology.

At the event, GAC Toyota revealed that the flagship EREV will use a battery custom-developed through its partnership with CATL, along with Huawei’s advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) and smart cockpit setup.

The EREV will be Toyota’s fifth “electrified” vehicle, joining battery electric vehicles (BEVs), plug-in hybrids (PHEVs), hybrids (HEVs), and fuel-cell electric vehicles (FCEVs).

Unlike fully electric vehicles, EREVs have a small gas engine that acts as a generator to charge the battery when it gets low, extending driving range.

According to Nikkei, Toyota aims to produce 200,000 EREVs in China in 2027, and about 400,000 units in 2028.

We will have to wait until closer to launch for battery and powertrain specifics, but local reports suggest Toyota’s EREV will deliver a combined CTLC range of over 621 miles (1,000 km) on a full tank of gas and a full charge.

You can catch a glimpse of what appears to be the extended-range vehicle in the video GAC Toyota posted confirming the new EREV tech.

Since the Highlander 9X will be built in China, Toyota will not sell the EREV in the US. Instead, it will launch the fully electric Highlander BEV in the US in 2027.

The all-electric Toyota Highlander BEV will be available with front-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive powertrains with two battery packs: 77 kWh or 95.8 kWh. The smaller (77 kWh) battery provides up to 287 miles of EPA-estimated range, while the larger (95.8 kWh) battery provides up to 320 miles in FWD models.

Like the outgoing version, the fifth-generation electric Toyota Highlander will offer three rows of seating and space for seven passengers.

#4352. VW Will Pay German Drivers To Plug In Their EVs. Even If The Grid Never Uses Their Power

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Plug your electric Volkswagen in at 8 in the evening, unplug it at 6 the next morning, and you could earn €2.40 while you sleep. How much electricity would your car have to send back to the grid for that money? Potentially none. Starting in December, VW’s charging subsidiary Elli will pay eligible German drivers for the hours their car spends plugged in at home, even if it doesn’t actually supply any power during that time.

We already wrote about Germany’s plan to allow parked EVs to earn money. New rules made it easier to account for electricity stored in a car and later sold back to the grid, even for homes that can generate their own power through solar panels. That left a fairly important question for anyone with an EV in the driveway: How much could you actually earn? Now, Volkswagen has put a number on it.

Elli will pay €0.24 for each hour the EV is plugged in, provided each session lasts at least three hours. The bonus tops out at €60 a month, or €720 yearly. Earning the full amount takes 250 hours a month, a little over eight hours a night. In the app, you tell Elli when you need the car and how much charge you want when you leave.

Elli will handle charging and discharging around your schedule, but to make this work you need its 11-kilowatt bidirectional charger with vehicle-to-grid (V2G) capability. That costs €1,995 without installation, and your home also needs a compatible smart electricity meter for everything to work. Owners can register now, then check eligibility at launch and get an installation quote before ordering.

The thing is, even if you collect every euro of the first-year bonus, that still leaves €1,275 of the charger’s price to cover, plus whatever the electrician charges to install it.

Not all VW EVs have bidirectional charging. It introduced this feature on its European models in 2023, but it says there are around one million eligible EVs in Europe, about a third of which are in Germany. The offer covers Volkswagen, Cupra and Škoda, and the charger supports 400- and 800-volt vehicles, even if the latter is not present in any of the three brands’ vehicles.

Elli says it plans to expand into more European markets in 2027 and offer a separate vehicle-to-home system so owners can save rooftop solar power for use after dark. A one-year trial involving 20 German households logged roughly 85,000 combined charger hours online and more than 6,500 charging and discharging sessions, the company said.

VW calculates that €720 could buy enough electricity to drive an ID.3 Neo nearly 10,000 miles (16,000 km), assuming €0.33 per kWh and the car’s official WLTP consumption. So it may not offset the full cost of the bidirectional charger, but that’s still a lot of free driving for just keeping the car plugged in overnight.

#4351. Electric Porsche Boxster Prototype Reviews Are Out. Here's What Critics Think

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

This is a big moment for the auto industry. Whether you're an EV fan, an EV doubter, or just a car enthusiast in general, the electric Porsche Boxster is a big deal. It marks the first time that a true, enthusiast-based roadster switches from piston to electric power. Its public reception will make a huge impact on the future of electric sports cars. Yesterday, that reception began. The review embargo lifted for the Boxster on Tuesday, so we can finally hear the thoughts of genuine gearheads and EV enthusiasts alike.

Before we dig into what critics think, it's important to note the tumultuous journey the electric Boxster has had. The will they/won't they discussion of whether Porsche would even build the damn thing, and whether an electric Boxster would be any good, seemed endless. There was also discussion of whether Porsche would build a gasoline Boxster alongside it, as that seemed to originally be the plan. But for now this is electric-only. So now that the electric Boxster is finally here, and Porsche has no gas-powered version to hide it behind, how is it?

The overall consensus is this: It's a proper Porsche Boxster. The Boxster might actually be the perfect sports car to electrify because its engine has always been secondary to its handling. A Boxster is supposed to be sharp, nimble, and thrilling on a twisty road. According to early reviews, this new "983" generation Boxster is all of those things.

"Whether you’re welcoming the Boxster’s EV transition or bemoaning the loss of its internal-combustion engines, particularly the iconic flat-six, we think anyone who drives the next-generation 983 Boxster will agree it’s fantastic. The steering, inherited from the 992.2 911 Carrera GTS, is eager and sharp, and rear-axle steering will also be available. You can feel the Boxster’s rear-biased weight distribution in the way its rear end steps out when lifting off the throttle," said Dave VanderWerp said for Car and Driver.

"The steering in the electric 718 Boxster is Carrera GTS good, obviously, since that’s where it’s from. Perfect weight, razor-sharp, with quick turn-in; it’s easy to place the car in and through a corner," Joel Feder wrote for The Drive. "It’s also extremely easy to kick the rear end of the electric 718 Boxster out and then control the slide through a corner. I imagine this thing will be a drift machine when given the opportunity without Porsche’s handlers watching my every move."

Autocar's Illya Verpraet had similar things to say: "The classic Porsche driving position and round wheel immediately sets the mood. At the lower speeds on our sighting lap, I didn’t immediately gel with the steering, which seems a bit too eager to bring the rear-steer into play, but as soon as we picked up the pace, it came alive in the way that the best 911 steering tends to: not crazy fast or heavy, but lightning-accurate and full of feedback."

Most reviewers also seem to note the Boxster's similarity to its gas-powered predecessor. It supposedly looks familiar inside (Porsche didn't allow photos of it, so we have to just take every reviewer's word for it), handles like a Boxster, and it feels as expensive as one.

"If you put a Boxster GTS 4.0 owner into this EV with the fake noise turned on, all they’d notice would be the slightly different interior and how much quicker the car is when they drop the hammer," said MotorTrend's Jonny Lieberman.

And it's said to be quick. Porsche didn't reveal exactly how much power the car has, nor which model it was. It could have been a regular Boxster, Boxster S, or even something spicier, like a Boxster GTS. Either way, this Boxster impressed with its performance, despite being a single-motor, rear-wheel drive car. That single motor pairs to a limited-slip differential, too, so it should feel pretty natural through corners for current Boxster owners.

Porsche didn't say what sort of battery powered the prototype Boxster, but we do know where the battery is. Rather than having a skateboard battery pack in the floor, Porsche stuffed it behind the driver, where the engine normally would be. That does two things. It gives the 983 the same sort of weight distribution as every other Boxster, while also allowing passengers to sit lower than a normal EV. The result is that the electric Boxster has a lower center of gravity than previous generations.

Overall, this new Boxster seems incredibly promising. It's fast, it's apparently very fun to drive, and it feels like a Boxster should. I can't wait to see what it's like when Porsche finally reveals it.

Every 4Runner now costs more than last year, but the base-level SR5’s $1220 price hike is the steepest.

The Toyota 4Runner’s starting price will clear $45,000 for the first time ever. That comes after the base-level SR5 trim receives a $1220 price increase, bringing the least expensive 4Runner up to $45,085. While every trim has increased in price, the SR5’s rise is the most substantial.

To help offset the upcharge, the base model now features standard heated front seats. The driver and front passenger seats also get standard eight-way power adjustments. Also, the Black exterior color has been renamed “Inked” on all trim levels. Fancy stuff.

#4349. Prevost unveils Electric coach bus: 600 hp, 540 kWh, 250-mile range

Prevost, the Quebec coach builder owned by Volvo Group, has unveiled the H3-45 Electric, its first battery-electric motorcoach. It gets a 540 kWh Volvo battery, 450 kW (600 hp) from two electric motors, and both CCS1 and MCS charging as standard.

The H3-45 is Prevost’s flagship and one of the most common highway coaches in North America. Prevost is pitching the electric version as the same coach drivers and technicians already know, with a different powertrain.

Prevost first committed to an electric coach back in April 2022, when it announced a five-year electrification program backed by the Quebec government. That plan included a 100% electric coach and a retrofit kit to convert existing diesel coaches. The coach is now here. Prevost hasn’t said anything new about the retrofit kit.

Everything that moves the coach comes from Volvo. Prevost’s product page describes a single drive unit that combines two electric motors, an 8-speed automated manual transmission, and an oil retarder, rated at 450 kW (600 hp). Prevost’s tagline for it is “more power than diesel.”

The gearbox is the interesting part. Volvo’s own BZR Electric coach chassis in Europe uses a 2-speed automated transmission, but a 45-foot North American coach spends most of its life at highway speed and on long grades, and more gears help keep the motors in their efficient range. Prevost claims 97% motor efficiency across the working range, and drivers get adjustable regenerative braking for descents.

The battery system is made of six Volvo Cube2 units on a 600V architecture, for 540 kWh of total capacity. The brochure specifies 459 kWh of usable energy “across the full battery life,” so Prevost is holding back about 15% as a buffer.

The packs are liquid-cooled and IP6K9K-rated, and they use the same VCS2B coolant as the diesel H3-45. Volvo also backs every battery for refurbishment, second life, or recycling.

Prevost rates the coach at “up to 250 miles (400 km)” of range. But the footnote under that number says typical energy use runs up to 2.25 kWh per mile (1.40 kWh/km).

Do the math with Prevost’s own figures: 459 kWh of usable energy at 2.25 kWh/mile is about 204 miles, or roughly 328 km. Reaching 250 miles requires averaging about 1.84 kWh/mile. So 250 miles is the best case, and operators should plan around closer to 200 miles before keeping any reserve for the return to the depot.

Also, an energy buffer of almost 80 kWh is quite massive.

On a CCS1 charger at up to 350 kW, a 20-80% charge takes about 55 minutes, according to Prevost. The Megawatt Charging System (MCS) cuts that to about 35 minutes. The charge port is positioned for pull-through truck-stop stalls, and Prevost says no adapter is needed on public networks.

Those numbers also tell you how fast MCS actually charges this coach. Going from 20% to 80% of 459 kWh means adding about 275 kWh. Doing that in 35 minutes averages roughly 470 kW. That’s a lot faster than CCS1, but nowhere near a megawatt.

The value of MCS here is access as much as speed. Megawatt chargers are being built for electric semi trucks, like the first MCS truck charge in North America at EV Realty’s San Bernardino hub, and newer dispensers like Kempower’s dual CCS and MCS charger serve both connectors. A coach that can pull into those stalls has a lot more charging options on the highway.

The rest of the spec sheet reads like a regular H3-45: up to 52 passengers, Cloud One Premium seating, Prevost Driver Assist, LED headlights, five monitors, automatic tag-axle unload, and a kneeling system. 360-degree cameras and a winter package are optional.

Prevost markets the coach as a certified zero-emission vehicle and leans hard on grant eligibility in its brochure. There’s one catch in the fine print. The optional cold-weather heater is diesel-fired, and it produces emissions when it runs. For Canadian and northern US operators, that’s probably the option most of them will tick.

Prevost didn’t include pricing or a delivery date in its announcement. Jay Menard, who runs Prevost’s ZEV programs, told Electric Autonomy that pilots start in early 2027 and that production deliveries should begin around mid-August 2027.

Prevost isn’t first here. Its main North American rival, MCI, unveiled its J4500 CHARGE electric coach in 2021 with a 544 kWh battery and more than 200 miles of rated range. So Prevost is arriving about five years later with essentially the same battery size.

What Prevost brings is a single-OEM drivetrain from Volvo, more power, a multi-speed gearbox, and MCS. It also keeps the electric version on the same platform as the diesel H3-45. And Prevost confirmed in September that its 2027 Volvo D13 diesel meets the new EPA and CARB standards. The diesel H3-45 isn’t going anywhere.

For more electric bus and coach coverage, check out our electric buses guide.

#4348. Audi Wants To Make Buttons That Deploy From Behind The Touch Screen

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Volkswagen is moving back to more physical buttons, after suffering some backlash from its touch-button-heavy design. Mercedes also publicly recognized that maybe the world went too far with touchscreens. Audi, too, seems to be eyeing more physical controls. But it isn't giving up its touchscreen ones to do so. The company just patented a technology that lets it have its cake and eat it, too, but creating a physical button panel that can hide behind a touchscreen.

Unearthed by CarMoses, this patent shows off a little button bar, which is just a strip of physical buttons and possibly one knob that lives below the touchscreen. At the press of a button, or even with voice control, the button bar can hide away behind the touchscreen, for anyone who prefers a simpler looking cabin. Once the buttons are hidden, the touchscreen creates a duplicate set of icons at the bottom, so button functionality isn't lost while hidden.

What sort of physical buttons will occupy such a button bar? There seems to be a circular knob in the center of the buttons, so that will likely be volume. The flanking buttons could be for climate control, maybe heated seats, or perhaps even some drive mode buttons. Whatever they end up being, it will be nice to see Audi's with high-quality physical buttons again.

In the '90s, 2000s, and 2010s, Audi had some of the best buttons, switches, and knobs in the industry, all with satisfying, high-quality clicks. The current crop of piano-black plastic touch buttons in most modern Audis feels like a slap in the face for fans of the brand. So to see the return of some buttons in places where they can be easily memorized and adjusted without looking would be wonderful.

Obviously, Audi can't use physical buttons for everything. There are far too many controls and features in modern cars for that to work. There'd be hundreds of buttons on the dashboard if that were the case. But the main buttons, the ones you use everyday, should be physical. And the beauty of this patent is that it, if you like a more high-tech vibe, you can hide them away. With this patent, Audi gets to make both camps happy.

#4347. BYD’s flagship electric minivan debuts with a new style and 559 miles of range

BYD’s new flagship MPV is not your average minivan. The Whale can drive over 559 miles (900 km) on a single charge, charge in as little as five minutes, and it’s packed with BYD’s latest tech.

The Whale is the first flagship multi-purpose vehicle (MPV) from BYD’s Ocean series. BYD has several sub-brands, including Denza, Yangwang, and Fang Cheng Bao, and sells vehicles under two primary lineups: Ocean and Dynasty.

BYD unveiled the Whale for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show on November 27, with a launch set for the first quarter of 2027.

Measuring 5,270 mm long, 1,996 mm wide, and 1,815 mm tall, with a 3,130 mm wheelbase, BYD’s newest minivan is slightly longer than the Chrysler Pacifica.

The Whale will be available in both plug-in hybrid (PHEV) and pure electric (EV) powertrains. Both will use BYD’s latest Blade Batteries 2.0. The PHEV version will offer a pure-electric CLTC range of 248 miles (400 km), while the EV variant offers over 559 miles (900 km) of range on a single charge.

With BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the electric minivan can charge from 10% to 70% in just five minutes.

For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes only nine minutes. Even in temperatures as low as -30°C(-22°F), it takes just 3 minutes longer, or 12 minutes total.

Leading up to its debut, camouflaged prototypes were spotted with a boxy design that looked closer to a traditional gas-powered MPV.

However, the Whale looks better than expected. It adopts BYD’s updated Ocean design with smooth edges and a double-layer staggered grille.

I'd buy one if they were available in the US, instead all we get are the overpriced Sienna and id buzz

BYD didn’t reveal many details outside of confirming the name and showcasing the design. With LiDAR on the roof, the Whale will offer BYD’s latest Advanced Driver Assistance System (ADAS).

The Whale will go on sale in the first quarter of 2027, joining the Dynasty Series Xia, Linghui M9, and Denza D9 as BYD’s fourth MPV.

Prices will be revealed closer to launch, but the Whale is expected to start at around 300,000 yuan ($45,000), filling the gap between the Xia, which starts at 249,800 yuan ($37,500), and the Denza D9 at 359,800 yuan ($54,000).

#4346. Acura Makes Japanese-Market Debut with the U.S.-Built Integra Type S

The Integra Type S is now for sale in Japan, making it the first Acura-branded vehicle to reach the Japanese market.

The 2026 Acura Integra Type S is officially for sale in Japan. That might not seem like big news, considering Honda Motor Company is headquartered in Japan, but the release marks the first Acura-branded vehicle to be exported to the Japanese market. While this is Acura’s first time in Japan, it’s strangely not the Integra’s, which spent a few decades wearing a Honda badge from 1985 to 2006.

Most Acuras are designed and built in the United States and sold throughout North America. The new Integras for sale in Japan are the same as those sold stateside, meaning they’ll be left-hand-drive anomalies in a predominantly right-hand-drive market.

See all results for new 2027 Acura Integra Type S for sale near 37040

That also means they’ll get the same 320-hp turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four that we’re quite fond of in the United States. The front-wheel-drive sport compact is only offered with a six-speed manual transmission and features a limited-slip differential, Brembo brakes, and 19-inch wheels wrapped in summer tires. The whole package comes together to reach 60 mph in a brisk 5.1 seconds.

Honda builds every Integra Type S at its assembly plant in Marysville, Ohio, and the engines come from Honda’s Anna Engine Plant, also located in Ohio. Honda began exporting vehicles from Ohio to Japan in 1988 and has shipped nearly 300,000 Hondas to Japan since then.

Honda says the Teg’s introduction in Japan marks a strong global demand for an enthusiast-centered performance sedan. If the Type S is well-received in the Japanese market, it’s likely that more Acuras could start making their way to Japan in the future. Pricing and the exact number of Integra Type S models available in Japan haven’t been released yet, but considering they’re identical to the Type S models sold on our shores, they’ll likely come in around $56,000.

#4345. Europe Gets This Tiny New Suzuki EV. It Makes A Mini Look Big

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Suzuki left the U.S. car market in 2012, but it still builds the kind of small hatchbacks European buyers have long favored, now also powered by electricity. Its latest is the Ignis EV, a city car that measures just 11 feet 9 inches long (3.57 meters). It’s due in Europe in summer 2027, when it will face a new generation of small EVs from both European and Chinese automakers.

The Ignis is Suzuki’s first subcompact electric car developed for global markets, but its roots are in Japan. The company recently launched the e Sky there, an electric kei car that supplies the basis for the Ignis’s body and powertrain. The Ignis still has the typical kei proportions (it's tall and narrow), but Suzuki says it took the car onto European city streets and winding roads to tune the suspension and power delivery, making it more appealing to the people it hopes will buy one.

A 26-kilowatt-hour lithium iron phosphate battery sits under the floor of Suzuki’s dedicated Heartect-e electric platform. Yes, that really is what it's called. Up front, the motor, inverter, and reduction gears share a single compact assembly that sends 90 horsepower and 98 pound-feet (133 Nm) to the front wheels. Suzuki says it chose LFP for safety and longevity, but it hasn’t given the European car a range or charging figure yet.

The Ignis EV has a very tight 29.5-foot (9-meter) turning circle. Its overhangs are tiny, giving it a wheel-at-each-corner stance that looks unique while maximizing available interior room. The LED signatures at both ends take their shape from digital numerals, and the dark pillars give the roof a floating look.

Inside, a curve runs from the dashboard into the doors, with a wide display and a ceramic-inspired storage tray across the dash. Suzuki President Toshihiro Suzuki credits the company’s decades of building Japanese mini vehicles for its ability to provide a genuinely usable cabin in such a small footprint.

For decades, European brands had most of this business to themselves. If you wanted an inexpensive car that could squeeze down a narrow street, Fiat would happily sell you a Panda, Renault a Twingo and Volkswagen an Up. Chinese automakers see an opening as those buyers go electric.

Leapmotor brought the T03 to Europe through its partnership with Stellantis, while BYD adapted its Chinese-market Seagull for Europe and called it the Dolphin Surf. Driving the latter, what stood out to me was how well it drove, how little felt cheap, and how much kit it had for its sub-€20,000 starting price.

By the time the Ignis arrives next year, European buyers will have had plenty of practice shopping for small EVs. Renault has revived both the 5 and the Twingo as electric cars, and there’s also the related Dacia Spring. Volkswagen has the ID. Polo, Cupra has the Raval, and Skoda has the Epiq, and there definitely seems to be demand for them. In September, a major VW dealer group reported more than 30,000 orders for the ID. Polo and a waiting list stretching to ten months.

That leaves one big question for the little Suzuki. What will it cost? Consider the redesigned Dacia Spring. Dacia moved production from China to Slovenia, shared the electric Twingo’s underpinnings, and produced a car that starts at €17,900 in Italy. It gets up to 155 miles (250 kilometers) of WLTP range from a battery only slightly larger than the one in the Ignis.

#4343. Editor’s Letter: The Benz Patent Motorwagen Has Big Perambulator Vibes

I love new cars, but lately I’m fixated on cars of the past.

From the November/December 2026 issue of Car and Driver.

These days, I’m particularly interested in cars of the past. By that I mean the distant past. Such is the case for the 1886 Benz Patent Motorwagen I drove during Monterey Car Week. Now when someone asks, “What’s the oldest car you’ve ever driven?” I have an unassailable answer. That is, unless you’ve driven Cugnot’s steam car. You did? No way. Was it cool?

The Patent Motorwagen gets credit for being first because Carl Benz designed it to be a car from the get-go. He didn’t simply take a horse-drawn carriage, add an engine and drivetrain, subtract the horse and reins, carry the oats.

I love primordial stuff because things we take for granted today had not yet been figured out. There were lots of guesses—some right, others not. Driving a vehicle that old is disorienting, challenging, and sometimes dangerous. Maybe something will explode. Maybe you’ll fall out. Boring hadn’t been engineered into the experience yet.

See all results for used cars for sale near 14221

The Patent Motorwagen gives big perambulator vibes, and baby, I am here for it. It has only three wheels, to keep it simple and light. Carriages turned their entire axle, since uprights and kingpins at the wheels were still years away. Steering the first car involves grabbing what appears to be the wood handle of an awl—the automotive steering wheel hadn’t been invented yet either. Also not in existence in 1886: carburetor jets, engine radiators, radios, tetanus shots.

Another hitherto unimagined concept: hiding the crankshaft and flywheel behind casings. The crank, connecting rod, cam gear, and drive belt all sit out in the open. Some of those parts have to be greased up before your drive. For others, oil is metered out onto the cylinder and the intake valve by drip lubricators before it runs over less critical parts and leaves behind a greasy trail on the road.

To start the Benz, switch on the ignition that sends energy to the roughly eight-inch-long spark plug, then grab the horizontal flywheel. Give that a Wheel of Fortune–worthy spin and wait. The air-hexane fuel mixture is adjustable, so you can richen it to help the car start (it originally ran on naphtha, which was available at apothecaries in 1886, right next to the laudanum). There’s no throttle, so the 1.0-liter doesn’t stray far from its 400-rpm operating speed. A 4.8-quart copper vessel perched over the engine holds the water that cools the cylinder. After about an hour of operation, the water boils over, and you stop and take a calf’s-head-stew break to let things cool.

To accelerate, push the long lever on the left side of the leather-trimmed park bench to engage the engine-driven leather strap to the axle. Feel the 0.88 horsepower. To stop, pull that lever back to actuate a shoe that drags on the axle. Not to sound like an 1886 infomercial, but driving the Patent Motorwagen is so easy, a toddler could do it. It’ll hit a claimed 13 mph, and it was the most amazing 13 mph I’ve ever experienced. There’s no way I’m going to be this fun when I’m 140 years old.

#4342. World’s largest electric bulk cargo shop packs MASSIVE 23.5 MWh battery

Moving millions of tons of coal, sugar, and other bulk cargo is serious business, and decarbonizing that business presents a number of unique problems – but if the new BRF Froan bulk carrier proves anything, it’s that battery size isn’t one of them. The new electric cargo ship is packing an impossibly huge, 23,500 kWh battery.

Fitted with the equivalent of nearly 300 long-range electric car batteries, 130 meter (426 ft.) BRF Froam built by SOHO Marine Heavy Industry for Norwegian shipping firm Berge Rederi Future (BRF) will use the ship to haul up to 13,250 deadweight tonnes (DWT) across the 230 nautical miles (or about 265, as the crow flies) between the ports at Brønnøy and Elnesvågen without burning a drop of diesel.

“It’s going to run back and forth, back and forth, just like a ferry,” explains Oivind Berge, co-owner of Berge Rederi Future, in a TradeWinds interview. He added that the round trip takes around 24 hours, with charging facilities installed at the loading and discharge ports. “Then we can go back and forth continuously.”

The 130M vessel BRF Froan left the shipyard at Jiangsu SOHO Marine Heavy Industry, in China last week, and is currently en route to Norway where it is set to begin shipping huge chunks of marble early next year.

The ship’s massive battery sends electrons to a 6,000 kW (about 8,000 hp) electric motors that turn the propellers. How that works is obvious – what might be less obvious is what those big stovepipe deals at the back of the BRF Froan are.

Those are called rotor, or rotary sails, and they one-up the old-school version by using something call the Magnus effect to produce forward thrust. Basically, as the tall cylinders spin, the wind flowing around them creates a pressure difference that generates lift perpendicular to the wind. That lift produces forward thrust, helping push the ship along and reducing the amount of electricity it needs to draw from its batteries once under way.

The company estimates the two rotary sails will save about 339 kW per trip, while the switch to battery power will save another 10,000 tons of harmful carbon emissions and 220 tons of nitrous oxides each year.

Pretty cool. It might not be trans-oceanic shipping yet, but it's nice to see electric vehicles of all types starting to become more common.

Interesting Engineering is reporting the total cost of the project at approximately USD 52 million (NOK 500 million). A second vessel, named BRF Frøya, is already under construction in China and is scheduled for delivery in 2027.

SOURCE | IMAGES: BRF, via Naval Porto Estaleiro.

#4341. Ionna Slashes EV Charging Prices For Thanksgiving

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Ionna, the EV charging network that ranked first in J.D. Power’s latest public charging satisfaction survey, has slashed prices at its stations across the country for Thanksgiving weekend.

The company, which usually charges an average of $0.40/kilowatt-hour, is now asking for $0.20/kWh plus tax at all its DC fast charging stations in the United States. That’s a 50% discount, and drivers don’t have to do anything special to get it—just plug in and pay, either through the automaker’s official smartphone app, the on-site payment terminals, or the Presto app for Tesla owners who want to enjoy the Autocharge function.

For long-distance travel, the slashed charging rates can make a big difference. A single 50-kilowatt-hour session that used to cost $20 will now be just $10 plus tax, but seeing how many people are traveling across the country these days, multiple sessions will be necessary, driving the cost savings even further.

And it’s not like the cost reduction comes with any strings attached. Ionna uses 400-kilowatt chargers from Alpitronic exclusively, so there’s plenty of wiggle room for even the most power-hungry EVs out there. What’s more, many stalls have dual cords for each port, with a CCS connector and a NACS connector, so charging adapters aren’t needed at most locations.

Separately, Ionna has discounts for several automakers, including Mercedes-Benz, BMW, General Motors, and Stellantis.

The charging operator installed its first stalls in 2024, and it has wasted no time expanding its footprint quickly. On its second anniversary, Ionna celebrated by opening its 100th site, and the company now has 229 sites and nearly 1,900 ports nationwide, according to the Department of Energy's Alternative Fuels Data Center (AFDC). Still, the charging network is not slowing down, with dozens of locations under construction and plans to introduce 500-kW chargers in the near future.

Most EV brands support Plug & Charge at Ionna, with Tesla recently getting Autocharge functionality through a third-party smartphone application. Ionna itself doesn’t have a smartphone app, instead relying on automakers and third-party apps to integrate its locations. So far, this approach has turned out to be quite successful, with J.D. Power’s latest public charging survey putting the operator first, ahead of Tesla and the rest of the competition.

#4340. Tested: New Lexus ES Hybrid Is Much Quicker Than the Old Version

With an extra 29 horsepower, it’s not an especially surprising result, though it is a welcome change.

Welcome to Car and Driver’s Testing Hub, where we zoom in on the test numbers. We’ve been pushing vehicles to their limits since 1956 to provide objective data to bolster our subjective impressions (you can see how we test here).

The debut of the 2026 Lexus ES brought a full overhaul to the luxury sedan, which included a revamped hybrid variant. The new generation comes with fresh styling, a longer wheelbase, and an updated powertrain. In our testing, a 2026 ES350h was considerably quicker than a 2023 Lexus ES300h F Sport Handling, which was the last ES hybrid we tested.

See all results for new 2026 Lexus ES for sale near 37040

In our recent test of the ES350h, the updated sedan sprinted to 60 mph in 6.6 seconds, while the 2023 car more or less jogged its way to the 60-mph mark in 7.9 seconds. That’s a huge improvement, and one that took us by surprise, given that the new car doesn’t look drastically more powerful than the old one on paper. That’s to say nothing of the additional 352 pounds of weight in the new car either.

So, where did all the extra quickness come from? Well, we can think of several places. For starters, the 2026 ES hybrid is more powerful, even if the numbers don’t jump off the page. The powertrain, which features a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine, now churns out 244 horsepower, up from 215 in the 2023 ES. Along with a more powerful engine, the updated hybrid system uses a larger and more powerful electric drive motor than the previous generation. Lexus also now offers the gas-electric ES with all-wheel drive for the first time, and that’s the version we tested, with the additional traction helping offset the new car’s weight gain.

The new generation also moved from a 3.39:1 axle ratio to a 3.44:1 axle ratio, a change that increases low-end torque at the wheels and makes the newer car somewhat punchier off the line. Lastly, the 2026 car gets a larger hybrid battery that can provide more horsepower than the smaller unit in the previous ES.

None of the changes are individually earth-shattering—especially with the extra 352 pounds of weight—but add them together, and the ES hybrid is a much quicker car than before.

Jack Fitzgerald’s love for cars stems from his as yet unshakable addiction to Formula 1. After a brief stint as a detailer for a local dealership group in college, he knew he needed a more permanent way to drive all the new cars he couldn’t afford and decided to pursue a career in auto writing. By hounding his college professors at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, he was able to travel Wisconsin seeking out stories in the auto world before landing his dream job at Car and Driver. His new goal is to delay the inevitable demise of his 2010 Volkswagen Golf.

#4339. Volvo Is Bringing Humanoid Robots Into Its Factories. Here's When They'll Start Working

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Volvo, the maker of the EX60 electric crossover, wants to replace some factory workers with humanoid robots that are capable of doing repetitive tasks without complaining about back pain.

To make that happen, the car manufacturer has brought in the first Aeon units at its factory in Ghent, Belgium, where humans are currently training them to do various tasks. Volvo said that it aims to support employees in repetitive and “ergonomically challenging work,” and it’s not the only car company that’s leaning towards replacing humans with robots.

Volvo Cars is training AEON humanoid robots for future work in factories

While fixed robotic arms have been a staple of automotive factories for decades, some brands are now investing a lot of time and money in artificial intelligence-powered robots that can do tasks where components don’t always land in the same exact spot. So-called pick-and-place jobs are gradually being taken over by robots, with Tesla, General Motors, Ford, and Rivian slowly but surely filling their factories with complex robots.

Volvo is no different, and while the first humanoids shipped to the company’s plant in Ghent are only being trained right now, they’ll gradually start going to work in real conditions starting in mid 2027, the Swedish manufacturer said.

Currently, Volvo Cars is using imitation learning to teach the robot how to pick up and place certain components into two fixtures with high precision. Through the learning process, the team will gradually make the work more challenging, adding multiple parts, moving around the production area, and interacting with the plant’s automated systems.

“Aeon’s humanoid design means it can fit into our production as it is today, alongside our teams and existing automation,” says Magnus Nilsson, Chief Manufacturing Officer at Volvo Cars. “Our aim is for humanoid robots to take on some of the most physically demanding tasks and help make work more ergonomic for our people.”

The robot chosen by Volvo looks like a human, but it doesn’t have feet. Instead, the 5.4-foot (1.65-meter) robot moves on wheels and is capable of reaching up to 5.3 miles per hour (8.6 kilometers per hour). It weighs 132 pounds (60 kilograms) and can carry up to 22 lbs (10 kg). Several cameras and sensors are used to capture its surroundings and handle parts with precision.

#4338. Zoomlion shows off SIXTY electrified, AI equipment assets at bauma 2026

Wit more than sixty (60!) new-energy models spanning everything from driverless excavators to cabless loaders and hybrid-electric mining trucks, the next generation of Zoomlion machinery is wowing everyone at bauma 2026.

Closing out a breakout year for the Chinese equipment brand, Zoomlion arrived at bauma China 2026 with more than 60 intelligent, new-energy heavy equipment options spanning eight product categories, highlighting both the company’s manufacturing prowess and establishing it as a leader in what it’s calling, “physical AI.”

And, while the company brought along a few examples of the Z01 and Z03 humanoid robots that are currently building a new equipment asset every six minutes, the real headliner was the cabless Zoomlion excavator robot shown, above.

Zoomlion says its proprietary RobotOps embodied AI operating system built around a vision-language-action (VLA) model that uses a comprehensive suite of sensors to give it “a 540-degree view” of the world around it.

Basically marketing-speak for, “better than just 360 degree camera views,” the sensors helps the Zoomlion machine correctly identify objects in a variety of conditions, determining their positions, orientations, and dimensions, then using the company’s Zbrain platform to translate that information into physical machine movements – and those movements are “just” being calculated for the excavator.

That 540-degree 3D vision system gives the autonomous excavator a much more complete picture of its surroundings, using multiple sensors to identify obstacles, understand distances, and navigate a constantly changing worksite.

The company says its intelligent Zbrain platform has been trained on millions of hours of operational data and tens of thousands of real-world scenarios, and allows Zoomlion’s autonomous machines to interpret natural-language job instructions, autonomously deconstructing complex tasks into simple step-by-step workflows before scanning the surrounding terrain, classifying the materials, and determining the right digging and gripping paths to deliver fully automate excavation, loading, slope dressing, brick paving, or material handling.

The bipedal humanoid Z01 robots will be at the show to guide visitors through the sprawling Zoomlion display, and will reportedly be using facial and gesture recognition to identify and remember individuals, while executing force-compliant motion planning and real-time obstacle avoidance to perform interactive gestures such as fist bumps and waves.

You can check out some photos of Zoomlion’s roboticized and electrified equipment display, below, then let us know what you think about someone else‘s claims about their AI and robotic sleadership status in the comments.

#4336. Volkswagen’s new ID. Buzz Beach electric camper goes on sale, starting at over $70,000

Volkswagen opened orders for the new ID. Buzz Beach in the UK, an electric van built for camping and overnight stays, with a fold-out mattress and more. It’s not exactly cheap, though, starting at over $70,000.

Volkswagen’s original microbus became a cultural icon thanks to its open, customizable interior, making it perfect for large families, road trips, camping, and, of course, music festivals.

The ID. Buzz brings the classic Type 2 microbus into the electric era with a retro-new style, modern tech, and a flexible, spacious cabin.

Building on its reputation as a symbol of freedom and adventure, Volkswagen is adding a new member to the electric people mover lineup.

The new ID. Buzz Beach “brings adventure into the electric age,” Volkswagen said after introducing the new variant on Thursday. Designed for camping, longer road trips, and overnight stays, the electric van will be available in 5-, 6-, and 7-seat configurations.

Volkswagen said it sleeps two comfortably with a removable bed frame and a custom-fitting folding mattress.

The mattress is a decent size at about 6.5 feet long by 4 feet wide (2.0m x 1.2m), roughly the size of an average small double bed.

In the 5-seat configuration, the bed frame tucks away in the trunk, while in the 6- and 7-seat layouts, it’s stored vertically behind the third row of seats.

For camping and other longer stays, Volkswagen added a new Overnight mode that uses the vehicle’s battery to provide up to 48 hours of continuous, off-grid climate control. The new mode can be accessed on the center touchscreen.

It also includes blackout curtains throughout the cabin and ventilation grilles on the front side windows.

The ID. Buzz Beach offers vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities. A 230V power socket adaptor comes standard, letting you power an e-bike, charge a smartphone, run camping equipment, or power other external electronic devices. A camping connector is available as an added option.

To top it off, Volkswagen added a hidden foldable table and chairs set that can be tucked away without taking up internal space.

Volkswagen opened orders for the new ID. Buzz Beach in the UK this week, starting at £53,955 (excluding VAT), or about $71,000. Including VAT and OTR costs, it starts at £65,837, or roughly $86,500.

Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles is offering a few financing deals to get you started, with prices from £555 ($726) a month, including a £6,500 ($8,500) deposit.

What about those in the US? Will Volkswagen bring the electric camper to the States?

Nice product at the wrong price. If VW can't lower the price because of the cost, then it has a lot more work to do to compete in this market.

VW introduced the 2027 ID. Buzz with a new Tourer model that was essentially the same as the Beach variant in the UK, with a fold-out mattress, Overnight mode, blackout curtains, and a table and chairs set.

However, VW told its US dealers in September that it would be delaying the ID. Buzz’s return until the 2028 model year.

The 2025 Volkswagen ID. Buzz started at about $60,000 in the US, which is one of the biggest reasons it failed to catch on with buyers. The original VW microbus was an affordable people mover.

A custom camper variant would likely cost more than $70,000. Would you pay $70,000 or more for Volkswagen’s electric camper van?

#4335. A Used Cybertruck Is Selling A Month Faster Than A Ford F-150

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

If you had to guess which used pickup found a buyer fastest in October, the Toyota Tacoma would be a sensible bet. It’s America’s best-selling midsize truck and has a reputation for holding its value. Or you might pick the super frugal Ford Maverick Hybrid. But the truck that beat them both was the Tesla Cybertruck.

The data from the new iSeeCars study covers 1.1 million used vehicles that changed hands in October, so this was before Tesla announced it would discontinue the Cybertruck in 2027. The study looked at one- to five-year-old vehicles and ranked models by how long they’d been listed before selling.

The Cybertruck surpassed all other pickups, averaging 39.1 days, compared to 65.5 days for used pickups overall. The Maverick Hybrid came closest at 43.3 days, followed by the Rivian R1T at 45.2 and the F-150 Lightning at 47.4. The Tacoma came in fifth position.

The gap between the two electric pickups at either end of the list was even more striking. A used Chevrolet Silverado EV took 107.5 days to sell, putting it last among the 24 trucks in the study. That’s a 68-day difference between two American electric pickups. Across the wider used market, EVs averaged about 46 days to find a buyer, around nine fewer than hybrids and 15 fewer than gas vehicles.

How quickly a used Cybertruck sold seems to have changed a lot since May 2024, when some sellers were cutting as much as $30,000 from their asking prices after listing their trucks for close to $200,000. By December of that year, we reported that used Cybertrucks were piling up on dealer lots, with data at the time showing they stayed for 75 days, up from 27 in May.

Then owners got a look at what Tesla itself would pay for a used Cybertruck trade-in. One year later, in May 2025, one owner of a $99,990 dual-motor Foundation Series truck got a trade-in estimate of $65,400 after driving it just 6,211 miles.

So even though the Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used pickup in iSeeCars’ new study, it didn’t report what buyers paid, so we don’t know whether owners got their asking price or had to lower it to sell.

Tesla will build the last Cybertrucks at the end of summer 2027, and this will reshape their used market. Elon Musk originally announced production would end around the middle of the year, but then extended the run to fill more orders. And if you order a Cybertruck now, the only one you can get is the $110,000 tri-motor Cyberbeast, so anyone who wants a less expensive dual-motor truck has to look for a used example.

Once the last new Cybertruck is sold, I’d expect collectors and everyday truck buyers to look at used ones differently. Someone after a clean Foundation Series truck with low miles might pay a little extra for one close to home, especially since it could be months before another comes up for sale nearby.

At the same time, someone who just needs an electric pickup to tow a trailer has more options. If a used dual-motor Cybertruck costs about the same as a Ford F-150 Lightning or a Rivian R1T, I suspect that buyer will care more about mileage, condition, and how much battery warranty is left than when Tesla built its last truck.

#4334. Tested: 1979 Buick Century Turbo Coupe Is a Rolling Contradiction

Buick goes after a bigger slice of the performance-image pie.

From the June 1979 issue of Car and Driver.

A paradox, according to a well­-thumbed copy of Webster’s New World, is a statement that seems contradictory, but may be true. Which brings us imme­diately to the Buick Century Turbo Coupe. On one hand it most definitely is a Buick, which is automatically a state­ment. As most of us were growing up, the Buicks in our lives belonged to the family doctor or other such community pillars. Buicks were sedate, relatively ex­pensive cars—stop-offs on the way up the GM ladder for the man with the growing bank account, or the highest reasonable aspirations for the workaday man who longed to rise out of Ford and Chevy land.

On the other hand we have this Tur­bo Coupe posturing about in its rackish, spoilered finery, squatting on its we­-mean-business fat tires, its twin pipes burbling, acting more Trans Am than Buick. A contradiction.

Buick started making out-of-character performance noises a few years ago when its chief engineer, Lloyd Reuss, and a band of enthusiastic young engi­neers decided to crank up a turbocharg­ing project for the V-6 engine. Their ef­forts were first seen in the 1975 Indy pace car, which also sported some very un-Buick-like suspension. In 1977 Buick offered a slick Sport Coupe variation on the LeSabre and Regal theme. The Le­Sabre version we tested was so good it elicited comments like “a breath of fresh air for people who’ve hungered to own a good-handling American car.” And one exuberant staffer said all it needed was a three-pointed star on the hood to make it a Mercedes-class piece. In 1978 the turbo motor went into pro­duction, and the stage was set for this year's Turbo Coupe.

See all results for used cars for sale near 37040

Bruce Robinson is a project engineer at Buick’s Flint, Michigan, headquar­ters, and one of those enthusiastic types Reuss brought in to spice up Buick’s slide-rule department. Reuss is gone now—he’s chief engineer over at Chev­rolet—but Robinson and the Reuss en­thusiasm still exist. Robinson was as­signed the Turbo Coupe. He didn’t build it single-handedly, but as much as any car that pops off the line can be said to be one man’s baby, the Turbo Coupe is his.

“We wanted to go from GT, like the LeSabre and Regal Sport Coupes, to All Out,” Robinson explains. “We wanted to make it go, and handle, and stop like no other Buick.”

He did it, he explains, by creating what Buick now calls the FE1 package, a giant step up from the existing FE2, which is Buick’s equivalent of Chevro­let’s famous F41 handling upgrade. The FE1, available only on the Turbo Coupe, is basically stiffer springs, steer­ing changes, and wider wheels. The front spring rates have been increased from the regular Sport Coupe specs of 365 pounds per inch to a giganto 440. Rear springs are up to 140 lbs/in from 125. (For further comparison, the base V-6 Century coupe has spring rates, front/rear, of 300/115.) Anti-roll bars are the same for FE1 and FE2: 32 mm front, 22 mm rear; but another big up­grade for the Turbo came in the rear upper-control-arm bushings, little de­vices we don’t think much about but which have a lot to do with transient re­sponse. The base and Sport Coupe ver­sions have bushings rated at 20,000 lbs/in; the Turbo Coupe is fitted with 35,000-lbs/in bushings. Rounding out the FE2 package is a quicker steering ra­tio, 14:1 instead of 15.13:1, and P205/70R-14 radials on seven-inch rims.

See all results for used cars for sale near 37040

But as much as we wanted to know all that good spring and tire stuff, we were even more curious about the exhaust system. It is, in a word, loud. We spent a lot of time playing with the throttle and letting off in low and second just to hear that sound-from-the-past, that Golden Oldie exhaust noise. How'd Robinson do it?

The sound, he reveals, was a specifi­cally planned part of the overall image. They got it by the simple expedient of routing the exhaust into a single con­verter and then out into a pair of ex­haust pipes that carry a resonator each. No mufflers.

“A delightful byproduct,” Robinson gleefully reveals, “was an extra ten horsepower due to the reduced back pressure.” The odds on finding ten horsepower these days without spend­ing ’leventeen trillion dollars in devel­opment are about the same as Bianca and her pals dropping by your place for dinner tonight: slim to none.

That throaty exhaust note, by the way, is more evident inside the Turbo Coupe than outside. The body acts as a sound chamber to increase the effect. “The noise level passed the EPA tests,” Robinson says, “but we’re not about to ask them to check it again to make sure.” Right.

So Robinson and his associates have built a Buick with all the right suspen­sion bits and pieces, they’ve come up with a creditable 175 horses to move it around, they’ve given it an exhaust sys­tem to warm the cockles of an old hot rodder’s heart, and they’ve dressed it up with spoilers and flat-black paint. Why, we had to wonder, after doing all that, did they leave out some traditional, mandatory even, performance-car parts, like a manual transmission and an in­strument panel with some gauges?

Adding a manual transmission would have required a complete 50,000-mile EPA durability test, and that costs hun­dreds of thousands. Ditto a different in­strument panel. Buick didn’t have any­thing on the shelf that would have bolt­ed in. Designing a new panel and tool­ing up to produce it would also have cost hundreds of thousands.

“Anything you spend on building a new model, or a new version of an exist­ing car,” Robinson explains, “you have to figure you can recover in sales.” And Buick doesn’t figure to sell too many Turbo Coupes, it turns out. It's an image car, a showroom-traffic build­er, so if you see one on the floor of your local Buick dealer, you’re probably looking at his allotment for the year. Should you jump at it?

The Turbo Coupe is easily the best-­looking of all the “aero” designs, which Buick and Olds offer in two- and four­-door versions. The improvement in looks seems to come from the simple addition of the rear-deck spoiler, which also happens to reduce overall drag, Buick reports, by a healthy 18 percent. (The two-door aero design, by the way, will be around at least through 1980; the ugly four-door is going away.)

Inside, as we’ve hinted, there is little to distinguish the Turbo Coupe from its lesser brethren. The handsome, but un­informative, instrument panel contains a tricolor turbo-boost indicator that reads out in one, A Little, and Whoosh. Our test car had vinyl buckets, and while they provide pretty good sup­port in all the right places, they are as slick as greased owl potty. Cloth is avail­able, however, and we recommend it.

Over the road, the Turbo’s yes-I-am, no-I’m-not nature surfaces again. De­spite all the good things Robinson and his merry band have wrought, the car’s manners are still rather Buick-like. Which isn’t necessarily all bad. Your teeth aren’t jarred by every tar strip, and the car is very quiet at cruise. But there is an unexpected numbness in the steering that should have been factored out. Response is good, but that all-important feel is missing.

Despite the suspension modifications, the Turbo Coupe is still an understeer­er. That’s to be expected, so no points lost there. General Motors is a firm be­liever that understeer is safer than over­steer. Better, the reasoning goes, the in­competents plow off the road nose-first, scrubbing speed all the way, than have the tail leading the procession at prodi­gious speed. Fair enough, because the knowledgeable Trans Am or Z28 driver can put the boot into his mount at the proper time and induce some very pleasant oversteer. Not so with the Tur­bo Coupe; the little engine-that-would­-be-a-V-8 just doesn’t produce enough torque quickly enough to let you play the tail-out game with much success. The boost gauge may be up there in Whoosh, but the tail will be dutifully following the furrow the front end is plowing. We’re talking about out there at the cop-baiting, wife-scaring, dog­-cowering limit, of course. In normal brisk motoring, the suspension does a good job. There’s no willow-wallow here, thank you.

The Coupe also does other good things. You’ll note that our comparison graphs show it at the top in acceleration ­and braking. Straight-line numbers will not disappoint.

The Turbo Coupe certainly has the flash and dash Buick wants for its show­rooms, and it’s sure to draw its share of peekers and pokers and hood lifters. The traditional Buick buyer will peek and poke and then head off to the Elec­tra or LeSabre four-doors. The curious that stopped off on their way to price Trans Am and Z28s will poke and peek with a good bit more interest. And when they learn they can have a bare-bones Turbo Coupe for a little more than $6000, they may even give it some seri­ous thought. But our best guess is they’ll eventually find their way back to those other showrooms. The Turbo Coupe, as good a Buick as it is, doesn’t seem to be right for either group.

What we want is Bruce Robinson and his boys to turn their attention to a new Skylark Sport Coupe. Turbo that little honey, slap the FE1 package on it, and stand back. When we suggested that to Robinson, his eyes lit up with what could only be engineer-type lust. So maybe it’ll happen. And maybe it’ll even have a tachometer.

I must admit, the first night I drove the Turbo Coupe I kept putting my foot into it and running up through the gears, then backing off and doing it again and again, all the way home. The pumped-up little six, all snarling and willing, was just too inviting for me to ignore. Sometimes I’d even drop it into low and back off just to listen to the popping of the exhaust as it simmered down. I acted as silly as a newly licensed adolescent that night, but you just can’t resist playing in the Turbo Coupe. It’s that kind of car.

But what turned me on the most was the message hidden within its sophisticat­ed mechanicals: a new generation of mus­cle cars, one that pays its respects to both ecology and our tight petroleum supply, is not only possible, it’s just around the corner. All Buick has to do is work its tur­bocharging wizardry on the half-ton-­lighter Skylark front-driver and we’ll have the first of that new breed. Let us pray. —Rich Ceppos

I happen to be a firm believer in turbo­charging and all the wonderful things it can do for our cars—David E. Davis, Jr., to the contrary—but this Turbo Coupe from Buick stretches the very heartstrings of my enthusiasm. Past the limit. It’s a horrible fate for any engine as spunky as Buick’s turbo V-6. This motor should be zapping around a 2000-pound sports car or burning the tires off Buick’s chic little Skyhawk. Instead, it’s sentenced to the homeliest hunchback sedan Buick has stamped out in recent history. Grown men wince at the sight of this TR7 garage on wheels. And I wince at the thought of such an eager engine straining its heart out against a 3500-pound curb weight and an automatic transmission, without so much as a tachometer or a boost gauge to register the effort. To finish off the in­sult, this Century’s all gussied up in what I assume is Buick’s idea of a performance disguise. It looks like something the local sheriff would use to sneak up on the kids down at Shakey's. They wouldn’t be con­vinced, and neither am I. —Don Sherman

Normally, when you dip the accelerator on a six-cylinder American car, it gives you the feeling you’re saving gas. Saving gas is a noble pastime but the feeling of saving gas is drudgery, right up there with Cometing out the sink.

That is why I think this Buick stands to give the American six-cylinder a good name. When you dip the pedal, things hap­pen. First off, the whole dashboard glows orange. (Knepper said the illumination comes from the boost light, but it’s hidden behind so many spokes and switches that I never actually saw it.) Then the exhaust turns mean and the bucket seat gets all pushy. Instead of saving gas, you get the feeling you’re hurrying.

Really, except for a count of the spark-­plug wires, there’s nothing six-cylinder about this car. It feels more like a high schooler’s hot rod, glass packs and all, and I had the urge to head on down to the drive-in and burn some rubber. I haven’t been in that mood for years. —Patrick Bedard

#4333. Volvo A40 Electric articulated haul trucks get to work in the UK

After becoming the world’s first all-electric 40 ton class articulated haul truck into regular series production earlier this year, the Volvo A40 has finally reached its first customers in the UK – and they wasted no time putting the big BEV to work on one of the nation’s largest, most important infrastructure projects.

More than sixty years after Volvo’s “Gravel Charlie” invented the articulated hauler, Volvo CE has delivered four customer A40 Electric articulated haul trucks to BMJV (a joint venture between Bouygues Travaux Publics and J Murphy & Sons) for use on the Lower Thames Crossing, further demonstrating that zero-emission machines are ready to move material at scale at major job sites right now.

“Going electric today is no longer about compromise, it’s about the benefits,” explains Shaun Pidcock, Lower Thames Crossing Programme Director at BMJV. “These remarkable machines show that even the heaviest jobs can be done cleanly, and in a way that is better for those working on or living near our sites.”

The Lower Thames Crossing project is approximately 14.3 miles long, and includes more than 2.5 miles of tunnels criss-crossing beneath the River Thames. Once finished, the project will connect the Kent and Essex meters, and promises to nearly double road capacity across the east side of London while becoming the first major infrastructure program in Britain completed with carbon-neutral construction.

By using the next generation of construction machinery to make the Lower Thames Crossing Britain’s greenest road today, we are helping the industry set a new standard for tomorrow and make diesel-powered sites a thing of the past.

Since grid power isn’t available on site, BMJV is using fuel cell generators fueled by British-manufactured green hydrogen to charge the A40s. The generators produce no exhaust emissions and are noticeably quieter than combustion machines, further improving living and working conditions for the humans around the site.

The “40” in the A40 Electric’s badge refers to the truck’s whopping 40 ton (39 tonne) payload capacity. Once loaded up, the hauler’s 350 kW (about 470 hp) electric motor sends power through a torque-amplifying gear reduction gearbox that, depending on how you do the math, delivers some 200,000 lb-ft of “at the wheel” torque. More than enough twisting force, in other words, to match the performance of diesel and possibly enough to have a measurable impact on the rotational speed of a planet.

That motor draws power from a 540 kWh li-ion battery good for up to six hours of continuous operation, but the hauler’s advanced regenerative braking system usually collects enough energy during operation to make it good for a full day’s shift. And, if there’s a Circle K nearby, operators can plug their A40 Electric into a 350 kW DC fast charger and get their battery from 10% to 90% in about an hour.

Rivian is discounting dozens of items in its online Gear Shop as part of a Winter Sale event that runs through December 4. The California startup is offering chargers, accessories, and apparel at prices that are between 15% and 30% lower than usual.

Charging equipment is front and center. The company’s hardwired wall chargers, which are capable of delivering up to 11.5 kilowatts either through a NACS or J1772 connector, can be had for $680, down from the regular $800. The Rivian Portable Charger with a NACS connector, which plugs into a household outlet and can deliver up to 7.6 kW, is now $340, $60 cheaper than usual.

Next up are charging adapters. The Gen 1 R1S and R1T came from the factory with a CCS1 charging port, so they need an adapter to top up at NACS-equipped chargers. Meanwhile, the R2 and Gen 2 R1 EVs have a NACS port, so they need an adapter to use CCS1-equipped stalls. Over the course of the Winter Sale, Rivian’s NACS and Combo CCS1 DC adapters are discounted to $170, down from $200.

The portable outdoor Travel Kitchen, which has two induction burners, an output of up to 1,500 watts, a cutting board, and a slide-out drawer, is now $1,190, down 15% from the usual $1,400 selling price.

Crossbars are also on sale, with a set of R1 or R2 bars starting at $595, down from $700. A set of all-weather floor mats for the R1T or R2 now costs $192, down from $225, while an R1S set goes for $213, down from $250.

Bundles get lower prices, too. For instance, an R2 protection bundle, which includes a windshield sunshade, a set of all-weather floor mats, and a protection film for the digital instrument cluster, has been discounted from $390 to $332.

Apparel can be had for cheap, with discounts as high as 58%. For instance, an Adventure Shirt is now $50, down from $120, while a T-Shirt is 50% cheaper than before, and a hat is $25, down from $35.

Rivian hasn’t included any of its vehicles in the Winter Sale promotion, but it is offering some discounts separately. Customers who order any new R1 vehicle between November 27 and November 30 get a $1,000 discount. Furthermore, some 2026 R1s can be financed at 1.99% APR.
