#4331. Respect Your Elders: The London to Brighton Car Tour, Michigan Style

We leave behind launch control and triple digits to experience slow thrills.

From the November/December 2026 issue of Car and Driver.

More than double that if you count New Londons. There are about 30 Brightons, which I think means there are somewhere around 700 ways one could set up a London-to-Brighton antique-car run. Which, of course, is a totally normal thing to plan, right?

Maybe a few of you with an interest in early automobiles recognize the combination of London and Brighton from the long-running English vintage-car meet that travels between those two cities every November. First run in 1896 by an intrepid group of early—very early—car enthusiasts, the Emancipation Run was held to mark one of the first increases in speed limits: from single digits (4 mph) to a downright scorching 14 mph.

The London-to-Brighton event, or, as it’s now known, the RM Sotheby’s London to Brighton Veteran Car Run, looks like fun, so we decided to have a go between our own London and Brighton in Michigan with some antique American cars.

See all results for used cars for sale near 29405

Several things lined up well. Our course between London Township and the cute main street of Brighton was 57 miles, which is a good parallel to the U.K.’s 97-km (60-mile) route. Plenty of tree-lined country lanes connect the towns, a benefit when organizing a road trip for vehicles whose max speed may be more than 14 mph but still lags behind modern highway pace. Most important, there’s a fantastic community of early-20th-century-car collectors in Michigan, so finding folks who were willing to take out their Fords, Oldsmobiles, Pullmans, and REOs was no problem.

What was a problem was finding a date. Every time I suggested a weekend, I’d get a flurry of texts and emails from the would-be participants. “So sorry,” said Mark Turner. “There’s a steam-car rally that weekend.” It might have also been Turner who couldn’t do another date because of a meet for vintage Bentleys. “I don’t know if I could do June 6th because we have an HCCA [Horseless Carriage Club of America] tour down in Georgia,” said Brent Terry, with apologies. Eventually, I just picked something and hoped a few of the crew would manage to fit it into their busy, brassy schedules.

An 1865 regulation required a flagger with a red warning cloth to walk ahead of any roadgoing mechanical vehicles and limited their max speed to just 4 mph on turnpikes and highways and 2 mph in cities, towns, and villages in the United Kingdom. The law was initially intended to apply to steam-powered road locomotives, which were growing in popularity in England and threatening traditional railways. As cars entered the chat, drivers chafed at the restrictions. An 1896 act of Parliament brought that speed limit up to 14 mph and was thus celebrated by English motoring clubs with a 60-mile rally, an annual tradition now under the 60-mile-long name of RM Sotheby’s London to Brighton Veteran Car Run.

See all results for used cars for sale near 29405

Michigan being Michigan, the day before our run brought pouring rain. It turns out vintage-car people are shockingly willing to brave weather. “I believe it rains a lot in England,” said Rick Lindner. So, we showed up, as did eight shining examples of the earliest entries in American motoring, from a 1904 Ford Model AC owned by Lindner to a late-model 1913 Buick Model 31 helmed by Larry and Joyce Schramm. On the Car and Driver side, we brought doughnuts, passengers, and a lot of questions about old cars.

After the third time I asked someone for the cubic-inch displacement of their engine, John Grace (who organizes his own vintage-car run in the fall and lent his 1911 Regal to teenage brothers Jonathan and Matthew Sinclair for our tour, and whose wife, Dorothy, once drove a Model T across America, making either one of the Graces very qualified to tell me what’s what in prewar car stuff) shook his head. He told me that while he can go look it up for me, owners of cars from this era don’t generally describe their engines in displacement. “We measure in horsepower,” he said. “I never hear anybody ask about cubic inches for early cars.”

It makes sense. In the modern era, cubic inches tend to reflect power output, but back in the days when a Curved Dash Oldsmobile might have a single jug measuring 95 cubic inches and making only four horsepower, it was more useful to announce your car’s 30 horsepower than, say, its 200 cubic inches.

Grace answered this, and all my other questions, with thoughtful enthusiasm, which is something I noticed about all the antique-car people I met that day.

“The older the cars, the nicer the people,” said Larry Schramm. For the hobby to have a future, he said, it needs younger people to ask questions and learn how to drive these cars. Plus, “we’re all in the same boat.” If your car isn’t the one broken on this run, it might be on the next.

Antique-car drives are a bit like off-roading; it’s best to go in pairs so someone can pick you up and get you to the finish. That happened to Ted O’Dell, when his 1913 Buick Model 31 started running a temperature. When I talked to him about it, he was unbothered. Breakdowns are just a part of the process, as they were when the cars were new. It’s historically accurate to get a flat tire.

Even though I’d invited people through different contacts, most of the participants knew one another. Many of these owners have multiple cars, maybe a big four-door for longer tours and a Model T for local runabouts. They loan one another parts and cars and smudgy business cards for the one place that still sells horsehair upholstery stuffing.

We all gathered in a parking lot across the street from Darana Dragway. The vehicle owners hunched over crank starters to coax engines into action amid a chorus of grunts and pops, both mechanical and human. Clouds of tire smoke drifted over from the drag-strip side as smooth-bodied race machines revved big V-8s to numbers that would reduce our two- and four-cylinders to steaming puddles of Babbitt. As an example of divergent evolution, it was stark, but a show of mutual interest implied that while the bodies and power outputs were different, there was a shared soul among us.

Once our great eight were puffing and clattering, we left the dragsters behind in our own clouds of smoke (oil, not tire). I rode in David Liepelt’s 1915 Model T Ford at the head of the line. For Liepelt and his T, this marks a return to C/D. They were the stars of our Model T versus Model S story back in February 2014, and Liepelt is still mad that then–tech director Don Sherman beat his Ford in a Tesla, so we let him lead the tour.

Liepelt set off at a pace that would have shaken the drivers of 1896. He was all limbs, pulling the throttle lever back to full acceleration, upping the spark advance, rocking the gear-selecting pedal into high, and adjusting his Ruckstell two-speed axle. It was like watching an octopus drive a car. I had to tell him to slow down to make sure we didn’t leave anyone behind. It’s impressive what 22 horsepower is capable of, and while acceleration wasn’t going to be the challenge, nobody in the early 1900s was much for a panic stop. “Not good, but better than nothing,” Liepelt said as he barreled through an Ann Arbor intersection. If we were braking, I wasn’t aware. A line in my notebook reads, “It’s a very specific thrill to be in a car you could fall out of.”

Thinking of joining the antiques road show? Here’s what to buy.

Affordability was a theme among the group, which may come as a surprise to people who’ve grown up hearing terms like “Brass Era” and “prewar” only in relation to megabuck Bugattis and Duesenbergs on concours lawns. Those cars still command big prices, but more common brands have come down as older owners die and pass on to their family a garage full of acetylene headlamps and wood-spoke wheels. Our group was unanimous in suggesting a Model T as a gateway drug, including lensman James Lipman, who is now on his second T purchase (the first is shown above).

“The Brass Era ones may be worth $15,000 to $20,000,” said T owner Brent Allen. “But you can pick up a running T for sometimes $7000, $8000 easily.” Learning to drive a Model T is a challenge, but Allen said that shouldn’t put anyone off. Other owners will be eager to teach you, and there are so many reproduction parts. If you have a frame and an engine block, you can build a whole car from catalogs.

That thrill was a recurring theme. It’s the caress of wind in your hair like the first time you rode a bicycle. It’s the nervy pleasure of sitting the canter on a horse. It’s the very real possibility that you’ll never be able to stop. In a world where most cars can hit 100 mph before the end of an on-ramp, it’s amazing how exciting 35 mph can be when it takes all your extremities and maybe one or two of your passenger’s to keep the vehicle out of the nearest hedge.

For Jonathan Sinclair, the youngest of our drivers at 16, learning on a vintage car ruined him for modern transportation. When he was told that he couldn’t take the driver’s test in the family Model T, his mom had to force him to do his remaining training hours in a newer car. “I don’t feel anything!” he complained. “After the involved process of driving an older car, you get in a modern car, and suddenly you don’t have to worry about anything. It feels odd.” He and his brother, Matthew, had been planning to bring their own project, a 1911 Brush, but then the Graces offered them the key to the Regal.

Our summer intern, Alayna Wilkening, joined the Sinclair brothers in the Regal, where she was given the job of watching the MotoMeter hood ornament for signs of overheating. Her official report was they experienced no difficulties aside from having to explain to multiple onlookers that the Regal was a Regal but not a Buick.

Behind them, senior news editor Caleb Miller was riding in luxurious and secure comfort, cushioned in the azure-blue cabin of Daniel Coffman’s 1910 Pullman. I noticed with no small amount of jealousy that he had a nice sturdy roof support bar to hold on to in the turns. His post-run report was that his desire to purchase a vehicle of this vintage has only increased with each exposure. He also rode back with Liepelt and declared the trip “probably the most exhilarating 53 mph I’ve ever experienced.”

Editor-in-chief Tony Quiroga was spared the terror of Liepelt’s sporty T, instead getting the full touring-car experience in Wes Raynard’s flashy red 1909 Oldsmobile Model X3, which cost about $2000 when it was new. “This is the only one known to still exist,” Raynard told me. A quick look at past auction prices shows that the cherry Olds changed hands earlier this year for $55,105, which is considerably more than its original purchase price but a downright bargain to own a one-of-one survivor.

“The ride is so smooth,” Quiroga told me at our rest stop. He looked mildly disappointed that things were going so well. “I was expecting the adventure to be more adventurous. All of these enthusiasts know their cars so well that they could tear down the entire thing and rebuild it on the side of the road. Only everything is working, and we’re ahead of schedule.”

Despite Quiroga’s desire for more chaos, the overall consensus was that the inaugural C/D London-to-Brighton (Michigan) was a great success, and the gang plans to do it again in 2027. Barring any conflicts with the steam-car rally.

Like a sleeper agent activated late in the game, Elana Scherr didn’t know her calling at a young age. Like many girls, she planned to be a vet-astronaut-artist, and came closest to that last one by attending UCLA art school. She painted images of cars, but did not own one. Elana reluctantly got a driver’s license at age 21 and discovered that she not only loved cars and wanted to drive them, but that other people loved cars and wanted to read about them, which meant somebody had to write about them. Since receiving activation codes, Elana has written for numerous car magazines and websites, covering classics, car culture, technology, motorsports, and new-car reviews. In 2020, she received a Best Feature award from the Motor Press Guild for the C/D story "A Drive through Classic Americana in a Polestar 2."  In 2023, her Car and Driver feature story "In Washington, D.C.'s Secret Carpool Cabal, It's a Daily Slug Fest" was awarded 1st place in the 16th Annual National Arts & Entertainment Journalism Awards by the Los Angeles Press Club.

#4329. This Audi E-Tron EV Has 125,000 Miles. Replacing Its Battery Was A Huge Pain

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Electric car batteries are known to last far longer than people often believe, but as always, there are outliers. This particular 2020 Audi e-tron Sportback is one of them, with its traction battery biting the dust after covering roughly 125,000 miles. The rest of the car is in great shape, but the dead battery meant that it couldn’t go anywhere, so Alex from Out of Spec Renew took on the job of replacing the pack.

The first step was to find out what actually caused the battery to fail. After a bit of digging in the diagnostics software, one module reported it had a 0% state of charge, yet the voltage reading was maxed out. A dozen other modules also reported voltage inconsistencies, sealing the fate of the unit.

A replacement battery from a crash-damaged EV that had roughly 30,000 miles on the clock was chosen as a swap-in replacement, and the work began to remove the dead pack. Like on most EVs, it was a fairly straightforward job, but when it came to installing the replacement unit, some minor problems transformed the whole thing into a multi-day affair. The replacement pack was slightly damaged at one corner, which compromised the seal.

As a result, the top lids had to be transferred from the dead battery to the replacement battery, which was quite the pain. A coolant fitting and the pyro fuse were also transferred, as they were also damaged.

But the job was far from over. After buttoning everything up, the car wouldn’t start because its brain wouldn’t authorize the replacement components, which had stored crash codes from the dismantled vehicle.

Alex tried to sort things out on his own, but ultimately external help was called in to program all of the replacement parts and convince them that they’re in the right place. With that done, a job that should have taken one or two days to complete needed nearly a week of labor and came with some unexpected extra costs.

All that being said, the car now works perfectly fine and should keep on going for many more miles.

#4328. Toyota’s Hyper Z Prototype Is So Extreme, It Has Aerodynamic Wings Instead of a Bed

Built as a nod to Thailand’s crazy pickup-truck customization scene, this one-off is maximum Hilux.

Even though Toyota’s Hilux pickup truck is not sold on this side of the Pacific, most people have a pretty good idea about what it represents. Thanks to the antics in Top Gear in which they were drowned, blown up, and even set on fire, the Hilux has a reputation for being rugged to the point of near indestructibility. What you don’t expect is for them to be fast.

Of course, things are completely different in Southeast Asia, especially in Thailand. There, a pickup truck isn’t just a rough-and-tumble tool for work, it’s also a canvas for personal expression. Thai customizers turn their trucks into insane builds that would rival anything you’d find at Daikoku Parking Area in Japan or on the floor in Vegas at SEMA.

See all results for used cars for sale near 97023

To put an exclamation point on the launch of its new Hilux Travo Z Edition, Toyota turned to its Australian design department. Said department reacted, to use the proper antipodean expression, by going off like a frog in a sock, building a Hilux that’s so crazy it’s not even really a pickup truck any more.

The Hyper Z prototype features massively wide bodywork that struggles to contain 325/35 series tires on 22-inch wheels, and more aerodynamic elements than a small regional airport. There’s a table-sized front splitter, a diffuser out back, ground effects tucked under the body, and a park bench of a wing out back.

Also out back, an X-shaped wing that occupies the entirety of the pickup truck’s bed. Planning a run to your local DIY center? Whatever you’re picking up better fit in the glovebox.

The standard Hilux Travo is powered by a 2.4-liter turbo-diesel engine good for 150 horsepower, but despite what looks like a huge Hilux-branded intercooler here, Toyota didn’t put any power numbers on the prototype. It’s more a love letter to Thailand’s custom truck culture, showing what can be done rather than what should be done.

Perhaps of more interest in a practical sense is how Toyota positions its Hilux in this market. Overseas, the truck is offered in both a high-floor and low-floor model, the latter riding low so that it is easier to load and unload for practical working conditions.

Conversely, in the U.S. market, pickups of all sizes have never been taller, which you’ll notice as soon as you need to load them up. Could Toyota successfully market a low-floor Tacoma model, one that’s a little easier to live with for commercial applications?

Either way, the Hyper Z Prototype is a cool way to shine a light on a slice of automotive culture that’s specific to a region. If you thought authentic Thai green curry was hot, just check out how spicy the country likes its pickup trucks.

#4326. EVs Outsold Gas And Diesel Cars Combined In The EU In October

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

The European Union registered about 24,000 more new cars last month than in October 2025. Fully electric cars alone added more than 106,000 to the tally, while sales of gasoline-only cars fell by nearly 30% and diesel sales dropped by 31%.

According to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), the EU registered 279,799 fully electric passenger cars in October, marking a significant year-over-year jump of 61.4%. Gasoline cars accounted for 158,970 registrations, and diesels added another 51,177.

This means that for every three new gas or diesel cars that hit EU roads last month, roughly four new EVs joined them. ACEA counts hybrids separately, including mild hybrids with a gasoline or diesel engine.

One year ago, in October 2025, the big news was that plug-in hybrids had overtaken diesel through the first ten months across the EU, UK and European Free Trade Association (EFTA) markets. Within the EU itself, fully electric cars still accounted for just 16.4% of registrations over that period. Even in October alone, gasoline cars comfortably outsold EVs, even before you added diesels.

Then came December 2025, when EVs outsold gasoline cars across the EU for the first time. By the third quarter of 2026, EVs had passed gas and diesel combined. The margin back then was about 55,000 cars across July, August and September. In October, EVs cleared that margin in a single month.

Significant EV sales growth in Germany and France explains much of the jump. Between them, they saw about 69,500 more electric car registrations than in October 2025, accounting for nearly two-thirds of the EU’s increase.

In Germany, more than 94,000 new EVs hit the road in October, making up 37% of the country’s new-car market that month. France registered nearly 62,000 EVs, enough to outsell conventional hybrids, which accounted for about 55,400 cars.

The same shift looks rather different in Romania. EV registrations rose almost 47% in October even as the overall car market shrank. That was enough for electric cars to beat gasoline cars by just seven registrations, 1,495 to 1,488. Add diesels back in and combustion still wins. Meanwhile, Romanians registered more than 6,600 conventional hybrids, comfortably ahead of either.

This reflects a broader trend across the EU, where hybrids remain the most popular choice. Full and mild hybrids accounted for 36% of registrations through October, against 23.4% for fully electric cars. Gas and diesel also retain a combined lead so far this year. What’s changed is how small that lead has become. At this point last year, gas and diesel together outsold EVs by more than two to one.

Ten months into 2026, the tally stands at 2.62 million to 2.21 million, and the most recent month went decisively to the cars with a plug and no engine.

The number of electric models on offer in Europe grew by about half in a year, and many of the new additions were small and affordable models. Buyers shopping for a small hatchback now have the Renault 5, Cupra Raval and Volkswagen ID. Polo to choose from.

Actually getting one is another matter. VW has reportedly taken more than 50,000 ID. Polo orders, with German buyers facing wait times of up to 21 months for the cheapest version.

#4325. Dually Noted: The Reasons Why Some Pickup Trucks and Vans Come with Dual Rear Wheels

Dually pickup trucks and vans may look tough, but these models have four rear wheels and tires for reasons that have nothing to do with vanity.

The term “dual rear wheels,” as applied to full-size pickup trucks and vans, raises as many questions as it answers. Namely, one: Don’t all vehicles have two rear wheels? Good work, detective. The dual part, however, refers to the number of rear wheels on each side. Confusing? Sure. But consider yourself a member of an elite club. Send away for your decoder ring now.

You’ll often see so-equipped vehicles referred to in official specs or on a build sheet as DRW, as opposed to single-rear-wheel (SRW) pickups and vans. Out in the real world, you’re likely to observe dually pickups towing big, heavy trailers, often using a gooseneck or fifth-wheel hitch.

DRW vans are usually the longest and tallest, used for both cargo and passenger hauling. Simply put, DRW vehicles are meant to handle big loads.

Automakers go the DRW route on configurations of their heavy-duty trucks and vans designed for hauling and/or towing heavy loads. Having those extra tires means more contact patch over which to distribute the weight. It’s the same basic principle that’s used on semi trucks—having 18 or so wheels spread across the semi tractor and its trailer allows the rig to carry literal tons.

See all results for used cars for sale near 37040

On dually trucks, the wider stance helps increase stability as well. You can think of the two extra wheels like outriggers, keeping the truck better planted in the face of crosswinds or in turns.

The main drawbacks of a dually setup are somewhat obvious. You have to worry about six tires instead of four, which in turn makes tire replacement more expensive. For dually trucks, the extra wheels sit outside the normal pickup-bed envelope, necessitating flared fenders to cover the extra rubber.

Maneuvering a big SRW truck or van is difficult enough. Predictably, the additional width of a DRW vehicle only adds to the challenge. It’s why many dually trucks end up with a blemish or two on at least one rear fender. The fenders of newer dually pickups are made from lighter-weight fiberglass instead of steel, so they’re less likely to bend and more prone to cracking when they meet a stationary object.

This isn’t the case with most dually full-size vans. So-equipped vans add their additional tires inboard, which eliminates the need for flared rear fenders. The consequence of this arrangement is a slight reduction in outright cargo space due to the wheel wells extending further into the cabin.

Ever wonder why the front wheels of a dually truck or van have a severe outward dish to them? It’s so that all the wheels match and are therefore interchangeable should you need to use the spare. This dished design allows the rear wheels on one side to mate up with each other, which enables the use of two rear tires on both sides of the vehicle.

See all results for used cars for sale near 37040

The need for a dually comes down to capability. DRWs may be necessary to comfortably pull a fully laden horse trailer, a giant camper, various types of farm equipment, or the crops they help sow and reap. To get an idea of how much more a dually can handle, an SRW heavy-duty truck may be rated for a little more than 20,000 pounds of trailer weight on a bumper-mounted hitch, while the DRW variant of the same basic truck with a gooseneck hitch can pull almost twice the weight.

The difference isn’t as great with dual-rear-wheel versus SRW vans, mostly because both use bumper-mounted hitches. A DRW van may be able to tow as much as 50 percent more weight than a comparable SRW version. With some vans, towing capacity actually goes down when you add two rear wheels. Why go the dually route, then? Because that extra rubber is advantageous to rear-end stability—particularly when a van’s loaded up at, or near, its maximum payload capacity.

Dually setups are available on heavy-duty versions of full-size pickups and some large vans. Those looking for a pickup truck with a bed can choose this setup on the Chevrolet Silverado HD, GMC Sierra HD, Ram HD, and Ford F-series Super Duty.

In the realm of enclosed passenger and cargo vans, only the Ford Transit and Mercedes-Benz Sprinter offer available DRW configurations. You’ll also often find DRWs in use on cutaway and chassis-cab versions of these trucks and vans, which are used in the aftermarket to build things such as box trucks, tow trucks, and RVs.

In some international markets, where full-size pickups are much less common, automakers produce DRW versions of their sub-full-size pickups.

As with any towing or hauling exercise, make sure you understand the limits of your specific vehicle before loading it up or hitching a trailer to the back. Consider what you’re likely to tow or haul when shopping for your workhorse, and follow the manufacturer’s guidance on loading so you stay safe and avoid putting too much strain on the vehicle.

Dually is a term used for a pickup truck or van with dual rear wheels (DRW).

A dually pickup truck or van has two wheels and tires on each side of its rear axle for a grand total of four rear wheels and tires.

You do not need a CDL to drive a full-size pickup truck or an enclosed cargo or passenger van with dual rear wheels (DRWs).

Pedants will note that even a rear-wheel-drive dually relies on its engine to power four wheels (the four back ones). In a technical sense, however, a rear-drive dually is a two-wheel-drive vehicle, since power is sent to the drive wheels via two axle shafts. Similarly, though a four-wheel-drive-equipped dually may power a total of six wheels, the engine’s power only reaches the drive wheels via a total of four axle shafts (two at each end).

#4324. Ford’s Next Le Mans Dream Is Finally Here: Meet the GT41

FoMoCo’s latest race car was built with one goal in mind: Get back on the top step of the Le Mans podium.

You’re probably aware that all the way back in 1963, Ford tried (unsuccessfully) to buy Ferrari from old Enzo. “Il Commendatore” quite famously used the offer to secure a better deal for himself with Fiat, angering and embarrassing “The Deuce” to the point that Ford wrote a blank check to beat Ferrari at the 24 Hours of Le Mans. While Ford achieved its goal in 1966, it seems the company still holds something of a grudge. Meet the Ford GT41, the new Hypercar that Ford is hoping will put it back on the top step at Le Mans.

See all results for used Ford for sale near 75062

The GT41 gets its name because, you guessed it, the air intake at the top of the car measures 41 inches above the ground. Well, technically, the GT41 stands at 41.7 inches tall, but Ford executives told Car and Driver that they preferred the sound of GT41 over GT41.7, and they had no interest in rounding up.

The GT41’s power is naturally aspirated, of course; this is an American race team, after all, though it is mated to a hybrid system as required by regulations. Still, the combustion part of the equation is handled by a Coyote V-8 engine that has been bored to 5.4 liters and developed in-house by Ford Racing engineers.

Despite a fair amount of grandstanding about how proudly American this program is—note the American flag, eagle, football, and Statue of Liberty graphics in the livery, along with timing the reveal to take place during the Detroit Lions game on the distinctly American holiday known as Thanksgiving—Ford still won’t commit to racing the GT41 in IMSA, here in North America. The final race livery will be revealed ahead of the 2027 WEC season’s opening race in Qatar, which will take place in March.

#4323. BMW Alpina Will Debut with a Sedan and SUV, but There’s More to Come

Along with gas-fed and electric versions of the B7 and XB7, an avant-garde two-door flagship and a V-12 are in the works.

Alpina returns next year under new ownership with the newly minted BMW Alpina 7-series-based B7 (G72) and the X7-based XB7, both in internal-combustion and electric form. While the sedan will be a four-seater unless you insist on a rear bench, the SUV comes with three rows and six seats standard, according to our inside sources.

Naturally, BMW Alpina buyers can choose from a wealth of fancy options, such as two-tone paint, gradient colors, a mix of matte and glossy shades, a choice of different wheel designs, variable-tint windows and glass roofs, bespoke lighting scenarios, and fully automatic remote-control doors. Alpina blue and green remain the traditional trademark hues. Both models will feature a fully adjustable, comfort-oriented, specially tuned adaptive suspension. Also, in the B7, a reprogrammed ECU will permit a higher top speed of over 186 mph.

BMW Alpina’s model line should read like this: B7 40, B7 60 and iB7 70. The same gas-fed engines—a turbocharged 3.0-liter straight-six with around 400 horsepower and a twin-turbo 4.4-liter V-8 rated at up to 600 horsepower—will be offered in the XB7, which boasts a bigger battery and more grunt in the fully electric iXB7 Alpina 100.

See all results for new 2029 BMW Alpina B7 for sale near 77429

What happened to the rumoured Alpina V-12, you ask? It’s still in the cards, but insiders don’t expect it to come to market anytime soon. The wait revolves around a life-cycle extension, a possible second facelift, and the late arrival of the new convergence platform dubbed CLAR Flex. But let’s start at the beginning. The current 7-series (G70), launched in 2022, was updated earlier this year and was due to be phased out in 2029, but this plan has apparently changed. Because of financial constraints and reduced demand, it now looks like the 7 must soldier on through 2032, which would stretch its lifespan to 10 years.

The follow-up, internally known as CF0, will likely be based on the CLAR Flex architecture, which reportedly offers significant weight, packaging, and cost advantages. The first model to tap this advanced matrix is said to be the next 5-series (codenamed CE0), which is scheduled to debut in 2031. CLAR Flex not only fuses pure-gas, plug-in hybrid, extended-range EVs, and fully electric elements in a superior, scalable manner, but it could also accommodate that coveted V-12 as one of the group’s few remaining upmarket unique selling points.

The Alpina brand launches next year, so by 2028, all markets should be able to sell all versions of both models. In terms of volume, we’re still talking low five figures here. Come 2029, the marque could do with an image boost for what’s next, which will almost certainly be at least one more new product.

If it gets the nod, the new B5 would, of course, also be based on CLAR Flex, which automatically puts the launch date back to 2031, at the earliest. Since the B05 GT costs close to the equivalent of roughly $220,000 before options, a B5 could be an attainable stepping stone for those who cannot quite afford the B7. On the other hand, a B3 is too small, not sufficiently prestigious, and not profitable enough. If it happens at all, we can only imagine it will be very low volume.

Although I was born the only son of an ornithologist and a postal clerk, it was clear from the beginning that birdwatching and stamp collecting were not my thing. Had I known that God wanted me to grow to 6’8", I also would have ruled out anything to do with cars, which are to blame for a couple of slipped discs, a torn ligament, and that stupid stooped posture behind the wheel. While working as a keeper in the Aberdeen Zoo, smuggling cheap cigarettes from Yugoslavia to Germany, and an embarrassing interlude with an amateur drama group also failed to yield fulfillment, driving and writing about cars became a much better option. And it still is now, many years later, as I approach my 70th birthday. I love every aspect of my job except long-haul travel on lousy airlines, and I hope it shows.

#4322. AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover

Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A new study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.

For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.

But the new findings raise an important question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?

"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a new study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity."

A New Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI

The York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.

If these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.

"Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," says Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.

The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.

Their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.

AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story

The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.

AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.

This difference was particularly revealing because the researchers did not observe the same problem when comparing neuronal activity across different brains.

"The results were striking. While AI models can predict the neurons we recorded in the brain fairly well, the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. Interestingly, this is not the case when neurons from one brain is compared against ones from another brain," says Kar.

The findings suggest that an AI system can produce results that closely resemble those of the brain while relying on very different internal mechanisms. In other words, matching the brain's responses does not necessarily mean that the underlying processes are the same.

Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence advances. If researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences between those models and actual primate brains could accumulate over time.

That would undermine one of the main reasons neuroscientists use these systems in the first place: to develop realistic explanations of how the brain works.

"The findings suggest that today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. Importantly, the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior," says Kar.

Why the Discovery Matters for Neuroscience and Human Behavior

The implications extend well beyond computer vision. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Many of these applications depend on the assumption that AI models process information in ways that resemble the human brain.

If that assumption is incorrect, researchers could draw misleading conclusions from models that appear accurate on the surface but operate differently underneath.

"Our findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. We show that models that were previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use. We provide a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field," says Muzellec.

Developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism. For now, however, the newly identified differences highlight the need for caution when using existing models to investigate human behavior or guide clinical research.

The concern may also apply to other areas of neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. If those systems also rely on internal processes that differ from biological ones, researchers may need to reconsider how much they can reveal about the nervous system.

Building AI That More Closely Matches the Human Brain

Rather than suggesting that artificial neural networks should be abandoned, the findings provide a way to make them more useful and scientifically reliable.

By identifying which features of an AI model correspond to real neural activity, researchers can focus on developing systems that more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms behind perception.

"Our approach helps identify which parts of an ANN truly match brain activity, allowing us to build more reliable models for understanding how people see and interpret the world," says Kar. "This is especially important for our autism research program, which builds on models of the neurotypical brain as a baseline."

A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical. Establishing accurate models of these patterns is important for researchers investigating how perception and information processing may differ in conditions such as autism.

To help other scientists put their findings into practice, the team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement.

Published in Nature Machine Intelligence, the study introduces a new approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as important.

The discovery could help guide the development of a new generation of AI models that not only recognize the world with impressive accuracy, but also offer a more faithful picture of how the human brain makes sense of what it sees.

#4321. Where Does the Chevy Blazer SS EV Fit in Chevrolet’s SS History?

See our list of worthy and unworthy SS models to find out.

I recently spent some time driving a 2026 Chevy Blazer EV SS, and the experience got me thinking about where Chevy’s electric family hot rod fits in the history of SS-badged machines. Chevy established the Super Sport trim in the 1960s with some legendary cars (Impala, Chevelle, Camaro, Nova) and then applied it scattershot over the decades, with some latter-day SS models worthy of the heritage and others an exercise in credibility dilution.

I am a self-appointed expert on which SS models rocked, and which ones should have been an RS at best (in high school, we all knew RS stood for Really Slow). So here are my SS rankings, grouped by Worthy of the Name and Should Have Been an RS. Fun fact: One SS was both.

I drove a Camaro SS 1LE at Carolina Motorsports Park for our How Fast Does Your Car Have to Be to Outrun a Cop? story. Our cop-evading candidates also included a Ferrari 488 GTB, and while the Ferrari was the quickest car of the day, the Camaro wasn’t as far behind as you might expect. It’s also possible that I just felt more comfortable pushing a Camaro than I did a Ferrari, but the SS 1LE remains the track-rat bargain of this century. I still want one.

See all results for new 2026 Chevrolet Blazer for sale near 90036

One of my high school hobbies was cadging test drives at car dealerships. Maybe I should have felt bad about wasting dealers’ time, but on some level I believed that I might actually buy whatever car I was begging for a drive. And I was arriving in my IROC, which was presentable enough to imply at least some trade-in value. I drove plenty of cars—the second-generation Ford Probe GT with its frisky V-6 was a pleasant surprise—but I did get shut down whenever I exceeded the threshold of deal-signing plausibility that was assigned when I rolled onto a given lot. That’s what happened when I asked to drive a 1994 Impala SS that was in the showroom of a local car dealer. I vividly remember what the salesman told me: “If everyone drives it, nobody buys it.” Instead, he gave me the keys to a Monte Carlo SS. I was amazed that a car with a similar engine to mine (the ubiquitous Chevy 5.0) could be so much slower. “Someday, I’ll write a story about how not all Chevys deserve an SS badge,” I probably didn’t say. But let’s imagine I did. What a perceptive lad!

I still haven’t driven a bubble-Caprice Impala SS. But I continue to revere them. They’re like a cop car, but cooler!

Speaking of cop-cars-but-cooler, the Chevy SS was the civilian version of the contemporary Caprice, and it was like Chevy’s version of an E39 BMW M5, complete with 415 horsepower and an available manual transmission. Of course, just right is never enough, so we had Lingenfelter Performance Engineering bolt on a supercharger before I took an SS on a multi-state investigation of the history of bootlegging. Sliding that car around on dirt roads out in moonshine country was so much fun I almost forgot I had a job to do. Which may or may not have involved bringing some things in the trunk back to Michigan. I get amnesia when I try to recall any details about that, but the SS—that I remember, and fondly. If you want one, maybe don’t wait too long, because the SS secret is out, based on what I see lurking on Bring a Trailer.

See all results for new 2026 Chevrolet Blazer for sale near 90036

I’ve never driven a Chevelle SS, but when we had one in a comparison test, it sounded like it was a royal handful. A 13.81-second quarter-mile at 102 mph isn’t super quick now, but consider that the first 500 feet of that run was probably devoted to wheelspin management as the 7.4-liter, 450-hp (gross-rated) V-8 abused the primitive tires of the day.

Of the Chevelle’s brakes, Sam Posey said, “While they’re working, they are predicta­ble.”

The Cobalt SS was a sneaky performance car when it debuted with a supercharged, 205-hp four-cylinder in 2005, and later got a 260-hp turbocharged upgrade. Chevy also built it in naturally aspirated form (hold that thought). This was around the time when GM started to figure out the concept of handling, and the Cobalt SS’s excellent all-around performance prompted me to conjure an unlikely contest in 2006. The premise: I race against Dale Earnhardt, Jr., around a tight road course at the Charlotte Motor Speedway infield. He’d get a Cobalt SS. And I’d get a 505-hp Corvette Z06. I beat him, but not for his lack of trying—he pushed that Cobalt so hard he pitted in with gravel falling out of the left-rear wheel because his track-out lines were starting to include real estate beyond the actual track.

Then we went Corvette to Corvette, and that went how you’d expect, as evidenced by his note in my Z06 press kit: “Good luck next time. Dale Jr., 30.8 (you 32.2).”

Dropping a dang Corvette engine in a family SUV is usually the sort of procedure that requires an engine hoist, a wrecked C4, and a long weekend. But in 2006 Chevy did that deed at the factory, giving us the Trailblazer SS, a 395-hp SUV that hit 60 mph in 5.5 seconds and conjured the casual menace of the ‘90s Impala SS. It also had upgraded brakes and suspension, modifications that our John Phillips described as “comprehensively testosteronated”. If you like the whole Trailblazer SS deal but wish it were weirder, GM also built a Saab version, the 9-7X Aero. It was about as Swedish as apple pie at a baseball game on the Fourth of July, and remains the most powerful Saab I can think of at the moment.

OK, the stopwatch doesn’t lie: the Blazer EV SS destroys its predecessors at the drag strip. The trip to 60 mph is over in 3.3 seconds, and the quarter-mile requires just 11.8 seconds. That beats an automatic 2019 Camaro SS (3.9 and 12.2 seconds for those respective runs), which itself was slightly quicker than the manual Camaro SSs we tested. On power alone—615 horsepower and 650 pound-feet of torque—the electric Blazer deserves entry to the SS club.

In other ways, it’s merely casually sporty, but that’s been the SS mien in a lot of cases. I appreciate that you can get it in habanero orange, an extroverted hue that caused one of my kids to mistake it for a Lamborghini Urus for about 50 milliseconds. And, in this age of inflation, the $395 performance package is a huge bargain for the upgrades it brings: 22-inch summer tires and high-friction brake pads and rotors. Those front rotors are 15.3 inches and are grabbed by six-piston Brembo calipers. That’s legit hardware, as evidenced by its 157-foot stop from 60 mph.

The Blazer EV SS interior gives you some SS branding on the seats and steering wheel but otherwise looks mostly like any other Blazer EV, which is to say mostly like any other Chevy SUV. Which is fine. If I were the person at GM in charge of cost-benefit analysis, I too would opt for cruddy lower door plastic as long as I got to keep Super Cruise.

The Blazer EV SS is worthy of the SS badge. Whether it’s worthy of the Blazer one is a different discussion that you can continue on your forum, K5 Freaks 4EVR.

The positive news here was that Chevy brought back a V-8-powered Impala SS that was good at doing burnouts. The bad news was that it could barely avoid doing burnouts at all times because it was front-wheel-drive. Yes, Chevy dropped a dang 303-hp LS engine in the front-drive Impala of the day, resulting in torque steer that made every ditch a possibility. Our own Tony Quiroga described that Impala SS as a car that “gives the feeling that it’s waging war with itself”. Other observations from that review:

-“Keeping an 18-year-old platform competitive is not an insubstantial task.”

-“Dive, squat, and roll control could be described as nautical.”

-On the skidpad, “The Impala leaned over far enough to be included in Who's Who in Body Roll.”

-“Impressed by the 154-mph top speed? Driving the SS at that speed is scary enough to be a stunt on NBC's Fear Factor.”

-“The front-strut suspension crashes over pavement imperfections as if someone had overlooked the advantages of bushings.”

At the time, my wife had an Impala as a company car. She was a pharma sales rep for Johnson & Johnson, and her trunk was always full of Tylenol PM and K-Y Jelly. It would have been funny if she ever got pulled over and searched. Also, the second “A” of the trunk badge fell off, so we fondly referred to her car as the Impal. That was the right assignment for that era of Impala.

During the early-2000s hot-truck heyday, there were some wicked creations. Ford said, “Let’s put a 380-hp supercharged V-8 in a regular-cab two-wheel-drive F-150, call it the Lightning and do some huge burnouts.” Over at Dodge, they said, “Let’s drop a 500-hp Viper V-10 in a regular-cab, two-wheel-drive Ram, call it the SRT-10 and do some even huger burnouts.” When Chevy got in on the game, it said, “Let’s build a Silverado with an extended cab, all-wheel-drive, and 345 hp. We’ll call it the SS, and it won’t do burnouts.” Eventually Chevy built a rear-drive version, but the Silverado SS still got noogies and purple nurples at recess from the Dodge and Ford.

We said the Maxx itself was “a runty-looking cross between a family sedan and an ice chest,” and the SS treatment didn’t do a whole lot to energize that off-putting shape. The Maxx SS was powered by an iron-block pushrod V-6 that made all of 240 horsepower, sloshed to the front wheels by a four-speed automatic. It hit 60 mph in 6.9 seconds and topped out at a governed 115 mph. This Malibu Maxx didn’t need to be called an SS. In fact, this Malibu Maxx didn’t need to be at all. It reminded me of when I bought reflective mailbox lettering decals and made my parents’ rusty 1989 Subaru DL wagon the DL SS.

How is the Cobalt SS on both the worthy list and the SS trash pile? Because for two years, Chevy offered a naturally aspirated version that wheezed out just 170 horsepower. (The good version was formally named the Cobalt SS Supercharged.) Chevy itself got embarrassed by this SS’s half-heartedness and renamed it the Cobalt Sport after two years, proving that even pre-bankruptcy GM had limits to its cynicism. Happily, no subsequent SS stooped to that level, and hopefully none ever will.

Ezra Dyer is a Car and Driver senior editor and columnist. He's now based in North Carolina but still remembers how to turn right. He owns a 2009 GEM e4 and once drove 206 mph. Those facts are mutually exclusive.

#4320. Buy This Custom 1978 GMC Van, and Elvis Is Your Co-Pilot

With this GMC Vandura on Bring a Trailer, every drive is like a trip to Graceland.

If your baby has left you, and you need to find a new place to dwell, may we suggest this rocking custom van? It's a 1978 GMC G2500 Vandura that’s a full-on Elvis tribute, and it's just turned up over at Bring a Trailer (which, like Car and Driver, is part of Hearst Autos).

The custom-van craze of the 1970s will no doubt be studied by future archaeologists, and maybe you’ll be able to find a Chevy with an airbrushed unicorn on its side in a museum someday. The vans of that era were rolling hangout spots, an extension of the hippie-friendly appeal of the Volkswagen Type 2 into the domestic market, and their broad sheetmetal sides were the perfect canvas for art of all kinds.

See all results for used cars for sale near 37040

You might expect a 1978 rock ’n’ roll tribute custom van to feature Led Zeppelin or maybe Foghat. However, there’s only one King of Rock ’n’ Roll, and even if Elvis had left the building by 1977, the creator of this van went all in on a rolling temple to their hero.

The exterior features porthole windows, a full-length airbrushed portrait of Elvis on both sides, musical notes, and record details. Out back, there's the King’s massively side-burned visage and his indisputable title “The King of Rock ’n’ Roll.” Chrome side pipes and five-spoke 15-inch chrome wheels finish out the look.

Powering this roving Graceland is a 350-cubic-inch small-block V-8 with a four-barrel Edelbrock carburetor. Power gets to the ground through a three-speed automatic transmission, and the odometer currently shows 42K miles. The original artwork dates back to the early 1980s, and the vehicle was comprehensively refurbished in 2019.

And, in case you have to ask, yes, it’s got an eight-track player for a stereo. Break out your collection of Elvis’s greatest hits and get ready to go cruise on through the night. One for the money, two for the show, three to get ready, then go, van, go.

#4319. Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis

A deadly form of blood cancer may begin taking shape more than 50 years before a person is diagnosed, according to new research revealing the surprisingly long and predictable path to leukemia.

Scientists have reconstructed how acute myeloid leukemia (AML) develops over a lifetime, discovering that in two-thirds of the cases studied, the first genetic mutation that helped drive the cancer appeared before age 20. These early changes could remain largely unnoticed for decades before eventually contributing to the disease.

The findings suggest that doctors may one day be able to identify people at risk of developing leukemia years or even decades before symptoms appear. They also raise the possibility of preventing the cancer by slowing the growth of abnormal blood cells long before the disease takes hold.

Blood Samples Reveal Leukemia's Hidden History

Published in Nature, the study was conducted by researchers at the University of Cambridge and University College London (UCL). By examining blood samples collected over many years, including some obtained as long as 15 years before diagnosis, the team pieced together a detailed history of how leukemia develops.

The scientists treated these stored samples as a kind of genetic fossil record. Using highly sensitive DNA sequencing and mathematical models, they worked backward to estimate when cancer-related mutations first appeared, how quickly the affected cells multiplied, and how they competed with other blood cells as the disease approached.

AML is an aggressive blood cancer that affects approximately 2,700 people in the UK annually. Its outlook is often poor, with only about one in six patients surviving at least five years after diagnosis.

Scientists have long known that many otherwise healthy older adults carry blood cells with mutations associated with leukemia. This condition, called clonal hematopoiesis, does not necessarily lead to cancer. In fact, most people with these mutations never develop AML. Until now, researchers have struggled to understand why some individuals progress to leukemia while others do not, partly because they lacked a detailed record of the genetic changes occurring in the years before diagnosis.

To investigate, the team turned to samples from the UK Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (UKCTOCS). That project involved approximately 50,000 women who provided blood samples annually for as long as 11 years.

For the new analysis, researchers examined samples from 47 women who eventually developed AML, with an average age at diagnosis of 72. They compared these findings with samples from 46 similar women who remained free of blood cancer.

Cancer Mutations Can Remain Hidden for Decades

The results revealed an extraordinary timeline. In two-thirds of the women who developed AML, the earliest mutation contributing to the disease was estimated to have occurred before their 20th birthday.

At first, the altered blood cells multiplied extremely slowly, sometimes taking several years just to double in number. But as additional cancer-driving mutations accumulated, their growth accelerated dramatically.

Each new mutation typically increased the rate of growth by roughly two to three times. By the time cells had acquired four mutations capable of driving cancer, their populations could double within weeks instead of years.

Perhaps even more surprising was how consistently these populations behaved.

Researchers found that groups of genetically related blood cells, known as clones, generally expanded at predictable rates once they became established. Their growth tended to slow only when they faced limited space or competition from another clone that was multiplying more quickly.

This consistency could have important medical implications. By measuring the growth of a particular clone using just a few blood samples, scientists may be able to estimate how large that population will become many years into the future, potentially even decades later.

The researchers also identified a striking pattern that appeared in some patients well before leukemia was diagnosed.

In at least one-third of AML cases, a single population of mutated blood cells had grown so extensively that it dominated the blood years before diagnosis. Scientists call this process a "somatic sweep."

None of the women in the comparison group who remained free of blood cancer showed the same pattern.

The researchers then examined data from the UK Biobank and confirmed that people showing evidence of these sweeps faced a substantially greater risk of developing AML.

This finding suggests that somatic sweeps could serve as an important early warning sign. However, conventional genetic testing can miss them because the mutations involved are sometimes incorrectly classified as inherited genetic variations.

Professor Jamie Blundell, who led the research at the University of Cambridge's Early Cancer Institute, explained how the team reconstructed the disease's history.

"Serial blood samples are a fossil record of the blood's evolution. They let us go back in time and reconstruct when each mutation arose and how fast it grew. What surprised us most is how predictable the growth of these clones is. Once a clone is established, its growth rate today tells you where it will be years, even decades, from now."

He added: "Because the growth is exponential, even modestly slowing a high-risk clone over the decade or more before diagnosis could substantially reduce the chance it becomes leukemia. This opens up strategies we can exploit to prevent these clones ever becoming leukemia."

Could Leukemia Be Prevented Before It Develops?

The discovery could change how doctors approach a disease that often appears to develop with little warning.

Dr. Caroline Watson, the study's first author and a researcher at the Early Cancer Institute, emphasized the contrast between the sudden impact of a leukemia diagnosis and the decades of biological changes that may precede it.

"As a hematologist, I've seen how suddenly AML can change someone's life. This study shows that the changes leading to AML can build over decades, with the affected cells growing in surprisingly predictable ways."

Watson is also an Honorary Consultant Haematologist who treats patients at the Cambridge Clonal Haematopoiesis Clinic at Addenbrooke's Hospital. The clinic is the first in Europe dedicated to leukemia prevention and already monitors people whose blood cell mutations place them at increased risk of developing the disease.

She added: "At our clinic, we already assess and monitor people who carry blood-cell mutations that increase their risk of leukemia. Today's findings give us real hope of improving how we identify which of them are at greatest risk and point to a window in which prevention could one day be possible."

Years of Blood Samples Unlock New Cancer Clues

A major reason the researchers could reconstruct leukemia's development was the availability of blood samples collected repeatedly from the same individuals over many years.

Professor Usha Menon of the UCL Institute of Clinical Trials and Methodology, who led the original UKCTOCS project, highlighted the unexpected scientific value of those samples.

"While UKCTOCS was designed to assess ovarian cancer screening, a key outcome was the establishment of a unique bioresource of serial serum samples. This resource has provided unprecedented opportunities to study how cancers develop over time and to discover and validate biomarkers for earlier detection. We owe an enormous debt of gratitude to the participants whose willingness to contribute their samples and data over many years made this possible. Their generosity is the foundation of this achievement."

The women who developed AML received their diagnoses between ages 53 and 83. Because the researchers did not have blood samples taken at the time of diagnosis, they could not directly examine the final stage of the disease's development in those patients.

The findings also showed that not every case followed the same extended timeline of detectable changes. In approximately one in five cases, growing populations of mutated blood cells became detectable only one to two years before diagnosis. This suggests that some patients may have a much shorter opportunity for early intervention.

Despite these limitations, the results offer an encouraging possibility: leukemia risk might be reduced by intervening long before the disease develops.

According to the researchers' mathematical models, even a modest reduction in the growth of high-risk blood cell clones could have a substantial effect over time. Because these cells multiply exponentially, slowing their expansion across the ten or more years between a second cancer-driving mutation and diagnosis could significantly reduce the likelihood that they eventually progress to leukemia.

This raises the prospect of preventive treatments designed to restrain dangerous cell populations rather than waiting until they have developed into cancer.

The next challenge is determining whether such an approach can be used safely and effectively in people identified as having an elevated risk of AML. Although the research provides a promising framework for earlier detection and prevention, clinical studies will be needed to establish whether slowing these abnormal cells actually prevents leukemia in humans.

The research was primarily supported by UK Research & Innovation and Cancer Research UK.

#4318. Gooseneck Hitches Explained

If a run-of-the-mill rear-mounted hitch won’t do, then a gooseneck hitch may be worth looking into.

Looking to tow a bigger and heavier trailer to carry the likes of livestock trailers, heavy equipment, or other vehicles? Then you’re probably going to need a heavy-duty pickup truck that’s both capable of pulling such a hefty load and compatible with towing a gooseneck-style trailer hitch.

This type of hitch gets its name from the high arch of steel that protrudes from the front end of the trailer. Goosenecks are designed to clear a pickup truck’s tailgate and sides, since the ball hitch the trailer connects to sits squarely in the middle of the tow-vehicle’s bed.

Placing the mount right over the truck’s rear axle enables more of the accompanying trailer’s weight to push down on the tow vehicle’s rear end. The result? The combined truck and trailer benefit from greater stability once on the move.

Fitting a gooseneck hitch to your truck is a completely different process relative to that of your typical rear-mounted hitch that hides under the bumper. You (or the manufacturer or service center) will need to drill right into the bed to install and mount the ball hitch and the accompanying safety chain attachment points.

See all results for used cars for sale near 37040

It’s a less invasive process than you may initially think, though. This is because the business end of a gooseneck is usually a long cylinder that sticks straight up from the bed.

In theory, this setup is similar to that of a fifth wheel hitch. In reality, a fifth wheel hitch is a different beast. Notably, fifth wheel setups require a much bulkier kingpin and jaw-style bed-mounted hitch. This setup provides quieter operation and additional stability at speed relative to a gooseneck hitch, and is often used for the towing of recreational trailers designed for the likes of camping.

The ball mount and coupler of a gooseneck, however, make this the heartier hitch for towing heavy tonnage. We’re talking north of 30,000 pounds in some instances.

Credit the fact that a gooseneck hitch pushes a large amount of the trailer’s mass downward onto the truck’s rear end, which allows the trailer to better resist sway than if it were mounted to a conventional tow hitch. The hitch’s in-bed location also allows the truck to handle heavier loads.

Another benefit of the in-bed ball hitch is that it takes up far less space than a fifth wheel. This means a majority of the bed remains available for its intended purpose: hauling cargo.

So, what can you haul with a hitch that’s ready for gooseneck trailering duty? Well, there are about as many options as there are jobs on a worksite. The most flexible choice is a flatbed trailer, which can carry anything from secured payloads to heavy construction equipment. Other options include livestock carriers, dumping trailers, and car haulers.

See all results for used cars for sale near 37040

Goosenecks also hold up well under abuse thanks to the tough but simple nature of the aforementioned ball hitch and coupler that connect the trailer and truck. It’s why gooseneck-style hitches are often used in agricultural and construction environments.

Installation aside, a gooseneck hitch is a simpler and safer way to tow big loads without having to sacrifice much in the way of in-bed utility. Not everyone needs a gooseneck hitch to tow with, but those who do are sure to benefit from the extra capability this style of hitch provides.

Both hitch types are sturdy options for towing heavy loads, but gooseneck hitches, the strongest of which can handle more than 30,000 pounds of weight, are generally regarded as the more capable heavy-duty hitch.

In theory, just about any pickup can be fitted with a gooseneck hitch. In practice, however, adding a gooseneck hitch to a light-duty pickup makes little sense given the lower payload and tow ratings of these trucks relative to their heavy-duty stablemates.

The in-bed connection point between the ball and the coupler of a gooseneck effectively makes towing with this type of hitch safer than towing with a run-of-the-mill bumper-pull hitch—particularly when towing especially heavy loads. Credit the fact that gooseneck hitches put more of the trailer’s weight directly over the tow vehicle’s rear axle. Because of this, gooseneck hitches typically offer far greater towing stability relative to that of a truck and trailer connected by a bumper-pull-type hitch.

#4317. Xenogears Is Finally Getting Remastered, But Not in the Way You Think

Murillo Zerbinatto is a JRPG enthusiast, writer, and editor. He has played over 300 RPGs during his gaming career, with 90% of them being JRPGs.

There are two perspectives on remasters and remakes. On one hand, we have those who complain whenever a developer announces a new one, wishing they would dedicate development efforts to bringing new IPs to life. On the other hand, we have those who rejoice and feel the nostalgia tingling whenever a game that shaped their tastes returns to the modern era. I fall into the latter camp, which is why I am extremely excited for the upcoming fanmade remaster of Xenogears.

The Elder Scrolls Travels: Shadowkey, the long-forgotten Nokia N-Gage RPG, is returning!

To be fair, three Xenogears remasters are currently being developed by fans, each with its own codename: Weltall, Exodus, and Atlas. Today I'll discuss the Atlas remaster because it seems to be the one the fanbase is most excited about, and it already has an imminent release date of 15 December 2026. However, keep in mind that since this is not an official remaster from Square Enix, you can only legally play it if you own an original copy of Xenogears at home.

The project could hardly be called a Xenogears remaster if it didn't include notable upgrades over the original. According to the creator, Reddit user Ok-Bed3203, the entire game has been rebuilt in the Godot engine and will run directly inside it, provided you supply your own copy of the game. Fans can experience Xenogears Atlas in two distinct visual styles, dubbed Canon and HD.

In Canon mode, the visuals remain faithful to the 1998 release, while incorporating technical fixes such as eliminating flickering triangles or textures, stabilizing sprites and images, and smoothing out screen fades. Meanwhile, High Definition mode introduces enhanced textures and sprites, 16:9 widescreen support (with menus, text, and FMVs preserved in their original 4:3 framing so nothing gets stretched), updated lighting and visual effects, and 3D Gears.

Both modes will support 60 FPS, 120 FPS, or your monitor's native refresh rate. They also include 2K CG cutscenes upscaled by Laichzeit (likely exclusive to HD mode, though not explicitly specified), subtitles in every language, fan translations, and quality-of-life options like text speed adjustments, quick loads, full-screen or windowed modes, and automatic pausing when running in the background.

Independent developer LoreanXavier, also known as Lorean The Gamer, has been working on an unofficial native PC port of P.T. for quite some time.

After the initial release, the developers plan to add a Mods menu that lets you load custom text patches and swap images or audio files by name, along with remastered music from Xenogears' iconic soundtrack and further touch-ups to the 2K movies. The community has also suggested several additions currently under consideration, including random encounter rate toggles, a reduced-flash mode, auto-advancing dialogue, optional voice-over via the Spoken Mirror fan dub (slated to arrive alongside the Disc 2 remake), and a dedicated Android port.

As you probably noticed, the developer mentioned a Disc 2 remake. That sounds like a tall order, because as anyone who played the game remembers, Xenogears features a pristine Disc 1, whereas the second disc was famously rushed after Square cut the budget before the project could be finished, which severely undermined the experience. Atlas aims to give Disc 2 the breathing room it never received. While it is not yet completely clear what that will entail or when it will arrive, it is easily the most intriguing prospect of this entire fanmade remaster.

While the project looks incredible and has me thoroughly hyped, one looming question always hangs in the air these days: was this project made using AI? The developer preemptively addressed that very concern:

“About AI, since it always comes up: yes, I used AI as a tool along the way, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But this is not a vibe-coded project. I checked every cutscene, every movement and every 16:9 margin by hand, then fixed it and compared it with the original. A huge part of the work was the boring part: tracking down the smallest glitches left over from the PS1 renderer, one by one, until they were gone. Monk work, honestly. I hope you'll feel it when you play.”

About AI, since it always comes up: yes, I used AI as a tool along the way, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

So there you have it. If you want to experience or revisit Xenogears with revamped visuals, quality-of-life additions, tweaks, and technical fixes, Xenogears Atlas might just be the way to go. This Xenogears remaster launches on 15 December 2026, via Godot for PC, though you will still need your original copy to get it running. Who knows, maybe this will finally wake Square Enix up to greenlight a full-fledged official remaster, or at least sell the IP back to Tetsuya Takahashi.

#4316. Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds

A major research review led by Curtin University has found that people with type 2 diabetes face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. The findings provide a clearer picture of the connection between diabetes and Alzheimer's, including how much the risk increases and how frequently new cases occur.

Researchers analyzed data from 40 studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis. They estimated that for every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes, approximately 4.7 would develop Alzheimer's disease over the course of one year.

A separate analysis found that people with type 2 diabetes had a 53 percent higher adjusted relative risk of developing Alzheimer's compared with those without the condition.

Understanding the Link Between Diabetes and Alzheimer's

Study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, an NHMRC Investigator Fellow at the Curtin School of Population Health, explained that the findings offer a more precise understanding of Alzheimer's risk among people with type 2 diabetes.

Unlike previous research reviews that often examined multiple forms of diabetes or dementia together, this analysis concentrated specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease. It also measured how frequently people with diabetes developed Alzheimer's, providing an additional perspective on the connection between the two conditions.

"While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease and estimated how often new cases occurred," Dr. Adewuyi said.

"Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer's disease among people living with type 2 diabetes."

The study, "Incidence and risk of Alzheimer's disease in individuals with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis," was published in Alzheimer's Research & Therapy.
